=== PAPER 288305d31b7d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit risk analysis (CRA) for portfolios, focusing on estimating Value at Risk (VaR) and Economic Capital (EC) for default losses using a quantum formulation of a portfolio loss model. It starts from an existing quantum CRA algorithm that offers a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods and seeks to make it compatible with more realistic multi-factor risk models used in practice, where expected loss is additive across assets and EC is defined as VaR minus expected loss.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-006, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-024]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is based on Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and its iterative variant to estimate loss distribution tail probabilities, by mapping CRA to a quantum operator A acting on n+1 qubits and using bisection on P[L ≤ x] to obtain VaR. The original circuit decomposes A into operators U, S, and C under a Basel II–style Gaussian conditional independence model, and the paper proposes two multi-factor uncertainty encodings (multiple-rotations with one register per factor, and single-rotation with a multivariate normal register) plus a modified comparator using LinearAmplitudeFunction and a piecewise linear function on amplitudes that reads default qubits directly and removes the S (sum) operator to allow flexible LGD inputs.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a toy example with two assets and two systemic risk factors, using the multiple-rotations scheme and non-integer LGDs, the authors simulate their circuit with iterative QAE and bisection, setting target precision ε = 0.002 and a 99% confidence interval, which required on average about 50,000 quantum samples and 9 qubits on a Qiskit simulator. They report that, for small portfolios, the modified multiple-rotations variant without a sum register offers a qubit advantage, and they emphasize that the use of non-integer LGD values empirically demonstrates increased input flexibility compared to the original integer-only design.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The work is framed against classical Monte Carlo–based CRA and EC estimation, where convergence is O(√n) and pseudo-random number generation can degrade simulation quality due to duplicates. The authors position QAE as providing a quadratic speedup for VaR estimation over these classical Monte Carlo methods and note that quantum hardware’s ability to generate true random samples addresses limitations of pseudo-random simulation, though the speedup is presented as a theoretical advantage rather than an empirically demonstrated one in this paper.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations. Classically, Monte Carlo CRA suffers from slow O(√n) convergence and pseudo-random duplication issues that can compromise simulation quality. On the quantum side, enriching the model with multiple risk factors via multiple-rotations significantly increases gate count, while the single-rotation design reduces depth at the cost of forcing all assets to share the same alpha vector, which is a modeling restriction. The original WeightedAdder-based approach restricts LGD inputs to integers and, for realistic LGD magnitudes, requires many qubits in the sum register. Their more flexible LGD encoding using LinearAmplitudeFunction adds one qubit per asset, effectively doubling per-asset qubit growth and causing circuit width to scale as O(2K) instead of O(K); although removing the sum register helps at small K, its overhead becomes negligible at larger scales. The number of risk factors also increases required qubits linearly with n_Z, and overall, the authors conclude that further scalability improvements are needed and that current real quantum hardware noise completely destroys the output, making meaningful results dependent on significant improvements in qubit coherence times.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-012, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work highlighted by the authors includes the need for significantly improved qubit coherence times to obtain meaningful results beyond ideal simulations, and the use of their enhanced algorithm—featuring flexible LGD inputs and a multi-factor uncertainty model aligned with large financial institutions’ practice—to enable realistic benchmarking studies against classical CRA models using real-world data.
    [codes: C-052, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims methodological contributions in extending an existing QAE-based CRA algorithm to support a more realistic multi-factor default model that accounts for several systemic risk factors, while preserving the theoretical quadratic speedup, and in increasing input flexibility by removing the constraint that LGD values be integers through a redesigned comparator that avoids the S operator. Although these enhancements increase circuit depth and width, the authors argue they demonstrate a path toward a more realistic quantum CRA software solution that better matches the custom multi-factor models used by large banks.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-024, C-026, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Experimentally, the paper uses a simulator-based evaluation on IBM’s Qiskit qasm_simulator with a clearly specified toy problem (two assets, two risk factors, non-integer LGDs) and reports concrete resource counts such as 9 qubits and roughly 50,000 quantum samples under stated precision and confidence targets, enhancing transparency. The authors employ iterative QAE with a standard bisection VaR search and explicitly discuss scalability of qubits and gates with respect to asset and risk-factor counts, but the study is limited to a very small synthetic instance without detailed classical benchmark results or large-scale empirical tests.
    [codes: C-016, C-018, C-019, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-047, C-049]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that quantum finance more broadly seeks to exploit quantum computing to outperform classical methods across a wide range of financial problems and reiterates that its more realistic multi-factor uncertainty model aligns with the models commonly used by large entities such as Intesa Sanpaolo, supporting external relevance of the chosen modeling assumptions.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-021, C-022]

=== PAPER 29f1f2555efe (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as both an opportunity and a risk for the financial system: it examines how quantum algorithms might improve stress testing, macroeconomic analysis, risk management, payments and portfolio optimisation, while also analysing how quantum-capable adversaries could undermine widely used cryptography and thereby financial stability. It emphasises that while quantum computers are still experimental, their future impact on financial institutions, infrastructures and macroeconomic outcomes could be profound, and highlights specific channels such as online/mobile banking, payment transactions and VPN communications as particularly vulnerable to quantum-enabled attacks.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-018, C-022, C-035, C-037, C-043]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors discuss families of quantum algorithms—such as quantum Fourier transform, amplitude amplification and quantum walks—as building blocks for potential financial applications, and note that quantum simulation and optimisation algorithms underpin use cases in stress testing, macroeconomic analysis and asset pricing. They also highlight quantum annealing as an implementation that can already solve certain dynamic programming problems faster than classical machines, and discuss quantum cryptography, including quantum key distribution, alongside classical post-quantum cryptographic schemes as key methods for addressing security risks. Throughout, they stress that quantum and classical computers are expected to complement each other, with redundancy via additional qubits used to address noise and error correction challenges.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-014, C-017, C-026, C-039, C-041, C-046, C-049]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that finance is projected to be an early beneficiary of quantum computing, with short‑term gains mainly in faster computation that leaves results largely unchanged. Cited examples include quadratic speedup expectations for some risk-management algorithms, a stylised VaR example where a quantum computer could compute risk for a one‑million‑asset portfolio in about 30 minutes, potential improvements in Monte Carlo-based risk assessment, and liquidity savings of roughly CAD 240–276 million in a quantum-optimised payment system study. The authors further cite work showing that a quantum annealer solved a real business cycle dynamic programming problem in about 3% of the classical computation time and discuss synergies with AI, including expected acceleration in reinforcement learning and deep learning training. On the risk side, they quote model-based estimates that a successful quantum-enabled cyberattack on financial infrastructures could generate expected GDP losses of about 0.1% within five years, rising to over 1% within 15–20 years, and report from Project Leap that post-quantum cryptography increased VPN setup latency, with implications for time-critical services such as instant payments.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-033, C-044, C-045, C-050, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors repeatedly benchmark quantum approaches against classical methods, typically emphasising speed gains rather than new outcome quality: they expect mostly faster computation with similar outputs in the short run and acknowledge that classical supercomputers may remain more cost‑effective for many tasks. For risk management, they describe anticipated quadratic speedups and illustrate classical intractability in systemic network-risk problems where classical computation would exceed the age of the universe. In macroeconomic modelling, they cite evidence that a quantum annealer solved an RBC dynamic programming problem in 3% of the classical runtime (around a 33x speedup), and in Project Leap they compare the latency of legacy versus post-quantum cryptography in VPN setup, finding additional overhead for the quantum-safe schemes.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-022, C-024, C-026, C-032, C-033, C-050]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses numerous limitations and caveats. Technically, practical quantum computers do not yet exist and it is impossible to know if or when they will; current devices are noisy, with fragile qubits requiring strong isolation and substantial redundancy, and there is no consensus that quantum supremacy has been achieved. Quantum computing is suitable only for a narrow class of tasks, and data loading and read‑out steps can become bottlenecks, so real‑life use cases with practical quantum advantage are expected to be few, with initial gains mostly modest speedups. Even where gains exist, classical supercomputers may remain more cost‑effective economically. The authors also highlight major obstacles to integrating quantum with AI, such as costs and technical limitations. On the security side, they emphasise that migrating to quantum‑safe cryptography is complex, time‑consuming and resource‑intensive; post‑quantum schemes can introduce latency that strains time‑critical use cases like instant payments; and quantum key distribution, though promising, currently faces scalability and integration challenges. In addition, they underline the harvest‑now‑decrypt‑later threat: data already being intercepted can be decrypted once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer—whose arrival is highly uncertain but possibly within 5–30 years—is available, making the cyber threat imminent even though functional quantum advantage in finance may be delayed.
    [codes: C-004, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-024, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-042, C-048, C-051, C-054]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors point to several forward-looking directions: hardware roadmaps towards systems with roughly 2,000 logical qubits and the uncertain but potentially 5–30‑year horizon for cryptographically relevant machines; deeper exploration of quantum algorithms in macroeconomic modelling and stress testing, building on early annealing results; and development of quantum‑enhanced AI techniques, such as reinforcement learning and quantum deep learning, despite current practical obstacles. Economically, they frame quantum computing as a potential future general purpose technology whose long‑run impact could rival historical transformations like electrification, even if near‑term benefits remain small. On the policy side, they call for designing flexible quantum‑readiness roadmaps, including migration milestones, and continued work on quantum‑resistant cryptography and quantum key distribution as technology matures.

  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is an integrated assessment for central banks and financial authorities of how quantum computing could both enhance and threaten the financial system: it synthesises emerging algorithmic opportunities in risk management, portfolio optimisation, payments and macroeconomic modelling with quantified examples, while also analysing the systemic risks to cryptography and financial stability, including GDP‑level loss projections. It further offers policy‑oriented guidance by outlining the need for quantum‑readiness roadmaps, skills and asset inventories, and by reporting an applied central‑bank experiment (Project Leap) that tests post‑quantum cryptography in cross‑border VPNs, thereby connecting high‑level technology trends to concrete operational and regulatory implications.

The authors explicitly recognise that many performance claims—such as quadratic speedups in risk management, payments liquidity savings, and macroeconomic modelling gains—are based on specific model setups or simulations rather than large‑scale production systems, and some examples (e.g. systemic risk networks or VaR for million‑asset portfolios) are highly stylised. === PAPER 2ae3455aa47b (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) as a key strategy to harness NISQ-era devices for solving classically intractable problems across domains, including finance modelling and specific financial tasks such as portfolio optimization and risk analysis. Financial use cases are formulated mainly as combinatorial optimization (Markowitz mean–variance) and sampling/estimation problems (risk analysis, derivative pricing), to be mapped into Hamiltonians or variational circuits within a hybrid quantum–classical framework.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-044, C-063, C-064, C-070]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors review several VQA families—VQE, QAOA, and QNNs—as hybrid quantum–classical algorithms built from parameterized quantum circuits with shallow-depth ansätze motivated by NISQ constraints. They detail how VQE relies on the Rayleigh–Ritz variational bound with an ansatz U(θ), QAOA uses a problem-specific alternating operator ansatz for combinatorial optimization, and QNNs are treated as parametrized circuits with specific layer structures and data-encoding schemes; optimization typically uses gradients via the parameter-shift rule or alternative optimizers, and noise is addressed through shallow circuits, error mitigation, and QEC methods such as QVECTOR.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-068, C-069]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The review reports that cited VQE experiments achieve chemical accuracy on small molecules such as H2, LiH, and BeH2, including a hardware H2 demonstration with dissociation energy error within chemical accuracy. For QAOA on MaxCut, the authors report an approximation ratio of ~0.755 at p=1 and above 0.9 at p=2 under ideal simulation, surpassing the Goemans–Williamson bound. They also cite QNN-based results, including 94.3% accuracy in thoracic CT classification, improved Sharpe ratios in quantum portfolio optimization, a benchmark table of QNN performance on molecular energy prediction, and NISQ-era VQA benchmarks across domains; further claims include strong ML correlations in material-science pipelines, significant error reduction via mitigation, polynomial scaling–driven screening efficiency, and high-fidelity quantum generative models with faster convergence. In finance specifically, they reference QAOA-based Markowitz optimization within 92% of classical solutions, 40% variance reduction in risk analysis relative to Monte Carlo, improved Sharpe ratios from quantum trading QNNs, and 30% Sharpe-ratio improvements from quantum portfolio optimization via efficient sampling.
    [codes: C-004, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-033, C-039, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-055, C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062, C-063, C-064]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout the survey, the authors contrast VQAs with classical baselines, typically reporting that cited quantum methods match or improve upon classical performance metrics on small instances. They note that higher-depth QAOA can exceed the classical Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio under ideal conditions, QNNs in clinical imaging outperform classical CNNs in accuracy with far fewer parameters, and quantum portfolio optimization and trading strategies achieve better Sharpe ratios than classical Markowitz models and classical trading counterparts. In risk analysis, they report that quantum approaches can reduce variance versus classical Monte Carlo, and in materials and chemistry they emphasize polynomial scaling of VQAs compared to exponential scaling of classical methods, presenting these as indications of potential practical advantage rather than definitive speedups.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper highlights several fundamental limitations of VQAs: barren plateaus arising from highly expressive ansätze that lead to exponentially vanishing gradients, substantial optimization overhead and highly non-convex landscapes with many local optima, and measurement overhead due to repeated sampling for expectation-value estimation. Hardware-related constraints are emphasized, including high error rates, short decoherence times, and limited qubit connectivity that restrict feasible circuit depth and motivate shallow circuits. In the context of QNNs, the authors point to practical difficulties with error mitigation and preserving qubit coherence. They also note broader efficiency issues around measurement frugality and explicitly acknowledge that for financial applications, current gate error rates (>10⁻³) limit circuit depth and require more robust error-mitigation techniques to ensure reliable decision-making.
    [codes: C-005, C-014, C-016, C-019, C-041, C-048, C-065, C-067]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Looking ahead, the authors discuss the trajectory from NISQ-era VQAs toward fault-tolerant quantum computing and emphasize that understanding the interplay between quantum noise models and variational parameter optimization is an open question with major implications for scalability and generalizability. They propose future innovation in noise-sensitive ansatz design, adaptive and problem-motivated circuit construction, and novel classical optimization heuristics as promising pathways to overcome current limitations and to enable more scalable, robust VQAs.
    [codes: C-007, C-071, C-072]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is presented as a comprehensive, NISQ-focused synthesis of variational quantum algorithms, comparing key variants (VQE, QAOA, QNNs) in terms of noise robustness, ansatz architecture, and hybrid optimization strategies across diverse application domains, including finance. The authors claim to highlight benchmarks suggesting potential practical quantum advantage, systematically analyze fundamental limiting factors such as barren plateaus and hardware constraints together with mitigation strategies like adaptive ansätze and QVECTOR, and to articulate how the hybrid quantum–classical paradigm offers, in principle, a practical route to tackling classically intractable chemistry, optimization, and machine-learning problems.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is a survey that summarizes experimental and simulation benchmarks from the literature rather than presenting a single unified experimental protocol, and it aggregates results across physics, chemistry, machine learning, and finance. It formalizes VQA components such as cost functions, ansätze, and optimization rules with mathematical detail, and includes benchmark tables (e.g., for QNN molecular energy prediction and selected NISQ VQA applications), but does not itself provide dataset specifications or reproducible pipelines for the cited financial case studies; instead, it relies on previously published benchmarks.

=== PAPER 2fe0d0f15604 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets a credit sales risk classification task: determining a customer’s reliability (whether goods can be issued or sales should be blocked) from selected decision variables, posed as a two-class problem that also contains additional subgroups of samples in each class and is not well separated in the original feature space.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)–based classifier for credit sales risk, in which classical data samples are first normalized and amplitude-encoded into normalized quantum states, then a parameterized ansatz circuit is trained via a VQE-style expectation minimization to produce class-specific pattern states, and finally a SWAP-Test–based similarity measurement plus a decision rule based on high |0⟩ probabilities on three qubits is used for classification. The method emphasizes suitability for NISQ-era hardware, using structurally simple VQA circuits, a low-complexity SWAP-Test, and ansatz designs explicitly constructed to recreate the entanglement structure observed in the encoded data, including a compact nine-qubit register layout with ancilla, VQE, and data sub-registers and two ansatz variants (a standard and a simplified, data-structure-aware circuit).
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their VQE+SWAP-Test classifier achieves high training-set accuracy on the proprietary credit-risk dataset, with best performance reaching 100% classification efficiency when classification thresholds are properly tuned. They find that the three-qubit amplitude encoding of eight features (with one padded zero feature) not only reduces the number of qubits but also speeds up the optimization process compared to an eight-qubit encoding. Analysis of the encoded samples shows that in most cases all three qubits are entangled, with distinct entanglement partitions for the two classes, and the authors claim the overall algorithm has polynomial complexity and requires only a logarithmically increasing number of qubits in the feature dimension.
    [codes: C-005, C-016, C-017, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Using classical exploratory analysis, the authors observe that although correlations between variables are weak and the raw classes are not well separated, PCA reveals class-based clustering. They further report that several classical classifiers can fit the same training data extremely well, with some models attaining 100% fit but being described as quite complex, which they implicitly contrast with their compact, logarithmic-qubit quantum representation.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors caution that the choice of acceptance threshold—the boundary distance from a class center to its most distant elements—is critical: if set too high it may cause class overlap and degrade classification quality. They also implicitly delimit the scope of their optimization findings by noting that the barren plateaus problem has not been observed for this problem instance, which should not be generalized beyond the studied setting.
    [codes: C-033, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future extensions, the authors suggest distributing observations across independent quantum circuits to realize parallel processing, which in principle could yield an additional linear speed-up for their classification procedure.
    [codes: C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is positioned as a compact, NISQ-feasible hybrid VQE-based classifier for credit sales risk that uses amplitude encoding to achieve logarithmic qubit scaling in the feature dimension, explicitly designs the ansatz to reproduce empirically observed class-specific entanglement patterns, and employs a low-depth SWAP-Test for similarity-based classification, thereby offering a resource-efficient alternative to complex classical models on this dataset.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a real but proprietary dataset from a Polish pharmaceutical wholesaler covering a specific period in 2003 and documents a two-step normalization (classical min–max to [0,1] followed by quantum amplitude normalization, with an additional zero-valued feature to match the three-qubit encoding). The authors perform classical exploratory analyses (correlations, separability, PCA) before designing the quantum ansatz to match observed entanglement, and they note that barren plateaus were not observed in their optimization runs. Reproducibility is supported by public availability of the full source code for all numerical experiments and plot generation in an online repository.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-041, C-042]

=== PAPER 342ce43a11d1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames Monte Carlo sampling as a core computational bottleneck in many numerical economic applications, including policy-relevant stress testing and dynamic macroeconomic models, which remain computationally infeasible under classical limitations for high accuracy. It formulates three economic use cases—bank stress testing with credit shocks and fire sales, a neoclassical investment problem, and a realistic macro model solved with deep neural networks—as expectation‑estimation tasks amenable to Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) and amplitude estimation. The stress testing problem is reduced to computing a polynomial operator of random default rates, while the macro deep-learning problems are expressed as expectations of (linear) random variables within Bellman‑error loss functions.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-038, C-041]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use the Quantum Monte Carlo (amplitude estimation) algorithm, which theoretically offers quadratic speedup in query complexity for expectation estimation compared with classical Monte Carlo, encoding the expectation value into the probability of an ancilla qubit and then applying phase estimation. They implement QMC by variationally preparing the underlying probability distribution with a parameterized circuit optimized to approximate the target distribution, exploiting product distributions to decompose multidimensional encodings, and constructing a controlled oracle Q without needing a controlled version of the underlying unitary F. The algorithm is simulated using PennyLane, including a template implementation for a simple example and resource tracking (gate depth, qubit counts) that is later mapped to physical runtime.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QMC retains its quadratic query‑complexity scaling relative to classical Monte Carlo, with oracle calls scaling as 1/ε, and in simulations the observed error exponents (≈−0.64 for an approximate encoding and ≈−1.0 for an exact encoding) both outperform classical Monte Carlo’s −0.5 scaling. In the bank stress‑testing use case, the QMC estimate of two‑period system‑wide loss (1.622% of assets) closely matches the theoretical value (1.618%), and even with only two estimation qubits the fractional error remains modest. For the more complex DSGE consumption‑saving model, the authors report very slow classical error scaling (≈−0.22), extreme sample requirements to reach 10⁻⁸ error, and claim that QMC’s quadratic speedup persists with multiple random variables, finding that additional variables do not fundamentally compromise scaling (within the small simulated range). Using their gate‑depth‑to‑runtime mapping, they further report that, at an assumed 1 ns gate time, the approximate QMC implementation can reach a computational error of 10⁻⁸ about 5.6 times faster than a strong HPC cluster accessible to an average researcher, and that under idealized noise‑free conditions high accuracy can be achieved with relatively few qubits.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-020, C-025, C-031, C-032, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly contrast QMC with classical Monte Carlo, noting that classical error scales as 1/√N (samples inversely proportional to the square of target error), whereas QMC requires only O(1/ε) oracle calls, yielding a quadratic theoretical speedup in expectation estimation. They benchmark physical runtimes by comparing QMC’s gate‑depth‑derived runtimes against classical Monte Carlo on a strong HPC cluster and show that, at an error of 10⁻⁸ and under optimistic gate‑time assumptions, QMC can be 5.6 times faster, with the advantage increasing as tighter error tolerances are demanded. For classical deep‑learning solutions of DSGE models, they emphasize that Monte Carlo sampling remains a major bottleneck—classical Bellman‑error convergence can be extremely slow and require astronomically many draws—while their observed QMC scaling exponents in both simplified and multivariate macro settings surpass the classical −0.5 rate.
    [codes: C-003, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-015, C-016, C-020, C-034, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-056]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper stresses that QMC’s quadratic speedup only holds if the decomposition of the core unitary operators is efficient; otherwise gate overhead can negate the theoretical advantage. Discretization of continuous distributions introduces an additional error term that must remain below the target Monte Carlo error, and some reparameterizations (such as renormalizing the payoff function to avoid a bimodal phase‑estimation output) reduce accuracy. The authors note that encoding Monte Carlo problems into quantum circuits without amplitude estimation yields no speedup, and that quantum arithmetic operations and the associated ancilla registers are costly in terms of gates and qubits, posing challenges for both hardware and simulators. They also report a fundamental hardware limitation: current quantum devices are noisy, with noise dominating outcomes after roughly 100 gates in their stress‑testing scenario, and emphasize that fast gate times, longer coherence, and sufficient qubit counts are essential for realizing any practical quantum speedup. Finally, they acknowledge that their multivariate simulations are limited to three random variables due to classical simulation constraints, so scalability claims beyond this regime remain untested.
    [codes: C-006, C-017, C-019, C-023, C-026, C-033, C-045, C-049, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that QMC could be integrated more deeply into deep‑learning pipelines for solving DSGE models by accelerating the Monte Carlo averaging over future shocks, thereby improving convergence of neural‑network–based solution methods. They argue that approximate QMC implementations requiring fewer quantum resources are likely to be realized first in practice, but highlight that further research is needed to optimize quantum arithmetic and amplitude‑estimation subroutines and to extend variational distribution‑encoding techniques from single distributions to encoding entire economic problems. They present these as open technical challenges and research directions that must be addressed before QMC can be deployed at scale in realistic macroeconomic and stress‑testing applications.
    [codes: C-035, C-048, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to be the first to study the potential runtime improvements of Quantum Monte Carlo for economic applications and to systematically examine the associated challenges, and more broadly the first to apply the QMC algorithm to economics and among the earliest applications of quantum computation in this field.     [codes: C-001, C-003, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-054]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study encodes three different economics use cases into quantum circuits, demonstrating how to translate stress‑testing models and deep‑learning–solved macro models into QMC‑compatible expectation‑estimation problems. === PAPER 34fc27290f18 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies a dynamic portfolio optimization problem where a portfolio of Na assets is rebalanced over Nt dates, explicitly incorporating transaction costs into the formulation and enforcing a total budget across all assets. To make this suitable for gate-based quantum computing, the authors construct an optimization objective function for maximization, include budget and allocation constraints, and then modify the transaction-cost term so the resulting problem can be cast into a QUBO form. Investments over time are encoded into binary variables, enabling a Hamiltonian representation for use in a VQE workflow.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors implement a Variational Quantum Eigensolver workflow, structured into five steps and executed on IBM Quantum hardware using the estimator primitive for expectation values and the sampler primitive for final solution sampling. They systematically explore several ansatz–optimizer pairs: a cyclic ansatz with a Conjugate Gradient optimizer, Real Amplitudes (RA) and Optimized Real Amplitudes (ORA) ansätze with a Differential Evolution (DE) optimizer chosen for its gradient-free, noise-robust properties, and finally a problem- and hardware-tailored ansatz that aligns QUBO variable couplings with qubit connectivity on the QPU. The tailored ansatz is explicitly constructed to exploit both problem structure and device connectivity, achieving the lowest circuit depth for the largest (XXL, 112-qubit) instance.
    [codes: C-002, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across the scaling study from 6 to 112 qubits, the best results are obtained by combining a Differential Evolution classical optimizer with an ansatz circuit tailored jointly to the DPO problem and the QPU properties, which yields the best Sharpe ratio among tested VQE configurations and the lowest depth for the XXL instance. Earlier configurations perform less well: the cyclic ansatz with Conjugate Gradient is assessed as not the best choice, and for the XXL problem its output cost distribution is close to a random (noise) distribution, whereas introducing DE with a Real Amplitudes ansatz is reported as the first scalable VQE setup that consistently produces a noticeable improvement over the random distribution for all sizes. The ORA ansatz further reduces depth compared to standard RA but at the cost of more variational parameters, while the final tailored ansatz shows a significantly biased and more concentrated cost distribution toward low optimization costs. Overall, the authors state that the DE optimizer is highly effective for VQE, achieving convergence in most cases.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum results are evaluated against several classical and quantum-inspired baselines. For classical solvers, exhaustive search is only able to obtain exact optimal solutions for the smaller XS, S, and M problem sizes, while Gurobi consistently finds the lowest optimization cost solutions and GEKKO performs worst on this formulation. In addition, a quantum-inspired tensor-network method (SAE) produces results close to those of Gurobi and DOCPLEX, and the authors note that SAE effectively biases the solution probability distribution toward lower-cost solutions. They also observe that minimizing the optimization cost used in their QUBO does not directly translate into maximizing the portfolio’s Sharpe ratio, which affects how both classical and quantum results should be interpreted.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The study is explicitly conducted without any quantum error mitigation techniques, which the authors present as a methodological caveat and later flag as an essential direction for future work. They also highlight that hardware transpilation can significantly increase circuit depth, potentially degrading VQE performance on real devices despite careful ansatz design. For the ORA ansatz, they acknowledge that its depth reduction comes at the price of a strong growth in the number of variational parameters with problem size, which increases optimization complexity. Finally, in their conclusions they generalize that larger problem instances require precise fine-tuning of VQE configuration, implying that the demonstrated setups may not transfer straightforwardly without substantial tuning effort.
    [codes: C-006, C-026, C-033, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors state that incorporating quantum error mitigation is essential and should be addressed in future work, suggesting that further advances in mitigation techniques could materially change the performance and scalability of their VQE approach.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as a scaling study of VQE for dynamic portfolio optimization that surpasses the so-called 100-qubit utility frontier by tackling instances up to 112 qubits on real hardware, and reports that the best-performing configuration combines a Differential Evolution optimizer with an ansatz circuit tailored to both the financial problem and the specific QPU. It further claims to provide the first scalable VQE implementation in this setting—in particular, the Real Amplitudes plus DE configuration—that clearly separates the outcome distribution from random noise across all tested sizes, and distills a broader methodological lesson that larger problems demand careful, problem-specific fine-tuning of VQE components.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors give a structured description of their VQE workflow in five steps and rely on IBM Quantum primitives (estimator and sampler) for expectation evaluation and final sampling, which supports reproducibility of the core algorithmic setup. They carefully describe the QUBO conversion process, including the quadratic approximation of absolute-value transaction costs, the soft-constraint encoding of the budget, and the binary encoding of investment trajectories, all of which shape the Hamiltonian used by VQE. The paper also explicitly discusses ansatz and optimizer choices in light of known issues such as barren plateaus for hardware-efficient circuits, and documents the impact of transpilation on circuit depth, reinforcing an emphasis on hardware-aware design. Finally, they benchmark against a range of classical and quantum-inspired solvers and analyze cost versus Sharpe ratio, indicating awareness that their mathematical objective is not perfectly aligned with the financial performance metric of interest.

=== PAPER 36432eaf1f31 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the problem that long-horizon financial return distributions (months to years) are often non-Gaussian, displaying persistent asymmetry and bimodality, contrary to the common assumption of Gaussian convergence at larger time scales. It specifically targets assets whose long-term return distributions exhibit clear asymmetry or bimodality, and aims to provide a more accurate probabilistic characterization of these long-term returns to support financial decision-making and risk analysis.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-034, C-041]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors model long-term return distributions using a discrete-time unitary quantum walk, described as a minimal extension of a classical diffusion process that incorporates quantum interference and thereby can generate bimodal and asymmetric probability distributions. They fix the number of time steps initially (n = 100) because changing n mainly affects distribution width rather than shape, smooth the discrete quantum-walk peaks by aggregating three adjacent positions, and fit four quantum-walk parameters (η, θ, φ, ω) to empirical return histograms using steepest-ascent hill climbing, with goodness of fit measured by mean absolute error. To improve fits, they later sample the walk length n from a normal distribution and average over these realizations; decoherence is deliberately excluded because of non-unique modeling choices and its tendency to wash out distinctive quantum-walk features.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the authors find that long-horizon return distributions (from about 100 trading days onward) for their sample assets remain strongly non-Gaussian, with persistent skewness around |γ1| ≳ 0.5 and clear bimodality emerging beyond roughly 50 trading days. Classical Gaussian-based models are reported to fail in capturing the pronounced asymmetry and bimodality, whereas fitted quantum-walk distributions generally reproduce the overall shape of the empirical distributions better than Gaussians, particularly after smoothing over a distribution of walk lengths n, which reduces peak overestimation and tail truncation. The fitted quantum-walk parameters also exhibit clustering in coin-parameter space that differentiates bimodal from asymmetric distributions, and in many asymmetric cases the model requires little or no drift when the initial position is near zero.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-029, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts its quantum-walk fits with classical Gaussian models, stating that Gaussian-based approaches fail to adequately capture strong asymmetry and bimodality in long-term returns, whereas quantum-walk fits better reproduce the overall behavior of these distributions. Quantitatively, the mean absolute error and Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics are reported to be lower for the quantum-walk fits than for Gaussian fits in most assets, especially for bimodal distributions where the KS statistic is consistently better for the quantum walk.
    [codes: C-020, C-025, C-029, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their modeling excludes decoherence, noting that there is no unique way to introduce decoherence into quantum walks and that even small decoherence rates cause the resulting distributions to resemble classical ones, erasing distinctive quantum features; this is presented as a methodological limitation and design choice. They also note a specific shortcoming of the initial fixed-n quantum-walk fits, which tend to overestimate peak heights and sharply truncate the tails, affecting the representation of extreme gains and losses that are important for risk analysis. More broadly, they state that achieving a perfect characterization of two-year return distributions is inherently challenging, implying that even their improved quantum-walk approach cannot fully capture all empirical nuances.
    [codes: C-027, C-028, C-030, C-034, C-041]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests extending the empirical analysis to larger data sets and exploring more refined fitting strategies to further improve quantum-walk fit quality. It also points to the inclusion of decoherence effects as a promising direction, particularly for modeling short-term returns with asymmetric distributions and heavier-than-Gaussian tails.
    [codes: C-040, C-042]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as introducing a quantum-walk-based framework to characterize long-term financial return distributions that remain non-Gaussian, emphasizing that quantum interference allows the model to generate the empirically observed asymmetric and bimodal shapes. They claim that this long-horizon, quantum-walk-based description complements traditional short-term models and provides opportunities to more accurately describe the probabilistic structure underlying long-term financial decisions, including cases where bimodality reflects two competing driving forces encoded via the quantum coin.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-006, C-009, C-033]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study focuses on assets explicitly selected for pronounced long-term asymmetry or bimodality and analyzes opening-price time series for 31 assets (stocks and funds) over periods up to 30 years, defining 'large' time scales as horizons of 100 trading days or more. The authors design custom metrics for distributional features: a bimodality measure that combines peak contrast and separation, and skewness to quantify asymmetry. They employ a discrete-time unitary quantum walk with fixed or randomized walk lengths, using smoothing of quantum-walk positions and histogram-based MAE (and KS) as fit metrics, optimized via steepest-ascent hill climbing over coin and initial-state parameters. The work is simulation-based, with no implementation on physical quantum hardware, and treats the quantum walk as an abstract probabilistic model rather than as an executable quantum algorithm on current devices.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates quantum walks within the historical evolution of financial time-series modeling by noting that Bachelier’s 1900 classical random walk was the first such model and emphasizing that classical diffusion processes are a benchmark from which their quantum-walk extension departs. It also interprets observed bimodality in long-term returns as reflecting two competing driving forces in the market, which the quantum coin is said to capture.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-033]

=== PAPER 374d8058ad85 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets tail-risk management in finance by focusing on Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) as a central risk measure for regulatory and portfolio-optimization purposes, and formulates CVaR minimization as a convex optimization problem requiring efficient estimation of subgradients for first-order methods such as projected stochastic gradient descent. The authors identify a specific gap in prior quantum finance work: the lack of a rigorous complexity analysis for CVaR optimization and, in particular, for the subgradient estimation needed for tail-risk minimization. This is anchored in the Rockafellar–Uryasev convex representation of CVaR, which underpins their gradient-based optimization formulation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-031]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum subgradient oracle for CVaR minimization built around Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), which leverages its quadratic improvement in expectation-estimation sample complexity to potentially accelerate tail-risk optimization. The oracle prepares a superposition over return scenarios, computes the loss reversibly, compares it to a VaR-like threshold to mark tail events, and then uses controlled rotations and payload amplitudes (after affine rescaling of returns) so that QAE can recover both tail probabilities and tail-weighted expectations whose ratio yields conditional expectations and hence CVaR subgradient coordinates. The implementation is QRAM-free, relying instead on basis-state sampling via a distribution-preparation unitary, fixed-point arithmetic for computing losses, simple comparators, and single-qubit controlled rotations, with VaR itself estimated via a QAE-powered bisection routine before being integrated into a staged oracle interface that combines VaR, tail probability, and payload estimation.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the theoretical side, the paper proves that CVaR subgradients in d dimensions can be estimated with O(d/ε log(1/η)) quantum queries, achieving an ℓ2-accurate subgradient with error at most ε and success probability at least 1−η, compared to a classical Monte Carlo complexity of O(d/ε²); the authors describe this as a near-quadratic improvement in query complexity. They analytically quantify how approximation error in the VaR threshold induces only a linear bias in the estimated CVaR subgradient and show that the full oracle’s estimation error can be bounded by a combination of threshold error and amplitude-estimation error terms. For optimization, they prove that projected stochastic subgradient descent using their noisy quantum oracle achieves a convergence guarantee of O(1/√T + ε) and that attaining an ε-optimal CVaR solution requires O(d/ε³) quantum queries end-to-end. Empirically, noiseless simulations show gradient-estimation errors decaying as O(1/M) for the QAE-style estimator versus O(1/√N) for Monte Carlo, with tabulated results indicating lower mean gradient error for the QAE-style method; optimization trajectories in simulated CVaR minimization are similar per iteration across methods, but when plotted against cumulative queries the QAE-style method reaches comparable CVaR reductions using fewer effective queries.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The classical baseline is standard Monte Carlo estimation of CVaR and its gradients, which the authors note has sample complexity O(1/ε²) for expectations and O(d/ε²) for d-dimensional subgradients, providing the reference point for their quantum query improvements. In theory, their QAE-based oracle achieves near-quadratic query savings, moving from O(d/ε²) to O(d/ε log(1/η)) for gradient estimation, and from classical MC’s O(1/√N) error scaling to QAE’s O(1/M) error scaling as the effective budget increases. In simulation, they compare a noiseless QAE-style estimator against a Monte Carlo baseline both for isolated gradient estimation and for use within projected stochastic subgradient descent: numerical results show higher mean gradient error for Monte Carlo than for the QAE-style estimator, while optimization trajectories over iterations show similar CVaR improvements for both, with query-normalized plots indicating that the QAE-style method achieves similar CVaR reduction with fewer queries.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that their evaluation is conducted entirely via noiseless simulation because current quantum hardware cannot support the query depth required for large-scale CVaR optimization, and they emphasize that the QAE-style estimator they simulate is idealized in the sense that it assumes quadratic scaling in an effective sample budget without modeling device noise or overhead. They further admit that their resource trade-off analysis is incomplete, calling for a more detailed study of circuit depth, qubit routing and measurement repetition overhead, and error-mitigation trade-offs across problem sizes. On the theoretical side, they highlight that a lower bound tailored to the conditional-expectation structure underlying CVaR gradients remains open, so the optimality of their query complexity is not fully resolved. In supplementary error-correction estimates they report that the physical qubit counts required are very large even for modest portfolio dimension (e.g., d=10 and precision around 10⁻²), leading them to conclude that near-term implementation on fault-tolerant hardware is out of reach, even though these estimates may inform hardware roadmaps.
    [codes: C-032, C-033, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper outlines several directions for future work: analyzing the noise-robustness of the quantum subgradient oracle under realistic noise models and potentially within fault-tolerant regimes; extending the framework from basic projected subgradient descent to accelerated methods such as Nesterov acceleration and to mirror-descent or dual-averaging schemes in non-Euclidean geometries; generalizing beyond linear loss functions to handle nonlinear payoffs, such as option portfolios or other derivative instruments; and exploring hybrid heuristics that combine the proposed oracle with variational or sampling-based subroutines to create more practical hybrid quantum–classical schemes.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim that their work provides the first rigorous complexity analysis of quantum subgradient methods for tail-risk minimization, specifically for CVaR optimization, by designing a quantum subgradient oracle and proving its statistical and computational properties. They position this as filling a gap in the existing quantum finance literature, which had not previously delivered a detailed complexity treatment of CVaR subgradient estimation for use in first-order methods.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-009]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the theoretical contribution is organized into three main propositions that formalize bias due to VaR approximation, accuracy and query complexity of the quantum gradient estimator, and convergence rates and overall query complexity of optimization with noisy quantum gradients; this structured approach clarifies the assumptions and guarantees at each stage. The empirical evaluation is explicitly presented as simulated evidence using synthetic correlated Gaussian returns, with results reported in two stages: first assessing gradient-estimation accuracy versus budget, then examining optimization dynamics of projected stochastic subgradient descent with simplex projection enforcing long-only constraints. The authors also stress that their circuits are QRAM-free, which is relevant for implementability, and provide a staged oracle interface that clearly separates VaR estimation, tail-probability estimation, and payload (gradient) estimation, which supports reproducibility of their algorithmic design even though hardware-level resource metrics are not fully specified.
    [codes: C-012, C-018, C-020, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-039]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several cross-cutting analytical observations do not neatly fall into the other dimensions: the authors use ratio perturbation bounds to control error when reconstructing subgradients from amplitude-estimated tail probabilities and payload expectations, and they highlight an intuitive explanation for why errors in the VaR threshold introduce only modest bias—namely, that only a thin tail slice of scenarios is misclassified when the threshold is perturbed. These analytic insights help justify the robustness of their estimator construction but are ancillary to the main problem framing, method description, or results.
    [codes: C-024, C-027]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is highly relevant to risk_management because it targets CVaR, a core tail-risk measure, and develops a quantum oracle for estimating CVaR subgradients and VaR thresholds that are directly used in tail-risk optimization. === PAPER 378c2a73ea46 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a combined problem of improving financial prediction (market anomaly detection, portfolio optimization, dimensionality reduction for high‑dimensional indicators, and time‑series forecasting) and strengthening transaction security against quantum attacks. It motivates quantum methods by claiming that classical cryptography and ML struggle with high‑dimensional data, complex optimization, and the coming quantum threat to RSA/ECC, and proposes integrating quantum machine learning with quantum‑resistant lattice cryptography for finance. The portfolio problem is explicitly posed as maximizing the Sharpe ratio under risk constraints, while security is posed as protecting financial transactions in a post‑quantum world.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-013, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use several gate‑based quantum approaches: QSVM with a quantum kernel defined as the overlap of data‑encoded quantum states to accelerate high‑dimensional classification and capture asset correlations via entanglement; QAOA encodes portfolio optimization as an Ising Hamiltonian over asset qubits to search allocations in superposition while targeting a high Sharpe ratio; QPCA represents the covariance matrix as a density matrix and uses phase‑estimation‑style routines to extract principal components; and QBM is used as a probabilistic time‑series model to capture short‑ and long‑run dependencies in financial data. For security, they specify lattice‑based cryptography grounded in SVP and LWE, detailing an LWE‑style encryption c = As + e + m and highlighting homomorphic properties for secure computation on encrypted financial records. All quantum ML components are evaluated in a hybrid quantum‑classical simulator setup.
    [codes: C-010, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-012, C-031, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QSVM improves classification accuracy by up to about 20% and reduces training time by around 50%, including 92.3% accuracy on S&P 500 anomaly detection and detection of 95% of anomalies in their summary. QAOA is claimed to improve portfolio optimization with a 10–15% Sharpe ratio uplift and 25% faster optimization, including a reported Sharpe ratio of 1.45 for a 50‑asset portfolio and an example allocation of 45% equities and 30% bonds. QPCA is reported to reduce dimensionality by ~90% while preserving around 95% variance (e.g., 95.2% variance retained on S&P 500 indicators), and QBM is said to increase forecasting accuracy by about 5–10% with 30% faster convergence, achieving roughly 88–88.5% stock‑price prediction accuracy. For security, lattice‑based cryptography is claimed to provide 99.9% security against classical and quantum attacks with roughly 10–15% extra execution time, yet still securing financial transactions with minimal overhead in their examples. The conclusion summarizes that all quantum‑enhanced components yield substantial gains in computing efficiency, predictive accuracy, and security.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-026, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout, the authors compare their quantum approaches to classical baselines, arguing that classical cryptography (e.g., RSA/ECC) and ML models are inadequate for high‑dimensional financial data and complex optimization. In their review and experiments, they state that QSVM and hybrid quantum–classical models outperform classical SVMs by 10–20% in accuracy and halve training time, QAOA improves Sharpe ratios over classical mean‑variance optimizers by about 10–15% and is claimed to reduce optimization time by 25%, QPCA retains more variance than classical PCA for equivalent dimensionality reduction, and QBM outperforms classical RNNs by 8–10% in prediction accuracy with around 30% faster convergence. For security, they emphasize that lattice‑based schemes resist both classical and quantum attacks, unlike legacy RSA/ECC, though at the cost of 10–15% higher encryption/decryption time versus classical schemes.
    [codes: C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-026, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several technical and organizational limitations. On the quantum side, it notes that current hardware noise and limited qubit coherence can seriously affect the performance and reliability of QSVM, QAOA, QPCA, and QBM, and that scalability to larger datasets remains unresolved because performance may degrade as data size and complexity grow. There is also an explicit admission that lattice‑based cryptography introduces a 10–15% increase in encryption and decryption time relative to classical schemes, and this overhead is reiterated in the comparative analysis. In terms of adoption barriers, the authors highlight a shortage of quantum‑trained professionals in the financial sector and the difficulty of embedding these quantum technologies into existing financial infrastructures, which together constrain near‑term deployment.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as a potentially important technology for solving high-value computational finance problems, focusing on a general multiperiod portfolio optimization problem with discrete integer holdings, transaction costs, and permanent/temporary market impact. The portfolio manager must choose how much to invest in each of N assets across T time steps, given forecasts of expected returns and risk, while accounting for rebalancing costs, making the problem a hard nonconvex combinatorial optimization that is naturally suited to a quantum annealer via a QUBO formulation. The author emphasizes that this multiperiod, discrete, impact-aware trajectory formulation aims to produce globally better portfolio paths than the common practice of solving a sequence of single-period mean–variance problems and then rounding continuous weights.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-010, C-028, C-030, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-055, C-058]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper uses the quantum annealing paradigm, specifically D-Wave hardware accessed via the 1QBit SDK, to solve the portfolio problem by casting it as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) over binary variables. The author explains that QUBO requires binary decision variables and a general (not necessarily positive definite) Q matrix with no explicit constraints, and that nontrivial encoding and embedding steps are needed to map the real-valued, constrained portfolio problem into this form, including choices of binary encodings that affect the effective problem size and the need to tune annealer parameters. Practically, the quantum annealer is operated at 12–17 mK to reduce noise, problems are solved multiple times (e.g., 200 runs), and the most frequently observed solution is taken as the final heuristic answer, with the SDK abstracting away much of the low-level hardware and physics complexity while exposing heuristics for building "quantum-ready" applications.
    [codes: C-012, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-047, C-049, C-052, C-059]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Using a small illustrative instance, the paper reports that existing quantum annealing technology can produce solutions to the discrete multiperiod portfolio problem that are equal to, or very close to, the optimal solution, despite the annealer being a heuristic solver. The author also claims that, conceptually, quantum annealing can exploit quantum tunneling to escape local minima in nonconvex landscapes and that ill-conditioned or degenerate covariance matrices do not pose numerical problems for the quantum annealer. Beyond the portfolio example, the author cites external work (e.g., Google 2015) indicating up to 10^8× speedup over classical computations for specific optimization problems and notes that, for some specialized problems, quantum hardware has already shown significant speed advantages over classical computers.
    [codes: C-006, C-019, C-031, C-032, C-045, C-051, C-053]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts quantum annealing with classical approaches by arguing that combinatorial optimization problems, such as the multiperiod portfolio construction problem (likened to the traveling salesman problem), are particularly hard for classical exhaustive search, which must check combinations often in series, whereas quantum superposition in principle allows exploration of all combinations simultaneously. Within finance, the paper argues that the naive classical approach of solving a sequence of single-period continuous mean–variance optimizations and then rounding to lot sizes is suboptimal because it ignores rebalancing costs and the nonconvex, discrete nature of the true problem, while the quantum-annealing-based discrete trajectory formulation can find globally better portfolio paths. The author also highlights that quantum annealing is less sensitive to ill-conditioned covariance matrices than classical numerical solvers and cites external empirical work showing large quantum speedups over classical methods for certain specialized optimization tasks.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-053]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several important limitations. On the hardware side, gate-model quantum computers are still extremely small (demonstrated 4-qubit grids) and are not expected to be commercially viable for 5–10 years, while quantum annealers, though larger, suffer from significant noise and require extreme operating conditions (12–17 mK and extensive shielding). The author notes ongoing debate about whether quantum annealers exhibit genuine quantum effects that yield true computational speedup, and emphasizes that the annealer is a heuristic solver that does not guarantee optimality, requiring multiple runs and careful interpretation of results. Usability is limited: using a quantum computer today is likened to classical computing 40+ years ago, with specialized expertise, possible machine-level programming, and nontrivial, time-consuming problem setup and parameter tuning. Methodologically, transforming realistic, constrained, real-valued portfolio optimization problems into QUBO is explicitly described as nontrivial, encoding choices affect the size of solvable problems, and the discrete formulation itself is nonconvex and harder to solve than continuous mean–variance counterparts. Finally, the author stresses that existing quantum annealing technology currently permits only small portfolio problems (few assets, time periods, and investment units) to be solved, and that the concrete portfolio example in the paper is correspondingly small in scale, even though the formulation is intended to be generic.

Shorter-term, the paper points to cloud-based access to quantum annealers via SDKs and advocates developing "quantum-ready" algorithms that run on classical hardware today but can later be switched to quantum backends, enabling a smooth transition. It also notes that industry leaders and researchers are beginning to investigate quantum applications for high-value commercial finance problems, particularly in portfolio and risk management, and suggests that the presented multiperiod, impact-aware formulation is designed to scale to generic large problems once hardware permits.

The author emphasizes that this formulation explicitly incorporates transaction costs and both temporary and permanent market impact, handles discrete lot-size constraints directly rather than via rounding, and is structured as a generic framework that, while presently limited to small instances, is intended for large-scale portfolio and risk-management problems as quantum hardware advances.

=== PAPER 3a13b1eecbf9 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core problem as reliably extracting high-quality samples and expectation values from noisy near-term quantum devices, which is a key scaling bottleneck for sample-based algorithms such as variational optimization and machine learning applied to risk and optimization tasks. The authors emphasize that noise on current hardware makes leveraging near-term quantum computers difficult, and they therefore seek to formally quantify the sampling overhead required to obtain ‘good’ samples under a specified noise model.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-007, C-009, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Methodologically, the work assumes a layered Pauli-Lindblad noise model and leverages a protocol that enables efficient learning of layerwise noise coefficients, summarized by an aggregate noise parameter γ that quantifies overall noise strength. Layer fidelity is used as a practical metric to relate this model to sampling costs, with per-layer fidelities multiplying across layers, and the authors extend their framework to diagonal and non-diagonal Hamiltonians via commuting-Pauli decompositions and to applications such as QAOA, fidelity estimation, and QSVM kernels. They also introduce the use of CVaR on noisy measurement distributions, possibly combined with problem-informed filter functions, to obtain provable bounds on noise-free expectation values and to post-select samples consistent with known problem structure.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The main theoretical result is that under the assumed noise model, obtaining a target bitstring from a noisy device requires a multiplicative sampling overhead scaling as √γ, where γ encodes noise strength, and that this scaling carries over to the sampling cost in CVaR-based expectation estimation. A central contribution is the proof that CVaR of noisy samples yields rigorous upper and lower bounds on noise-free expectation values; for diagonal Hamiltonians these bounds apply directly, and in the special case where the ideal state is a ground state, the lower CVaR bound becomes tight and furthermore lower bounds the fidelity between noisy and ideal states at level α when CVaR equals the ground energy. The variance of the CVaR estimator is shown to be bounded as O(1/α²) in general and O(1/α) for Bernoulli and normal-like cases, and the authors show that exploiting problem structure via filtered Hamiltonians and constraint-preserving ansätze can significantly tighten these bounds and ensure that post-selected averages remain within filtered CVaR intervals. They demonstrate that their results directly apply to QAOA and argue that, given a √γ sampling overhead, known QAOA approximation guarantees can be retained in the presence of noise, with experiments up to 40 and 127 qubits confirming the CVaR-bound behavior and revealing that fitted effective γ can be smaller than conservative layer-fidelity estimates. Additional experiments validate the variance-scaling predictions via bootstrapping and show that 40-qubit QAOA MAXCUT CVaR values upper-bound ideal expectations as predicted, while 127-qubit tests highlight that applying the analytic CVaR bounds requires shot counts that are currently impractical.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-004]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their CVaR-based bounding approach against classical and quantum baselines by noting that, under the assumed noise model, a √γ sampling overhead can in principle recover known classical QAOA approximation guarantees even in the noisy regime, provided sufficient samples are taken. They explicitly compare their sampling overhead to that of probabilistic error cancellation, stating that their method requires considerably fewer samples—scaling like √γ rather than γ²—but only provides bounds on expectation values rather than unbiased estimators, implying a trade-off between sample efficiency and estimator bias relative to more resource-intensive quantum error mitigation schemes.
    [codes: C-032, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper emphasizes that implementing full quantum error correction on current devices is infeasible, motivating the need for mitigation but also constraining achievable accuracy. The authors acknowledge that their core analysis focuses on gate and circuit noise and largely omits state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors, explicitly noting that SPAM is a separate issue and that their primary focus is on errors during circuit execution. They further recognize that, for some problem sizes and hardware qualities, the √γ sampling overhead required to combat noise may exceed the cost of brute-force classical search, undermining any practical advantage, and they show that for their 127-qubit experiments the number of shots required to apply the analytic CVaR bounds is ‘significantly higher’ and currently impractical to run. They also highlight that hardware quality thresholds and low layer fidelities can lead to enormous required sampling overheads, limiting near-term applicability even if the theoretical bounds hold.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-033, C-040, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest exploring hybrid workflows where classical optimization is used to determine variational parameters and quantum hardware is employed only for sampling good solutions, leveraging their sampling and CVaR guarantees in a more hardware-efficient way. They also propose extending their methodology to explicitly account for SPAM errors, indicating that adapting the CVaR-based framework and noise modeling to include SPAM is a natural direction for future research.
    [codes: C-031, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution a formal quantification of the sampling overhead needed to obtain high-quality samples from noisy quantum computers, expressed in terms of an aggregate noise parameter γ and linked to experimentally accessible layer fidelities. Building on this, the authors introduce the use of CVaR of noisy samples to derive provable bounds on noise-free expectation values, extending these bounds to diagonal and general Hamiltonians, and show how problem-specific filters and constraint-preserving ansätze can tighten the bounds and even infer fidelity guarantees in ground-state settings. They further highlight that their √γ sampling and variance scaling represent a more favorable overhead than probabilistic error cancellation for obtaining informative (though biased) estimates, and that they validate these theoretical guarantees on real hardware up to 127 qubits.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-037, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-004]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study grounds its analysis in a Pauli-Lindblad layered noise model that admits efficient learning of its coefficients and defines a single parameter γ to summarize noise strength, which is then related to experimentally observable layer fidelities that compose multiplicatively across layers. The CVaR-based framework is developed with formal lemmas linking noisy and ideal distributions, explicit bounds on estimator variance, and distribution-specific refinements (e.g., for Bernoulli and normal distributions), and it is systematically extended from diagonal to general Hamiltonians and to practical settings like QAOA, fidelity estimation, and QSVM kernels. The authors emphasize experimental validation on real IBM hardware up to 127 qubits, including constraint-preserving QAOA instances and bootstrapping studies that confirm the predicted variance scaling, and they are transparent about scope by explicitly separating SPAM from the main analysis and by discussing when layer-fidelity-based estimates are conservative compared to fitted effective γ.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-016, C-004]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Error mitigation is explicitly framed as a key strategy to bridge the gap between noisy near-term hardware and fully error-corrected quantum computing, and the authors also note that many variational algorithms effectively treat measurement outcomes as direct candidate solutions in optimization contexts. These broader contextual points motivate their focus on sampling and CVaR-based postprocessing.
    [codes: C-007, C-029]

The focus is on high-level planning for quantum‑safe software/hardware and quantum‑ready data frameworks, not on concrete algorithmic or hardware implementations.
