=== PAPER 3ee4e2ce5b7d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses high‑dimensional Monte Carlo simulation problems in finance, motivated in particular by credit portfolio loss estimation where the number of obligors – and thus required random numbers – can be on the order of 10^6, creating prohibitive qubit requirements in prior quantum Monte Carlo schemes that allocate a register per random number (C-002, C-003, C-019). It formulates these problems as expectations of integrands that depend on many random variables but can be computed sequentially in Nran steps, a structure that includes credit portfolio risk measurement under a Merton‑type model (C-013, C-023, C-037, C-038). The framing leverages the known quadratic error scaling advantage of quantum Monte Carlo over classical Monte Carlo as the underlying motivation for seeking a more qubit‑efficient implementation (C-001).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-013, C-019, C-023, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum Monte Carlo scheme that effectively performs classical Monte Carlo on a quantum computer: they prepare a uniform superposition over sample indices, then, for each branch, sequentially generate pseudo‑random numbers via a quantum PRNG and update the integrand, finally encoding the sampled integrand value into the amplitude of an ancilla qubit for quantum amplitude estimation (C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021). Instead of storing all random numbers in parallel registers, they sequentially generate pseudo‑random bit strings on a single PRN register and compute the integrand into another register, which reduces qubit usage at the cost of greater depth (C-004, C-009, C-019). As a concrete PRNG they choose the permuted congruential generator (PCG), whose sequence is realized via linear congruential updates and permutations implemented as modular multiplication, controlled swaps (random rotation), and xorshift using CNOTs, with dedicated gates PPRN and JPRN and an LCG jump‑ahead formula to initialize subsequences (C-006, C-007, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035).
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim that their PRNG‑based quantum Monte Carlo procedure yields the same estimation result as classical Monte Carlo but with quadratic speedup in terms of oracle calls, preserving the O(N^{-1}) error scaling of amplitude estimation compared with the O(N^{-1/2}) scaling of classical Monte Carlo (C-001, C-005, C-027). They decompose the total error into sampling error, which scales as the inverse square root of the number of samples Nsamp, and amplitude‑estimation error, which decreases inversely with the number of oracle calls, showing how both contribute to the final estimation accuracy (C-024, C-025, C-026). For their PCG implementation, they report that the dominant resource cost comes from modular multiplication, which scales linearly in qubits and quadratically in circuit depth with the bit‑length n (C-036). In a small simulator demonstration on a toy multivariable integral, they observe that the quantum estimate closely matches the sampled average over PRNG‑generated points, as intended (C-041, C-045, C-049).
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-036, C-041, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The method is explicitly compared with classical Monte Carlo: the authors emphasize that classical Monte Carlo samples only a subset of all possible random‑number patterns and approximates the true expectation Etrue with a simple arithmetic mean Esamp, whereas their quantum procedure reproduces this same Esamp but with quadratic speedup via amplitude estimation (C-010, C-011, C-005). They analytically contrast error scalings, showing that classical Monte Carlo’s error is proportional to N_orac^{-1/2}, while the quantum approach achieves an error term that scales as N_orac^{-1}, leading to a claimed quadratic improvement in oracle complexity (C-001, C-024, C-027, C-028). They also note that previous quantum Monte Carlo methods targeted the true expectation Etrue directly using parallel random‑number registers, providing a conceptual baseline for their qubit‑reduced, Esamp‑oriented scheme (C-019, C-029).
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-019, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that their approach relies on the assumption that the integrand can be written in a sequential form in Nran steps, and explicitly acknowledge that not all functions fit this assumption, limiting the method’s applicability beyond cases like credit portfolio loss (C-013, C-022, C-023). They point out a circuit‑design constraint: modular multiplication in the PRNG must be implemented in a self‑updating fashion to avoid outputting to an extra register, otherwise qubit usage would increase and undermine the intended reduction (C-033). They further recognize that the proposed qubit reduction inevitably increases circuit depth, and argue that such deep circuits will not be performable on near‑term quantum hardware without full quantum error correction, which they do not expect to be available soon (C-050, C-051). In their simulator demonstration, they also concede that the very small‑scale PRNG and limited number of samples raise statistical concerns about the robustness of the estimate, framing that example as a proof‑of‑concept rather than a statistically strong validation (C-041, C-048).
    [codes: C-013, C-022, C-023, C-033, C-041, C-048, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a mitigation strategy for the depth–qubit trade‑off, the authors suggest partially parallelizing the PRNG: instead of fully sequential generation of all Nran random numbers, they propose generating Nran/n pseudo‑random sequences in parallel, each of length n, and computing corresponding parts of the integrand one‑by‑one, which interpolates between full qubit reduction and full parallelization (C-052).
    [codes: C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is a qubit‑reduction strategy for quantum Monte Carlo that replaces the standard one‑register‑per‑random‑number design with a sequential quantum pseudo‑random number generator, allowing the same sampled expectation Esamp as classical Monte Carlo to be estimated with quadratic speedup while using significantly fewer qubits (C-002, C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-021). A second aspect of novelty is the concrete proposal to use the permuted congruential generator on a quantum circuit, chosen because its combination of LCG and bit permutations offers advantages in both required qubit number (memory) and circuit depth, along with explicit gate‑level constructions of the needed PRNG operations (C-006, C-007, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035). The application of this framework to credit portfolio loss under the Merton model, justified by the sequential structure of the loss computation, is presented as an illustrative financial use‑case of the general method (C-023, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040).
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-019, C-021, C-023, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper provides a step‑by‑step description of the quantum algorithm, including preparation of the sample superposition, PRNG subsequence initialization with JPRN, sequential PRNG and integrand updates, and final amplitude encoding, as well as a detailed gate‑level construction for PCG and the credit‑loss circuit, which enhances conceptual transparency (C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-044). For the simulator experiment, they describe a simple multivariable integral, approximate it using PRN‑sampled grid points, and use likelihood‑based amplitude estimation, but also directly acknowledge that the experiment relies on a very small LCG and small sample size, flagging statistical concerns and underscoring the proof‑of‑concept nature rather than a rigorous benchmark (C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049).
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The requirement to convert uniform pseudo‑random numbers into target distributions, such as normal variables needed in many financial models, is noted as an additional step in the integrand computation, and while treated as implementable, it is not deeply analyzed in terms of quantum resource overhead (C-020).
    [codes: C-020]

=== PAPER 413125f4264b (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets derivative pricing, credit risk, and a dynamic portfolio problem in a regime‑switching economy, motivated by the fact that current quantum computers cannot yet provide an advantage for realistic continuous‑time diffusion models commonly used in finance. To make quantum implementation more tractable, the authors focus on discrete-state Markov regime‑switching models with observable states, arguing that these are both more realistic for macro/volatility regimes and more amenable to quantum algorithms based on amplitude estimation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-018, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-031]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The core quantum approach is Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), pursued for its theoretical quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo, with accurate state preparation identified as the crucial prerequisite. The authors design and analyze state‑preparation circuits for discrete Markov chains (including two‑state and multi‑state cases), using RY/CRY rotations parameterized by transition probabilities (estimated from NBER business cycle data), and study one‑hot versus binary encodings that trade qubit count against gate complexity. These Markov‑controlled circuits are then embedded into application‑specific architectures: a static credit‑risk state‑preparation circuit with regime‑dependent default probabilities; an option‑pricing circuit with Brownian, price, and payoff registers plus regime‑controlled price updates; and a dynamic portfolio circuit combining a Markov chain, a QFT‑based growth register, and rescaled loss encoding, with MLAE adopted as a near‑term alternative to canonical QAE.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On real hardware (IBM torino and Honeywell H1), the authors show that their Markov‑chain state‑preparation circuits achieve low mean squared error (MSE), with accuracy improving for larger transition probabilities and error growth mainly driven by the exponential increase in bins and reduced effective shots. For the static regime‑dependent credit‑risk application and regime‑switching derivative pricing, they report MSE tables for specific parameter choices and observe that one‑hot encoding is preferable up to moderate state counts on current IBM hardware. In the dynamic portfolio example, Honeywell H1’s higher fidelity and connectivity yield lower MSE than IBM, and applying MLAE to the credit‑risk amplitude on H1 produces an estimate within about 2.5% of the exact value.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-017, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum approach is positioned against classical Monte Carlo, with QAE cited as offering an estimation error that scales quadratically better in the number of samples. For the dynamic portfolio/credit‑risk amplitude, the MLAE‑based quantum estimate on Honeywell H1 is compared to the exact (classically computed) value and reported to be within 2.5%, but the paper does not present detailed runtime or resource benchmarks versus classical implementations of the same regime‑switching models.
    [codes: C-004, C-025, C-037, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that current quantum hardware cannot yet deliver a computational advantage for realistic stochastic diffusion models and that standard Euler/Milstein discretizations of continuous‑time diffusions introduce biases that complicate quantum implementations. They deliberately assume observable regimes to avoid the added complexity of filtering latent states, and note that current processors are still too small to implement discrete‑state models with a realistically large number of time steps or states. Canonical QAE circuits for their empirical example are described as prohibitively large for existing devices, forcing reliance on approximate or alternative estimation methods. Overall, they argue that achieving practical advantage will require hardware capable of deeper circuits and more qubits to realize realistic Markov chains and time horizons.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-020, C-025, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the authors suggest extending their framework beyond the stationary two‑state observable Markov setting to models with heterogeneous Markov chains and more than two regimes, which would increase realism but demand more sophisticated state‑preparation and encoding schemes.
    [codes: C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as developing and experimentally validating state‑preparation circuits for regime‑switching Markov models tailored to amplitude estimation–based quantum finance, including explicit constructions for derivative pricing, static credit risk, and a dynamic portfolio example. The work compares one‑hot and binary encodings for Markov chains on actual devices, evaluates application‑level performance on IBM torino and Honeywell H1, and argues that regime‑switching credit‑risk estimation via MLAE is currently a stronger candidate for near‑term useful amplitude‑estimation results than more demanding derivative‑pricing circuits.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper derives Markov transition probabilities from NBER U.S. business‑cycle data to parameterize its circuits, and evaluates accuracy via MSE computed from repeated hardware runs with specified numbers of iterations and shots. It reports circuit depths and gate counts for different encodings on IBM torino and Honeywell H1, and links error behavior to bin growth and shot allocation, while also motivating classical rescaling of payoff distributions to reduce qubit requirements. The adoption of MLAE instead of canonical QAE is explicitly justified by current hardware constraints, and the authors provide closed‑form classical solutions for portfolio weights as a reference, though detailed reproducibility information (e.g., full code listings) is not discussed in the extracted codes.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all extracted codes fit within the other reporting dimensions.

=== PAPER 41d2d7bb257a (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit risk prediction, arguing that accurate assessment is essential for financial health, default minimisation, and regulatory compliance, and that current credit models struggle with nonlinear relationships in high-dimensional data and poor recall on the minority (defaulter) class. It formulates the task as a binary loan default classification problem on a real-world credit risk dataset, aiming to improve AUC and minority-class recall via a quantum-assisted model. The work is framed within a broader move from traditional risk models, whose shortcomings were highlighted in the 2008 crisis, toward machine learning and quantum-enhanced approaches in financial risk management.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid quantum–classical transfer learning model in which a classical neural network compresses 24-dimensional input features into a 4-dimensional latent representation that is then encoded into 4 qubits via angle encoding with RY gates. The quantum component is a parameterized variational circuit comprising an embedding layer, entanglement (e.g., CNOT) layer, and trainable rotation gates; this circuit, together with the classical feature extractor and output layer, is co-trained end-to-end with binary cross-entropy loss using PennyLane’s TorchLayer inside a PyTorch pipeline. Only a selected subset of computationally significant features is encoded into quantum states, addressing data-encoding inefficiency, and all parameters (classical, quantum, and output) are updated jointly via backpropagation through the hybrid architecture.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The co-trained hybrid QTL model is reported to achieve an AUC of 0.9134 and a test accuracy of 91.17%, with substantially improved recall for the minority defaulter class (0.73) compared to baselines. It demonstrates strong ROC performance and high overall classification accuracy, reaching its best performance at epoch 8, and the authors emphasise that it significantly boosts minority-class detection while maintaining strong metrics on the majority class. An additional empirical finding is that training on the original unbalanced dataset, rather than SMOTE-resampled data, yields higher accuracy, which the authors attribute to overfitting in synthetic samples.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-012, C-013, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid co-trained QTL model is compared against a standalone QNN baseline and a conventional classical neural network, with the co-trained model claimed to significantly outperform these baselines. Relative to the standalone QNN, the hybrid model shows higher accuracy (0.9117 vs 0.8097), higher AUC (0.9134 vs 0.7446), and much better minority-class recall (0.73 vs 0.16). The standalone QNN, trained directly on raw credit data with limited preprocessing, is said to suffer from poor recall and unstable convergence, while also requiring nearly twice the training time of the hybrid model, leading the authors to describe the hybrid as both more accurate and more time-efficient.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-012, C-013, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note several limitations: at the field level, QML is constrained by hardware limits such as qubit count, coherence time, and noise, as well as data encoding inefficiencies, generalization gaps between theory and practice, and scarce benchmarking on real datasets. At the implementation level, they highlight that data encoding inefficiency is a critical barrier and that quantum circuit simulation, especially parameter-shift gradient computation on a CPU-based simulator, is the dominant computational bottleneck. For the standalone QNN, they report poor recall, unstable convergence, high computational demands, and the need to restrict training data to 1,000 samples because of parameter-shift overhead. For the hybrid model, they acknowledge higher computational cost due to joint training of classical and quantum layers and more variable convergence behaviour, which they attribute to non-convex circuit training and high-variance gradients, explicitly stating that this variability calls for careful optimization strategies.
    [codes: C-004, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-036, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-052]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future methodological work is implied in the authors’ observation that convergence fluctuations in the hybrid model and high-variance gradients from parameter-shift rules "highlight the need for careful optimization strategies," suggesting further research into more robust training procedures for co-trained quantum–classical models.
    [codes: C-052, C-049]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main claimed contribution is a fully co-trained hybrid quantum–classical transfer learning architecture applied to real-world financial credit risk data, where both classical and quantum components are trained simultaneously rather than using a frozen classical feature extractor. The authors argue that this end-to-end co-training enables mutual adaptation between classical representations and the quantum circuit, improves minority-class detection and AUC, and demonstrates that quantum-assisted learning can be feasibly integrated into financial decision pipelines under current simulator and hardware constraints. They further position hybrid architectures as a meaningful near-term path that balances performance gains with existing quantum technology limitations.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-014, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-015, C-012, C-013, C-053]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study uses a public Kaggle credit risk dataset with 24 features and 32,580 instances, applies EDA and Min–Max normalization, and considers SMOTE to address class imbalance, ultimately opting for the unbalanced dataset after observing SMOTE-induced overfitting. The experimental setup includes a stratified 80/20 train–test split for the hybrid model; the standalone QNN baseline is trained on a reduced subset of 1,000 samples due to computational overheads.   DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses derivative pricing and credit risk measurement in financial markets by proposing regime-switching models that are both more realistic and more compatible with near-term quantum hardware. It replaces continuous-time diffusion models, which are viewed as currently impractical for quantum advantage, with discrete-time, discrete-state Markov-chain regime-switching processes whose states represent good and bad economic conditions, and uses these to frame option pricing, portfolio loss distributions, and VaR calculations for quantum algorithms.

  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors work on gate-based quantum computers, encoding observable two-state Markov chains and associated financial quantities using discrete-time circuits whose depth scales with the number of periods. Across applications, they rely on amplitude estimation (canonical and iterative QAE/IQAE) to estimate probabilities or expectations, with additional hybrid structure such as classical preprocessing to reduce qubit counts and a dynamic-portfolio circuit that combines a Markov-chain register with a QFT-based growth register.

At the hardware level, they state that the practical example circuit is prohibitively large for canonical QAE on current processors, that connectivity constraints approximately double the complexity of the transpiled circuits, and that NISQ-era limitations such as the need for error mitigation and tight qubit budgets remain significant obstacles.

=== PAPER 50989fdc9ad1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core obstacle for quantum algorithms in finance and statistics as the lack of efficient, updatable state-preparation routines for loading classical probability distributions into quantum states, particularly when worst‑case arbitrary states are prohibitively deep and ancilla‑intensive and when existing methods require updating many circuit parameters each time model parameters change (C-001, C-002, C-004). It formulates the problem as preparing quantum states that encode statistical distributions and mixtures, Odistr|0⟩ = ∑x p(x)|x⟩, with p(x) arising from parametric or maximum‑entropy models, and then using these states for downstream tasks like derivative pricing and risk analysis (C-012, C-035, C-038).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-012, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit (SI‑PQC) framework that links quantum state preparation to intrinsic statistical symmetries via the maximum entropy principle, using observables with conservative expectations as symmetry‑defining constraints (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015). Within this framework, they decompose distributional information into fixed constraint functions fk (encoding prior model knowledge) and tunable parameters λk (encoding data uncertainty), and implement a maximum entropy distribution loader (MEDL) in three steps: unitary dilation of normalized constraint functions, linear combination of these via block encoding, and QSVT‑based imaginary‑time evolution to approximate the exponential form (C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020). The circuit architecture is a static state‑preparation structure with model parameters explicitly encoded as rotation angles, enabling reuse, deep compilation, and compatibility with a weighted distribution mixer (WDM) that reuses MEDL components and encodes parameter uncertainty in latent registers for mixture models, as well as with a variational learning protocol and QMCI/QAE for finance applications (C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038).
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that SI‑PQC, via MEDL, achieves universal expressiveness with an optimally dimensioned learning space and classical preprocessing complexity that is optimal in the number of model parameters M, since only O(M) rotation angles must be updated (C-011, C-019). For single distributions, the MEDL theorem gives single‑shot circuit depth O(n M df log(1/ε)) with success probability F²/4, improved to depth O(n M df log(1/ε)/F) with amplitude amplification, and analogous complexity bounds hold for mixtures under the WDM theorem with only logarithmic additional depth in the number of mixture components (C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028). SI‑PQC‑based learning is argued to reduce training complexity and improve generalization because it uses only Npara = M ≪ n independent gates and a repetition count Nrepeat independent of qubit number, leading to generalization error bounds driven by the small parameter count (C-033, C-034). In finance applications, the authors state that QMCI with SI‑PQC enables a quantum extension of incremental computing for pricing, yielding a favorable end‑to‑end resource expression, and that Greeks can be obtained directly via parameter‑shift rules on the SI‑PQC parameters (C-035, C-036, C-037). For risk analysis, they show numerically that slowly varying observables such as E[X] and E[ln X] serve as conservative constraints and that SI‑PQC can efficiently and accurately approximate empirical distributions to recover quantities like empirical VaR from simulated data (C-039, C-040).
    [codes: C-011, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical or existing quantum‑assisted pipelines that rely on heavy preprocessing, the authors argue that a static SI‑PQC structure with only M tunable parameters avoids recomputing large preprocessed artifacts and thus preserves potential speed‑ups in time‑dependent models (C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023). For mixture models, they explicitly contrast WDM with straightforward QSP+LCU combinations that require Nθ repetitions of full circuits, claiming that WDM needs only logarithmic additional depth, leading to an exponential reduction in time and quantum resources for mixtures (C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010). In learning, they position SI‑PQC favorably against generic QML models whose generalization error scales with a larger parameter count, emphasizing that SI‑PQC uses only M independent gates (C-033, C-034). In pricing and VaR estimation, SI‑PQC‑based QMCI is presented as a quantum analogue of classical incremental computing and classical Monte Carlo, with the resource expression TTSSI−PQC intended to be lower end‑to‑end than approaches where state preparation dominates (C-035, C-036).
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023, C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that classical pre-processing approaches are fragile in time‑dependent settings because previously computed artifacts quickly become obsolete, erasing any prospective quantum speed‑ups; SI‑PQC is partly motivated as a remedy but they treat this as a limitation of many current methods (C-005). They also note that a simple combination of QSP routines with LCU for mixtures incurs prohibitive overhead, motivating but not fully eliminating mixture‑model complexity concerns (C-006). For their own proposal, they state that for small qubit numbers n, the asymptotic resource advantage of SI‑PQC can be diminished by larger constant prefactors, so practical gains may only materialize at moderate or large scales (C-041). They further mention that block‑encoding of certain linear functions can be viewed as a limitation of SI‑PQC, suggesting the need to hybridize with pre‑trained PQCs to address this gap (C-042).
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a way to mitigate current limitations in implementing linear functions within SI‑PQC, the authors suggest combining SI‑PQC with a pre‑trained PQC used specifically for block encoding, effectively proposing hybrid architectures as future work (C-042). They also state that SI‑PQC could be extended beyond the paper’s concrete tasks to loading and simulating time series and to designing quantum algorithms for non‑parametric and semi‑parametric statistical tests, indicating broader statistical and financial applications (C-043). Additionally, they point to a possible but unexplored connection between SI‑PQC and quantum state tomography or verification, explicitly leaving this line of inquiry open (C-044).
    [codes: C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit that embeds prior knowledge about data symmetries via observables with conservative expectations and the maximum entropy principle, yielding maximum‑entropy distributions as the ‘best unbiased guess’ when explicit formulas are unavailable (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016). They further claim that this design leads to universal expressiveness with an optimally dimensioned learning space and a static circuit structure in which all model parameters appear only as rotation angles, enabling advanced compilation, reuse, and precise phase calculation (C-009, C-011, C-023). For mixtures, they present the WDM construction as novel in reusing MEDL components to encode parameter uncertainty in a latent space, achieving only logarithmic additional depth and, according to their analysis, exponential savings in time and quantum resources compared with naive QSP+LCU schemes (C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-010). Finally, they emphasize that SI‑PQC supports simultaneous learning of classical model parameters and quantum states, improving interpretability and potentially offering better generalization due to the small number of independent parameters (C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034).
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-009, C-011, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-010, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the framework is grounded in a clear separation between fixed prior knowledge (encoded in constraint functions fk) and tunable data‑driven parameters λk, which dictates both circuit design and learning strategy and is explicitly aligned with the maximum entropy principle (C-014, C-015, C-016). The MEDL construction is specified as a three‑step, block‑encoding‑based process with formal theorems providing circuit depth and success probabilities, and the use of amplitude amplification and imaginary‑time evolution approximated via QSVT is analytically characterized (C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022). For learning, the authors employ a fidelity‑based loss that allows parameter extraction proportional to the number of free parameters, and they explicitly tie generalization bounds to the parameter count, emphasizing that SI‑PQC contains only M independent gates repeated O(log(1/εF)) times (C-029, C-030, C-033, C-034). In the financial experiments, they adopt a sliding‑window incremental scheme for online risk analysis and identify slowly varying observables such as E[X] and E[ln X] as conservative constraints for maximum‑entropy fitting, arguing that this yields accurate approximations of empirical distributions and VaR estimates, although detailed benchmarking against real financial data is not discussed in the codes provided (C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039, C-040).

=== PAPER 55cbe84d64e7 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets Monte Carlo integration for high-dimensional, separable integrands, noting that many similar term evaluations are repeated when many random numbers are used, and applies this to credit portfolio risk measurement. In the finance use case, portfolio loss is modeled as a sum over obligors and risk measures such as VaR and CVaR are represented as functions of this loss, fitting the separable structure required by the method.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach builds on quantum Monte Carlo via quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), where a superposition over inputs is prepared and the integrand is encoded into an ancilla-qubit amplitude, yielding quadratic error scaling in the number of integrand-circuit calls. The authors introduce a nested QAE scheme: an inner QAE estimates per-sample sums over dimensions in quantum parallel using separability and pseudorandom numbers (PRNs), and an outer QAE aggregates over samples; the PRN-based construction reduces qubit requirements and exploits a separable map over indices, with a concrete implementation using a PCG generator and its jump formula, and T-count is used as the main runtime proxy.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the nested QAE scheme can reduce the number of calls to the circuit for each separated term from O(D) to O(δ⁻¹) when the dimension exceeds the required precision scale, while standard QAE retains quadratic error scaling in oracle calls. Because the PRN-based encoding makes qubit requirements independent of the problem dimension, the authors estimate in a typical credit-risk parameter setting that the new method can cut the total T-count by several tens of percent relative to their previous PRN-based construction.
    [codes: C-007, C-013, C-014, C-024, C-034]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The work positions its method within the standard claim that QAE-based quantum Monte Carlo achieves a quadratic reduction in the number of integrand-oracle calls compared with classical Monte Carlo sampling, by achieving worst-case error scaling as M⁻¹ with O(M) oracle calls rather than the classical O(N⁻1/2) behavior. The detailed quantitative comparison in the paper, however, focuses primarily on improvements over a previous quantum PRN-based Monte Carlo implementation rather than over a specific classical codebase.
    [codes: C-001, C-013, C-014, C-019, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that a reduction in the number of circuit calls does not automatically imply shorter computational time, since their new method replaces a recursive PRN progression with a jump formula that is typically more expensive per use. They note that the previous method computes the inner sum over dimensions exactly, whereas the inner QAE in the new scheme introduces approximation error and outputs a superposition of nearby values, so the method only behaves well when the inner-QAE resolution parameter M is large enough that 1/M is small compared to the typical per-sample sum S_j. This, in turn, requires M > (l δ_rel)⁻¹ and the improvement in term evaluations only materializes when (l δ_rel)⁻¹ < D, and they emphasize that PRN jumps usually incur much larger cost than sequential progress. Finally, applicability is limited to cases where the integrand is separable in the form they require.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-009, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The conclusion points to exploring additional ways to exploit distinctive features of the PRN-based construction in future quantum Monte Carlo algorithms.
    [codes: C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s main contribution is a nested QAE architecture that leverages separable integrands and PRN-based quantum parallelism over term indices to reduce the number of repeated evaluations in high-dimensional Monte Carlo integration, with a concrete instantiation for credit portfolio risk where loss is decomposed into obligor-level terms. It extends prior PRN-based work by introducing an inner QAE for per-sample dimensional sums, using a jump-capable PCG random generator and analyzing how this impacts query complexity and T-count.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The study is entirely analytical: it specifies circuit constructions (including how superpositions are prepared and amplitudes encoded) and uses T-count as the proxy for computational time, together with explicit parameter choices to characterize a “typical” credit-risk setting, but does not report hardware executions or empirical error measurements. The analysis carefully separates inner and outer QAE roles and contrasts the new jump-based design with the previous sequential PRN scheme in terms of exactness versus approximation and gate-count formulas, supporting reproducibility of the complexity estimates though not of runtime benchmarks.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper includes a brief outline of its organization, marking the transition from introduction to technical sections.

=== PAPER 58e7ea9324df (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The work targets quantum enhancements for core quantitative finance tasks, specifically derivative pricing and Value at Risk (VaR), by formulating them as expectation‑estimation problems amenable to Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) and amplitude estimation; VaR/Expected Shortfall is further reduced to a pricing‑type problem by encoding a step function oracle whose measurement probabilities correspond to tail probabilities of the loss distribution.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors study QAMC with a "standard encoding" and propose a modified encoding plus a new Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm. The standard encoding prepares a superposition matching classical path probabilities and uses an oracle to encode payoffs, with amplitude estimation providing the quadratic Monte Carlo speedup; the new encoding instead directly loads probabilities and payoffs (not their square roots) and adds one extra qubit, while RQAE is designed to estimate both amplitude magnitude and sign by being sensitive to the underlying phase. They emphasize that oracle efficiency and the tunable depth–accuracy trade‑off in RQAE (via parameter q) are central to overall algorithmic performance.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that the new encoding and RQAE enable pricing of derivatives and other financial products with negative payoffs or values, where standard encodings fail: the new encoding converges to the correct Riemann sum for negative payoffs, and RQAE is the only tested AE variant that converges to the exact solution on a negative‑price example. Quantitatively, they restate that QAMC with amplitude estimation yields a Monte Carlo error scaling of order 1/Noracle, and they find that RQAE attains performance similar to well‑known AE algorithms in terms of convergence behavior.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-018, C-026, C-030, C-034, C-007]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical Monte Carlo, the authors highlight the known quadratic improvement in error scaling when using amplitude estimation, contrasting the classical ε_MC ∼ 1/√Npaths and overall ε ∼ 1/√C behavior with the quantum ε_MC ∼ 1/Noracle scaling, under the usual assumptions about oracle efficiency. They stress, however, that despite this theoretical advantage, their concrete algorithms—especially when implemented on current NISQ devices—are not yet competitive with classical Monte Carlo methods in practical pricing and VaR computations.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors underscore multiple limitations. First, the new encoding suffers from a large constant‑factor overhead proportional to Npaths, which can overshadow or even nullify the quadratic speedup and yields worse performance than the standard encoding in many settings. Second, their proposals are not yet applicable or competitive on current NISQ hardware due to excessive qubit requirements for oracles, circuit depths incompatible with decoherence times, and gate counts that demand error rates beyond today’s capabilities. Third, while RQAE matches other AE algorithms in asymptotic performance and uniquely handles negative amplitudes, it often requires more oracle calls than the most advanced competitors, further limiting its practicality.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the authors call for improved stochastic differential equation (SDE) solvers tailored to quantum Monte Carlo pipelines and, critically, new techniques to implement oracles with significantly reduced depth and qubit counts. They frame the main ongoing challenge as simultaneously advancing these algorithmic and implementation aspects so that QAMC‑based pricing and risk algorithms become more realistic for future hardware.
    [codes: C-037, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims two primary contributions: a new encoding protocol for QAMC and a new Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm. The encoding is presented as a way to correctly handle payoffs that can take negative values by loading payoffs and probabilities directly, while RQAE is introduced as an AE variant explicitly sensitive to amplitude sign (via phase information), enabling pricing of financial products with negative values. They further argue that RQAE achieves convergence comparable to state‑of‑the‑art AE algorithms while adding this sign‑sensitivity capability.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-007]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds on the standard Riemann‑sum discretization of payoff expectations and makes explicit the error‑scaling analysis for both classical Monte Carlo and quantum amplitude estimation, which clarifies the theoretical benchmark. The authors also discuss in detail where standard encoding fails—through the absolute‑value effect in the amplitudes—and how the new encoding plus RQAE fix this on test problems, indicating a careful diagnostic of algorithmic failure modes rather than only showcasing successful cases.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-026, C-030, C-032]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper highlights that the efficiency of the state‑preparation oracle is a key determinant of end‑to‑end performance in QAMC, and that RQAE’s tunable parameter q introduces an explicit trade‑off between circuit depth and convergence speed, offering a knob for adapting to different hardware constraints.
    [codes: C-015, C-033]

=== PAPER 5f1b1731f44b (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum financial modeling as simulating random walks relevant to asset price dynamics under strict NISQ constraints, emphasizing that effective algorithms are limited by gate depth and compounded noise, and that experiments are currently small due to qubit scarcity and gate inaccuracies. It targets the reproduction of stylized facts such as heavy-tailed return distributions and liquidity–volatility relationships, comparing quantum-generated price-change distributions to stock indices and housing market behavior.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-030, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose approximate quantum counting circuits for quantum walks that deliberately reduce the number of 2‑qubit entangling gates by avoiding exact binary arithmetic. They introduce several design variants: an arc counter using only single‑qubit rotations with higher‑order qubits rotating at half the rate of lower ones, an arc walk that adds a Hadamard ‘coin’ and controlled rotations, a random jump scheme where target qubits are chosen via weighted random sampling introducing both classical and quantum randomness, and cascading disjunction components that propagate lower‑order qubit values upward to preserve progress. Two‑way walks are implemented via separate ‘up’ and ‘down’ circuits combined through classical subtraction, and approximate counting generally trades exact stepwise updates for probabilistic position increments.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that its approximate counting circuits are robust to noise, with ideal vs noisy simulations and QPU runs showing that arc counter and arc walk circuits most reliably produce monotonically increasing positions, while traditional binary counters fail under noise and quickly converge to a random midpoint. Random jump circuits increase on average but tend to plateau and fluctuate, and cascading disjunctions improve the reliability of progress in these walks. Hardware experiments show arc counter results staying close to ideal simulations, and quantum-generated distributions from arc walk and random jump circuits qualitatively match heavy-tailed daily price-change patterns better than normal approximations. The authors also observe that arc counters yield monotonic growth with occasional jumps due to high-order bit measurements, mid-measurement in walks reduces the average distance traveled and suppresses transitions in a Zeno-like fashion, and housing market data reveal that lower liquidity (lower transaction volume) is associated with higher price volatility and larger discrepancies between list and sale prices.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-016, C-017, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classically inspired exact binary positional encoding is used as a baseline, and the authors argue it is too costly and noise-sensitive on NISQ devices because binary full adders require many entangling gates, making quantum counting highly susceptible to 2‑qubit gate errors. In contrast, the arc counter uses no entangling gates and is therefore easy to simulate classically, so the authors explicitly note that it offers no physical quantum advantage despite lower error rates. For two‑way walks, they employ classical post-processing—subtracting ‘down’ from ‘up’ circuit outputs—to achieve bidirectional motion rather than encoding true quantum superposition of directions, and they remark that simple non‑quantum models could also explain the observed housing-market behaviors, underscoring the lack of demonstrated classical outperformance.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-015, C-018, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize several limitations: current NISQ hardware restricts experiments to small scales due to limited qubit availability, high gate error rates (with compounded error estimated at at least 40%), and especially the scarcity and unreliability of 2‑qubit entangling gates. They acknowledge that binary positional encoding is impractical on such hardware because binary adders require many entangling gates, making counting highly vulnerable to noise, and that their arc counter—while low-error—is straightforward to model classically and thus does not provide a physical quantum advantage. They also note that the tuning and appearance of quantum-generated distributions depend on averaging choices, such as number of shots and numbers of random-jump circuits, and that simple non-quantum models can plausibly explain the empirical housing-market correlations, limiting the strength of any uniquely quantum interpretation.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-015, C-031, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work is framed around more rigorous quantitative evaluation of the proposed circuits, particularly by systematically comparing NISQ hardware results with ideal and noisy simulations to understand expected behavior as systems scale. The authors also call for structured comparison of quantum-generated random-walk distributions against real market distributions to assess how well these approximate counting schemes capture empirical financial phenomena.
    [codes: C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing quantum approximate counting circuits for random-walk-based financial modeling that dramatically reduce the use of 2‑qubit entangling gates compared to traditional binary-based quantum counting, and in demonstrating their robustness to noise on NISQ hardware. It further presents specific new circuit families—arc counters with single‑qubit rotations, arc walks with coin-toss dynamics, random jump schemes, and cascading disjunction mechanisms—as alternative encodings tailored to noisy devices, and explores their connection to heavy-tailed financial returns and liquidity–volatility effects.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-030, C-035]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is explicitly NISQ-driven, defining scarce resources to include both qubit count and, critically, the number of 2‑qubit entangling gates, which directly shapes the circuit designs. The authors distinguish between ideal and noisy simulations and provide tabulated comparisons across circuit types, including QPU runs, to support claims about robustness, and they highlight that random jump circuits incorporate both quantum measurement randomness and classical randomness in circuit generation. They note that quantum job results and random-jump outputs are averaged over shots and sampled circuits, indicating sensitivity to these choices, and in the housing-market analysis they compute and interpret empirical correlations, while explicitly conceding that non-quantum explanations remain plausible, which signals some caution about over-interpreting the modeling link.
    [codes: C-008, C-021, C-024, C-029, C-031, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes were incorporated into dimensions 1–8.

=== PAPER 629ad7ff1054 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as modeling financial market dynamics and volatility risk in a way that captures empirically observed deviations from Gaussian random walks, such as excess kurtosis, turbulence, volatility clustering and price jumps. It links price formation to unbalanced market orders decomposed into a binary market polarization component and multiple binary trading-volume-related volatility components, arguing that probabilistic descriptions of such dynamics should incorporate quantum interference terms reflecting cognitively motivated quantum-like decision behavior.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-012]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce Quantum Artificial Neural Networks (QuANNs), specifically recurrent QuANNs arranged as a Quantum Neural Automaton where each market component is modeled by a three‑neuron quantum network that evolves via unitary, conditionally applied single‑neuron gates (phase transforms and rotations) on qubit‑encoded neuron states. The overall market state is represented as a normalized superposition over neural firing patterns, with quantum interference affecting amplitude updates; probabilities are not fixed ex ante but are updated round‑by‑round via a nonlinear deterministic (and, with noisy gates, stochastic) map induced by the quantum dynamics, and noisy unitary gates are further modeled via stochastic Hamiltonians leading to stochastic rotation angles.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030, C-031, C-041, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Simulations of the QuANN-based market model reportedly generate financial turbulence markers, including volatility bursts, clustering volatility and price jumps, along with excess kurtosis in returns distributions over a wide parameter range; the degree of leptokurtosis and turbulence is especially sensitive to the baseline volatility parameter v0 and to the number of volatility components, with higher v0 values tending to suppress excess kurtosis and turbulence. The authors show that expected returns emerge as probability‑weighted averages over eigenvalues of a returns operator, that ensemble averages of projections match projection weights, and that quantum interference in amplitude updates yields nonlinear deterministic probability dynamics; they also claim that introducing noisy quantum gates induces a stochastic nonlinear probability map while having limited impact on the transition between leptokurtic and platykurtic regimes. More broadly, they argue that the same quantum computational structure simultaneously generates nonlinear deterministic dynamics and nonlinear stochastic processes, providing a synthesized description of financial dynamics.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts its quantum market model with the classical Gaussian random walk framework, emphasizing that the empirically relevant excess kurtosis and volatility‑related turbulence constitute statistically significant deviations from Gaussian behavior that motivate the quantum approach. However, it does not report any explicit quantitative benchmarking or computational performance comparison against specific classical econometric or machine‑learning models, instead positioning the quantum model conceptually as an alternative that can reproduce non‑Gaussian features.
    [codes: C-004, C-009, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that even when the simulated returns distribution approximates a Gaussian, this normality is not robust: the Gaussian fit depends on the particular sample path and cannot be assumed as a dynamically fixed probability law holding indefinitely. They further indicate that the model’s parameter regimes can eliminate excess kurtosis and turbulence markers (e.g., at higher v0), implying sensitivity and potential instability in reproducing heavy‑tailed behavior, and they explicitly describe the lack of a stable Gaussian law as a caveat rather than a firm prediction.
    [codes: C-035, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future extensions, the paper proposes allowing the rotation angle in the unitary neuron gates to change stochastically, effectively using stochastic Hamiltonians to model external noise and thereby inducing noisy unitary gates and a stochastic nonlinear map in the probability dynamics, as a way to better capture random external influences on market behavior.
    [codes: C-040, C-041]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is framed as introducing QuANNs—specifically recurrent QuANNs organized as a Quantum Neural Automaton—for financial market dynamics and volatility risk modeling, thereby embedding quantum interference and quantum adaptive computation directly into the probabilistic description of returns. The authors also claim novelty in showing how this quantum AI structure can bridge deterministic nonlinear dynamics and stochastic nonlinear processes in finance, providing a unifying framework that connects quantum cognition–motivated nonlinear probability updates with financial risk modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-023, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper develops a detailed quantum neural formalism: neuron firing states are encoded as qubits in two‑dimensional Hilbert spaces, network states are normalized superpositions, and evolution is governed by conditional unitary link operators with single‑neuron phase and rotation gates, from which explicit transition tables for amplitudes are derived. The probabilistic interpretation is given via projection norms as decision weights and ensemble averages, and the model specifies how returns are represented as eigenvalues of a returns operator and how probabilities are updated round‑by‑round rather than imposed ex ante; at the same time, the work is entirely simulation‑based with synthetic dynamics and does not describe empirical datasets or code release, so reproducibility relies on the analytic update rules rather than shared implementations.

=== PAPER 674c681a57d0 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The report frames the problem as the heavy computational burden of pricing financial derivatives and computing risk measures such as Value at Risk (VaR), which commonly rely on Monte Carlo simulation and PDE solvers, and surveys quantum computing techniques that might accelerate these tasks, with a particular focus on developments since a prior NEASQC deliverable. It also notes a separate line of work that seeks to build quantum-inspired models of financial markets rather than just speeding up classical methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors review several gate-based quantum approaches: (i) quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC), which uses an oracle U to load the path probability distribution and a unitary V to encode the payoff, together with amplitude estimation schemes; (ii) quantum algorithms for PDE-based pricing that map option pricing PDEs to imaginary-time evolution under a Hermitian Hamiltonian and then simulate this evolution variationally on NISQ hardware; and (iii) other approaches such as quantum finance modelling based on a Merton–Schrödinger equation, quantum deep hedging via quantum reinforcement learning layers, and martingale pricing via quantum linear programming and density-operator-based “quantum assets.” All of these are discussed under an explicit NISQ-computing focus because of limits in qubit counts, circuit depth, and noise.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-011, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the algorithmic side, the report emphasizes that quantum amplitude estimation (AE) can in principle reduce the number of oracle calls compared to standard Monte Carlo, while parallel AE variants typically offer better depth control for NISQ devices. However, empirical and theoretical analyses cited in the report show that even low-strength noise can prevent achieving the quadratic speedup, with error saturating beyond a certain number of Grover applications, and that linear AE schedules tend to perform best under realistic noise. The report also highlights that approximate state loading may yield lower overall error than exact loading on noisy hardware, that engineered likelihood functions combined with Bayesian inference improve performance over conventional likelihoods, and that a variational PDE solver for option pricing can be implemented with poly(d·log(1/ε)) few-qubit gates on small quantum computers.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-034, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The report repeatedly benchmarks quantum proposals against classical Monte Carlo and PDE methods: Monte Carlo is described as the de facto industry standard because it is easy to implement, general, and scales well with dimension, while PDE solvers can converge faster in low-dimensional cases. Quantum amplitude estimation is presented as promising a quadratic reduction in required samples/oracle calls versus classical Monte Carlo in ideal conditions, and some PDE-based quantum solvers are said to potentially offer exponential speedups in very specific cases, though the authors stress that most of the observed performance improvements in recent work are only up to constant factors rather than changes in asymptotic scaling. They also caution that when realistic noise and error correction are taken into account, the effective speedup over classical methods may disappear for all practical instance sizes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-019, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors enumerate multiple limitations. Hardware-wise, current NISQ devices suffer from limited qubit counts, restricted circuit depths, and significant noise, which motivates focusing on shallow, NISQ-compatible algorithms and leads to observations such as noise being the main limiting factor in AE experiments and the saturation of error improvements beyond a small number of Grover iterations. Methodologically, unitary-synthesis-based initialization is only applicable when the payoff evolution can be represented as a unitary, and initialization procedures must preserve relative phases—something that variational methods risk violating by introducing arbitrary phases. Both parallel and sequential MLAE approaches exhibit fundamental issues: depth limits on NISQ hardware stop error reduction beyond a certain point; critical points can make MLAE estimators biased and prevent further error reduction even without noise. For PDE-based quantum pricing, extracting a single amplitude in high-dimensional grids becomes a readout bottleneck that can eliminate any theoretical quantum advantage. Quantum deep hedging is constrained by the need for at least one qubit per time step and additional challenges when modelling rough paths. Finally, in a longer-term, fault-tolerant regime, the authors argue that the overhead of error correction may render quadratic speedups ineffective by pushing the problem sizes at which any speedup appears into an impractically large regime.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-037, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Looking ahead, the report suggests that near-term practical benefits from quantum computing in pricing and VaR may come less from speedups and more from reductions in energy consumption, implying an agenda of studying energy–accuracy trade-offs for quantum versus classical methods. The authors also implicitly point to further research on NISQ-friendly techniques such as approximate state loading, improved amplitude estimation under noise, and more efficient variational PDE solvers, though they do not lay out a detailed roadmap.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Conceptually, the survey highlights that several quantum algorithms offer asymptotic advantages: quadratic improvements for Monte Carlo-style integration and risk metric estimation via quantum amplitude estimation, potential exponential scaling benefits for quantum linear-systems-based PDE solvers and certain convex optimization formulations, and polynomial or higher speedups in various machine learning and generative modeling tasks (e.g., quantum k-means, quantum Bayesian networks, quantum GANs). Experimentally, it reports hardware demonstrations of risk analysis using QAE on superconducting devices, reverse quantum annealing for portfolio optimization that yields orders-of-magnitude reductions in time-to-solution relative to forward annealing, and a NISQ-adapted HHL-style portfolio solver on trapped-ion hardware that reduces circuit resources while sacrificing formal asymptotic speedups. Across these, the authors emphasize that observed performance gains are either theoretical, heuristic, or limited to small toy instances rather than full-scale financial problems.

In regression, convex portfolio optimization, spectral clustering, Bayesian inference, and various quantum ML models, the quantum methods are presented as enhancements to classical linear algebra or optimization routines rather than outright replacements, often assuming access models similar to those in classical oracle-based analyses. Hardware case studies compare quantum implementations to classical Monte Carlo or heuristic optimizers (e.g., genetic algorithms in portfolio optimization), framing any empirical advantage as problem- and instance-specific rather than universal.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The survey is explicit that practical quantum advantage in finance has not yet been demonstrated, emphasizing that current NISQ hardware is noisy, limited in circuit depth, constrained by qubit connectivity and gate-speed/fidelity tradeoffs, and therefore unable to solve real-life-scale financial problems more efficiently and accurately than classical systems. It underscores methodological limitations: variational and annealing approaches are fundamentally heuristic; many QLSA- and quantum-ML-based speedups rely on strong data-loading and oracle assumptions; nonlinear PDEs usually require linearization to fit QLSA; and path-dependent derivatives pose complexity for both classical and quantum pricing. The paper further notes that data movement between classical and quantum devices and efficient state preparation are critical bottlenecks; that some experiments, such as QAE-based risk analysis, cannot achieve practical advantage on NISQ devices; and that near-term HHL variants trade away formal asymptotic speedups for implementability. === PAPER 69b8b36d8aad (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets end‑to‑end quantitative risk management, framing three core finance problems for quantum computation: (i) tail‑risk estimation of VaR/CVaR via quantum amplitude estimation on a loss distribution, (ii) systemic risk monitoring on an exposure network via entanglement and purity observables, and (iii) risk‑aware portfolio optimization formulated as a constrained binary optimization problem with risk‑adjusted objectives. These are motivated by classical bottlenecks in Monte Carlo VaR/CVaR, stress testing, and network cascade modeling.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-010, C-013, C-014, C-016]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Methodologically, the framework combines three quantum submodules: QRAE encodes the loss distribution via amplitude encoding and uses amplitude estimation plus binary search and conditional estimation to compute VaR and CVaR; QSRA encodes the financial exposure network as a bipartite entangled state, measures node‑wise reduced‑density‑matrix purity (via a SWAP‑test circuit), and formulates cascade‑mitigating partitions as a QAOA‑compatible Ising model; VQRO uses a basis‑encoded binary optimization Hamiltonian with a quantum‑enhanced risk matrix derived from two‑qubit parameterized entangled states, optimized by a variational circuit with constraint‑aware penalties. The paper provides explicit circuit architectures for each module and an integrated algorithm with phased execution.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that QRAE attains quadratic sample‑complexity scaling O(1/ε log 1/δ) versus classical Monte Carlo and, empirically, reduces sampling requirements for VaR/CVaR by up to about 55×–150× at ε≈0.01 on a 15‑asset portfolio (45–83 amplitude‑estimation calls vs thousands of classical samples), with mean absolute error around 0.008–0.009 and most estimates within one standard deviation. QSRA shows a theoretical correspondence between purity responses and contagion path‑sums and achieves higher AUC (0.847) for early‑warning classification than centrality baselines, as well as analytic bounds on detection sensitivity. VQRO is shown to converge under stochastic gradient descent at O(1/√T) for convex surrogates and yields improved out‑of‑sample Sharpe ratios (1.23±0.087) and risk metrics relative to classical mean‑variance and equal‑weight portfolios, supported by penalty and feasibility bounds. The integrated QRMF is claimed to maintain bounded cross‑component error propagation, to achieve an information coefficient of 0.34 vs 0.22 for standalone components, and to obtain statistically significant improvements (p<0.01) in Sharpe ratios. Error‑mitigation analysis yields formal robustness bounds and empirical error reductions of about 73%, while the quantum risk matrix exhibits stronger correlation with realized financial metrics than classical correlations.
    [codes: C-002, C-006, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Throughout, the quantum methods are benchmarked against classical baselines: QRAE’s sample complexity O(1/ε log 1/δ) is explicitly contrasted with Monte Carlo’s O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)), and empirical results report large reductions in required samples for comparable VaR/CVaR accuracy. For systemic risk, purity‑based monitors and QAOA‑based partitioning are compared to degree, eigenvector, and betweenness centrality as well as modularity‑based methods, showing higher AUC and greater cascade‑size reduction. In portfolio optimization, the quantum‑enhanced optimizer’s Sharpe ratio and other performance metrics are compared to classical mean‑variance and naive benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements. At the workflow level, the authors note that the quantum pipeline currently has longer total runtime (47 minutes) than a classical workflow (≈12–26 minutes), but they argue the classical workflow offers reduced accuracy and less comprehensive risk coverage.
    [codes: C-002, C-020, C-021, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-047]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The discussion acknowledges several implementation limitations: counterdiabatic schedules are only emulated and not yet realizable on available QPUs due to limited API support and programmability; quantum risk modeling currently relies on two‑qubit proxies for higher‑dimensional entanglement, simplifying the risk matrix construction but limiting expressiveness; and embedding overhead plus circuit‑depth growth pose practical scalability challenges, with the authors estimating that near‑term hardware likely caps portfolio sizes at roughly 20–50 assets despite theoretical asymptotic advantages. Near‑term scalability is further bounded by current circuit depths (<300 gates) and asset universes up to about 20 instruments.
    [codes: C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions include implementing counterdiabatic protocols directly on quantum hardware, extending quantum risk metrics beyond two‑qubit proxies to multi‑qubit measures with efficient estimation, developing more advanced embedding strategies to handle larger and denser financial networks, and incorporating more realistic trading frictions and regulatory constraints into the risk‑optimization framework.
    [codes: C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its main novelty a unified three‑module Quantum Risk Management Framework that jointly integrates quantum amplitude estimation for VaR/CVaR (QRAE), entanglement‑based systemic risk analytics (QSRA), and a constraint‑aware variational quantum risk optimizer (VQRO) into a single risk workflow, along with formal complexity theorems under explicit QRAM/QROM cost models, convergence guarantees for the variational component, and coupling bounds that ensure stability of the integrated system. The authors also emphasize the introduction of purity‑based early‑warning observables and QAOA‑based cascade‑mitigation partitioning, as well as the construction and empirical validation of a quantum risk matrix derived from entanglement features.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-008, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work places emphasis on formalism and empirical design: it defines risk measures like VaR precisely and formulates quantum encodings and observables (loss amplitude encoding, bipartite entanglement encodings, node‑specific reduced density matrices and purities) with explicit mathematical detail. The authors highlight rigorous cost modeling, comprehensive error analysis, and validated experimental protocols across modules, including theoretical complexity and convergence bounds, penalty conditions for feasibility, and error‑mitigation guarantees. The empirical studies use real‑market daily data for a 15‑asset universe with a clear in‑sample/out‑of‑sample split, and they report statistical significance (paired t‑tests with p<0.01) for performance improvements. Circuit‑level architectures are specified for each quantum component, and the integrated algorithm is described phase‑by‑phase, though some advanced elements (e.g., counterdiabatic schedules) remain in emulation only.

=== PAPER 69bfce9095d0 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the challenge of efficiently encoding financial market data—specifically stock prices and returns—into quantum states so that quantities like SVD entropy of the stock correlation matrix can be computed for applications such as risk management, asset allocation, and market forecasting. It formulates the problem as preparing a |data⟩ state carrying a matrix of normalised log-returns from which a stock density matrix and its SVD entropy can be derived on a quantum computer.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose using the GASP (Genetic Algorithm for State Preparation) framework to generate low-depth approximate amplitude-encoding circuits for the |data⟩ state, which are then integrated into a variational QSVD pipeline. The method constructs a joint stock–time statevector, extracts the stock density matrix via a partial trace, and applies a VQSVD procedure that uses parameterised circuits U(θ) and V(θ′) to map Schmidt bases to the computational basis while minimising a Hamming-distance-based cost function. GASP circuits are compared against qGAN-based encoders and AAE, which respectively learn probability distributions and full real-valued amplitudes via variational training with MMD-based costs, and the full GASP+QSVD circuit is executed on both simulators and real hardware in a NISQ-relevant, low-depth regime.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-007, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that GASP-generated circuits achieve improved fidelity and efficiency in encoding stock price data, and that these circuits are shallow enough to be feasible on actual hardware. Across rolling five‑month windows and a range of target fidelities, higher-fidelity GASP encodings yield more accurate singular values than qGAN and AAE, leading to better reconstruction of the correlation matrix and SVD entropy estimates; however, the accuracy of SVD entropy shows minimal improvement beyond about 90% state-preparation fidelity, indicating diminishing returns from pushing fidelity toward perfection. The authors conclude that approximate state preparation at around 90% fidelity can maintain accurate SVD entropy estimates while keeping resource usage modest.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-012, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: As baselines, the work evaluates qGAN and AAE-based state-preparation methods and finds that, for higher target fidelities, GASP circuits produce more accurate singular values and improved correlation-matrix reconstruction relative to these alternatives. The paper frames these comparisons in terms of downstream SVD entropy accuracy rather than direct classical runtime speedups.
    [codes: C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that exact state-synthesis techniques often generate circuits with depths that are infeasible on current hardware and that ancilla-based methods are constrained by limited qubit counts, motivating their focus on approximate, low-depth state preparation. They further note that achieving very high fidelities (e.g., 99%) with GASP incurs substantially higher time and gate costs—especially in CNOT and total gate counts—than generating ~90% fidelity circuits, while offering only marginal improvements in SVD entropy accuracy; they suggest that, in practice, the diminishing returns associated with perfect state preparation may not justify the additional resource expenditure.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper states that its findings on approximate state preparation for SVD entropy in financial correlation matrices open avenues for further research and practical implementation in quantum finance, implying future extensions to more complex indicators, larger datasets, and real-world financial workflows.
    [codes: C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is presented as extending prior approximate amplitude-encoding work for financial market indicators by using the GASP framework to engineer low-depth, hardware-feasible |data⟩ preparation circuits and integrating them with a QSVD-based entropy estimation pipeline. The authors emphasise that GASP can enhance both fidelity and efficiency of encoding relative to existing generative and amplitude-encoding approaches, while still respecting NISQ constraints.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-012]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds a clear data pipeline: monthly opening prices for four stocks (XOM, WMT, PG, MSFT) are retrieved from Yahoo Finance over March 2008–March 2009, log-returns are computed and normalised to form a matrix used to construct a positive semidefinite, normalised correlation matrix whose properties underpin the SVD entropy definition. These data are encoded into a 4-qubit |data⟩ state, and experiments are repeated across all possible five‑month windows and multiple GASP target fidelities, with circuits run on both simulators and real hardware, suggesting a structured but small-scale, proof‑of‑concept design.
    [codes: C-004, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all codes were integrated into the other dimensions.
