=== PAPER 6b2b4f6ba298 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a broad range of portfolio optimization and risk-management tasks as convex conic programs—specifically LP, SOCP, and SDP formulations—and then reduces these optimization problems to sequences of feasibility problems suitable for multiplicative-weights–based solvers. It catalogues standard portfolio problems (including mean–variance, CVaR, and Sharpe-ratio optimization) according to whether they are LP/SOCP/SDP-representable, and highlights a quasi-convex Sharpe-ratio formulation that can be reduced to SOCP feasibility via bisection.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-011, C-016, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The methodological core is a multiplicative-weights (MW) framework for conic feasibility, interpreted in the matrix setting where MW updates produce Gibbs states of accumulated losses, with explicit use of matrix Gibbs states ρ(H) = e^{-βH}/Tr(e^{-βH}). For SOCPs, the authors design a specialized MW feasibility algorithm that exploits Lorentz-cone arrowhead matrix embeddings and their low-rank spectrum, and then discuss classical and quantum Gibbs-state preparation options, including a proposed quantum MW variant that aims to leverage faster Gibbs preparation under favorable input models.
    [codes: C-002, C-018, C-020, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the paper provides regret bounds and iteration complexity for MW in both SDP and SOCP settings, showing that matrix MW finds ε-feasible SDP solutions in T = O(R^2 log d / ε^2) iterations and that the specialized SOCP MW algorithm achieves T = O(R^2 log N / ε^2). It derives detailed spectral and Gibbs-state structure for Lorentz cone arrowhead matrices—including explicit eigenvalues, a rank-two nontrivial Gibbs component, and the irrelevance of identity shifts—which leads to O(N) total Gibbs computation using stable asymptotic formulas in low-temperature regimes. The comparison table reports that quantum MW could in principle scale in iterations as O(√r / ε^2), in contrast to classical MW’s O(R^2 / ε^2), and the analysis clarifies how conditioning and width parameters affect MW convergence.
    [codes: C-003, C-019, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-040, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare MW-based solvers with classical interior-point methods (IPMs), summarizing that classical MW requires O(R^2 / ε^2) iterations, while IPMs typically need O(√r log(1/ε)) iterations with higher per-iteration cost. They also argue that exploiting SOCP-specific arrowhead structure yields O(N) classical Gibbs-state computation versus O(N^3) for naive dense SDP embeddings, and note that for cardinality-constrained problems, practical experience suggests mixed-integer solvers like Gurobi or CPLEX are often fastest up to moderate asset counts (n ≤ 500).
    [codes: C-022, C-031, C-043, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper emphasizes several limitations and caveats. First, the SOCP MW efficiency relies on an oracle that returns violation certificates preserving the arrowhead matrix structure; losing this structure would undermine the low-rank Gibbs advantage. Second, the claimed quantum SOCP speedup is explicitly labeled as informal and theoretical, and its practical relevance depends critically on strong data-access assumptions, such as sample-and-query models that may not always hold in financial datasets. Third, MW performance is sensitive to problem conditioning and the choice of learning rate: poorly scaled constraints inflate the width parameter and slow convergence, while an excessively large or small learning rate can respectively cause instability or slow progress. Finally, cardinality-constrained mean–variance optimization is NP-hard, and the authors note that even with SDP relaxations, mixed-integer methods may be more practical at realistic portfolio sizes, highlighting complexity barriers for sparse portfolios.
    [codes: C-032, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future directions, the authors highlight extending the conic/Gibbs framework toward discrete portfolio constraints—particularly cardinality constraints—via SDP relaxations, while acknowledging associated complexity barriers and the need for practical implementation guidance. They also imply that further work is needed to understand and realize the informal quantum SOCP speedups under realistic financial data-access models.
    [codes: C-009, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in unifying a wide class of portfolio construction problems under conic (LP/SOCP/SDP) formulations and connecting them to multiplicative-weights methods that generate Gibbs states, with an emphasis on Jordan-algebraic exponentials for symmetric cones. It presents a finance-forward catalog of conic-representable portfolio problems, including a Sharpe-ratio formulation reducible to SOCP feasibility, and develops a SOCP-specific MW algorithm with complete proofs, explicit complexity bounds, and detailed algorithmic specifications. The authors further claim that exploiting the Lorentz-cone arrowhead structure yields low-rank Gibbs decompositions that improve both classical and prospective quantum Gibbs-state preparation for financial conic optimization.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-029]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is analytical rather than empirical: the authors emphasize providing complete proofs of all key results, explicit complexity bounds, and detailed algorithmic specifications suitable for implementation. They analyze the impact of conditioning on MW via the width parameter and offer practical guidance on scaling and whitening, as well as on numerically stable computation of arrowhead Gibbs states using asymptotic formulas. The paper also discusses the choice of MW learning rate and compares MW’s theoretical complexity to interior-point methods in a structured way, but it does not report numerical experiments or benchmark datasets.
    [codes: C-005, C-014, C-040, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates LP, SOCP, and SDP within a symmetric cone hierarchy and notes that finance covariance matrices often exhibit factor structure that preserves sparsity, potentially helping with data access and sampling for both classical and quantum methods. It also observes that certain financial data, such as factor-structured covariance matrices, may naturally support sample-and-query access models beneficial for quantum algorithms, and reiterates that Gibbs states in the MW framework arise from accumulated loss operators, highlighting a conceptual bridge between online learning and thermodynamic-like structures.
    [codes: C-012, C-014, C-034, C-039]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is relevant to risk_management because it gives conic-program formulations and solver machinery for CVaR and Sharpe-ratio problems, both central to downside-risk measurement and risk-adjusted performance. It also highlights feasibility-based reductions and complexity caveats that matter when risk models must be solved repeatedly or under practical data-access constraints.
    [silo_relevance_score: high]
  KEY_POINT 1: CVaR is explicitly reformulated as a linear program, making a core risk metric directly compatible with the paper’s conic optimization framework.
    [codes: C-016, C-001, C-006  dim_source: dimension_1]
  KEY_POINT 2: Sharpe-ratio optimization is reduced to SOCP feasibility via bisection, giving a structured way to solve a risk-adjusted performance problem.

=== PAPER 6f139839ae4c (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies whether a quantum reservoir computing (QRC) architecture can tackle statistical and financially motivated classification and regression tasks, including identifying the underlying distribution of i.i.d. samples, estimating tail-heaviness, and detecting volatility regimes in time series. Concretely, it formulates three problems: binary discrimination between Normal and Laplace distributions given T samples, regression of Student‑t degrees of freedom from samples to capture heavy tails, and multi-class classification of GARCH(1,1) time series into three persistence bands relevant for volatility regime identification in economics and finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use an analog quantum reservoir computing scheme implemented in a model of two superconducting islands coupled via their charge degrees of freedom, whose effective low‑energy description is a Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian with Josephson junctions providing the key nonlinearity. The circuit is operated in the transmon regime EJ ≫ EC, enabling a rotating‑wave approximation, and data are encoded as analog inputs through the gate voltage; numerical simulations truncate each bosonic mode at occupancy nc = 5, with open‑system dynamics treated via a density‑matrix Lindblad evolution including decay at rates chosen to be realistic for current superconducting devices. Features are obtained by statistical pooling of selected occupation probabilities (avoiding full state tomography), and a classical linear readout is trained by pseudo‑inverse to produce task outputs evaluated via accuracy for classification and RMSE for regression.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across all three tasks, the simulations show that the QRC can accurately classify complex distributions (including heavy‑tailed ones) and identify volatility regimes in correlated time series, exhibiting particularly strong performance when only short sequences are available. For Normal vs. Laplace discrimination, both QRC and the classical GLRT display stretched‑exponential accuracy scaling with T, with QRC competitive overall but converging to a slightly lower asymptotic accuracy than the classical test. For Student‑t parameter regression, QRC achieves systematically lower RMSE than the likelihood‑based baseline over a broad interval of T, with errors decaying approximately as a power law T^-p with exponent near 0.5, consistent with central‑limit scaling. In GARCH band classification, QRC yields a clear advantage for short and moderately short time series but becomes comparable to or slightly outperformed by the classical method at large T, and its accuracy vs‑T curve exhibits a peculiar swing, which the authors tentatively link to the intrinsic time correlations in GARCH models. Summarizing across tasks, the authors report that QRC improves over classical algorithms in the limited‑data regime, whereas classical methods marginally dominate when abundant data are available.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QRC’s performance is systematically compared against strong classical baselines: a generalized likelihood ratio test for Normal vs. Laplace classification, likelihood‑based estimation for Student‑t parameters, and a feature‑based supervised classifier for GARCH regime bands. In the Normal–Laplace task, QRC is reported as competitive with GLRT and particularly strong at small T, but GLRT achieves higher asymptotic accuracy for large T, with both methods following stretched‑exponential convergence. For Student‑t regression, QRC shows a systematic RMSE advantage over the likelihood protocol across a broad range of T, even though both exhibit similar power‑law scaling exponents near 0.5. In GARCH band classification, QRC again provides a benefit for short and moderately short time series, while at the largest T the classical classifier slightly exceeds QRC, albeit with overlapping error bars. Overall, the authors explicitly summarize that QRC improves on classical algorithms in the limited‑data regime but is marginally outperformed when the amount of data is large.
    [codes: C-006, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and caveats. Numerically, they truncate each bosonic mode at occupancy nc = 5 to keep simulations feasible, and they explicitly note that this cutoff may prevent them from capturing stronger nonlinear evolution, especially since the Bose–Hubbard model itself may break down for larger cutoffs where a rotor model would be needed. Conceptually, they emphasize that there is no general theoretical guarantee that QRC will saturate to unit accuracy in the infinite‑data limit, consistent with their empirical finding that classical methods can ultimately outperform QRC at large T. Regarding hardware, they argue that there is no need to push coherence times much further because QRC can benefit from moderate noise, but this also implies a trade‑off between reservoir memory and decoherence, particularly in time‑correlated tasks such as GARCH classification.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-025, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose running their QRC algorithm on real superconducting hardware to exploit reservoirs with a much larger Hilbert space and a larger effective number of neurons, which they expect would improve performance. They also suggest algorithmic and architectural enhancements, including adding more nonlinearities to the reservoir dynamics and exploring architectures with all‑to‑all couplings, as well as refining the implementation on actual devices to better leverage these extensions.
    [codes: C-008, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its main contribution as a numerical demonstration that a physically realistic superconducting‑circuit QRC, built from two Josephson‑junction islands modeled by a Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian, can tackle nontrivial statistical and financial tasks, including classification of heavy‑tailed and correlated data and volatility regime identification, with performance that can outperform strong classical methods in limited‑information regimes. They further claim that the observed robustness and even potential benefit from moderate noise indicates that QRC can serve as a noise‑resilient quantum learning approach suitable for realistic near‑term superconducting platforms.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-021, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is based on open‑system density‑matrix simulations using a Lindblad master equation with decay rates calibrated to be reasonable for current superconducting circuits, which enables explicit treatment of decoherence and exploration of noise effects. The feature extraction relies on statistical pooling of measured occupation probabilities in a truncated bosonic subspace, and the readout is a simple linear layer trained via Moore–Penrose pseudo‑inverse, making the learning pipeline transparent and easy to reproduce in principle. The authors note that full state tomography is not required—only occupation probabilities of selected reservoir states—highlighting a practical consideration for experimental implementation. They also report that QRC is robust to and can even benefit from moderate amounts of noise, and they offer a qualitative interpretation of the trade‑off between time correlations and noise‑induced decay in the GARCH task, while acknowledging numerical truncation choices and providing quantitative scaling analyses of performance versus sample size.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-045]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes were assigned to other dimensions.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 71dc25d5ac6a (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the problem of estimating financial crashes and distress propagation in a network of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that are customers of a Turkish bank, motivated by the need for accurate and timely crash estimation to preserve stability and mitigate risk. It formulates this as a nonlinear, quadratically constrained quadratic optimization problem on an SME network, capturing domino-style contagion effects and multiple equilibrium points in firms’ market values and failures.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-011, C-035, C-036, C-048, C-050]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use D-Wave’s hybrid constrained quadratic model (CQM) solvers to tackle the QCQP formulation, arguing that CQM is a good fit due to constraints, high complexity, and integer decision variables. Quantum computing is used within this hybrid framework to explore the solution space and obtain decision variables indicating firms’ likelihood of financial distress, with repeated runs necessitated by randomness in the quantum processing mechanism and the presence of multiple equilibrium points.
    [codes: C-004, C-020, C-022, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-038, C-042]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On 2019 financial data, the model identifies 90.04 million TL of non-performing loans out of 107 million TL and reports an overall prediction accuracy of about 91.2%, with quarterly accuracy figures also reported. Using D-Wave’s hybrid solver, the authors state they can obtain a feasible solution in roughly 7 seconds of solve time, and they present concrete examples of failure propagation between firms in the network, such as firm D’s failure increasing its own and another firm’s unpaid debt.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-010, C-039, C-045, C-049]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper claims that classical computing solutions to this type of crash-estimation problem would be computationally infeasible, citing an estimate of 13.7 billion years of runtime for classical methods on similar problems. In contrast, the hybrid quantum approach reportedly solves the formulated optimization problem in seconds, though the extreme classical runtime figure is drawn from prior literature rather than measured directly in this study.
    [codes: C-006, C-012, C-019, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: inadequate and incomplete financial information and inter-firm relations in the available data constrain the quality and feasibility of the constructed networks and require post-processing of equilibrium points. The hybrid solver exhibits sensitivity to solve time: shorter-than-recommended times yield infeasible solutions with constraint violations, while longer runtimes do not improve results beyond obtaining feasible solutions. They also note the stochasticity of the quantum processing mechanism and multiple equilibrium points, necessitating repeated runs, and argue that standard machine learning metrics like precision and recall are not meaningful for evaluating their model, which restricts the evaluation toolkit.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-050, C-051]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include improving data quality by more frequent and complete collection of companies’ trial balances, expanding the network to include large companies alongside SMEs for more realistic projections, and enhancing the statistical modeling by involving domain experts and incorporating more diverse financial documents beyond trial balances.
    [codes: C-053, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as a pioneering, interdisciplinary demonstration of the applicability of quantum computing to one of the most challenging problems in finance—predicting financial crashes in complex SME networks—and suggest that combining quantum optimization with financial network modeling has the potential to improve the robustness and reliability of crash predictions for practitioners and policymakers.
    [codes: C-013, C-015, C-016]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper constructs an SME network from proprietary bank financial records, selecting nodes based on database analysis and classifying customers into three risk types (including NPL and watchlist categories) defined by payment delay thresholds. It introduces detailed model parameters such as crossholding ratios and self-holdings, binary failure indicators, and integer-restricted market values, with an equilibrium-based objective and constraints linking failures to value thresholds. For evaluation, the authors reject classical ML metrics in favor of real unpaid debt as the primary metric, focusing on end-of-year quarters because they provide more comprehensive financial statements and validating model predictions against unpaid debts observed in subsequent quarters of 2020. They also use a dependency matrix to visualize and interpret cascade effects, and repeat each solver configuration multiple times due to stochasticity and multiple equilibria.
    [codes: C-024, C-025, C-026, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047, C-048]

=== PAPER 76ee3cb38743 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets high-dimensional Monte Carlo integration problems in finance where computing a single sample requires many similar per-dimension or per-obligor operations, exemplified by credit portfolio risk measurement in a Merton-style setting. It formalizes a class of integrals with separable structure F(ε_com, {ε_i}; {c_i}) = g(∑_{i=1}^D f(ε_com, ε_i; c_i)), and argues that credit portfolio loss integrands fit this separable form. The aim is to exploit this structure, together with pseudorandom numbers, to reduce the cost of repeated calculations over dimensions/obligors in quantum Monte Carlo integration.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-013, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors build on quantum amplitude estimation (QAE)–based Monte Carlo integration using amplitude encoding, then introduce a new nested QAE scheme tailored to separable integrands. Their method uses pseudorandom numbers (PRNs) so that a quantum circuit takes an index i as input and produces the corresponding term f(…) in superposition, enabling quantum-parallel evaluation over terms; an inner QAE sums contributions over term indices, and an outer QAE estimates the sample average over j. They rely on a PCG-based PRN generator with a jump formula to implement a jump operator that can directly access PRN states associated with arbitrary indices without sequential progression, and they adopt T-count as the main gate-based cost metric in their analysis.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-011, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-024, C-025]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Analytically, the paper reiterates that QAE yields a quadratic reduction in oracle calls versus classical Monte Carlo, with O(δ⁻¹) versus O(δ⁻²) scaling for a target error δ. For the separable integrand setting, the proposed method reduces calls to the per-term circuit from O(D) to O(δ⁻¹), i.e., a reduction factor of roughly O(δ⁻¹/D), at the cost that the inner QAE produces an approximate per-sample sum S_j with a sharply peaked but not exact value. Comparing total T-counts for a concrete credit portfolio setup, they estimate that despite a higher per–f-evaluation cost, the overall T-count can be reduced by a factor on the order of 0.64, i.e., several tens of percent, in a typical high-dimensional credit risk configuration.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-010, C-016, C-019, C-021, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper contrasts its nested-QAE-based method with both classical Monte Carlo and a previous quantum PRN-based scheme that performs simple sequential summation. Relative to classical Monte Carlo, it relies on the standard QAE result that oracle-call complexity improves from O(δ⁻²) to O(δ⁻¹). Relative to the previous PRN-based quantum method, where contributions f(ε_com, ε_i; c_i) are evaluated and summed exactly and sequentially over i, the new method replaces exact iteration with QAE-based summation over i and j, reducing the number of f-evaluations when δ⁻¹ ≲ D but making each f-evaluation more expensive in T-count due to jump-operator overhead.
    [codes: C-001, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-027, C-029]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize several limitations and caveats. First, their new method applies only when the integrand is separable into a sum over terms, which restricts the class of financial problems it can handle. Second, it depends critically on PRNs and on having an efficient jump formula for the PRN generator; jump formulas can be significantly more costly than recursive progression, so the per-call cost of f may increase substantially. Third, the inner QAE introduces approximation error: per-sample sums S_j are not exact but concentrated distributions around the true value, and to keep this error small a sufficiently large inner-QAE register is required, with M > (l δ_rel)⁻¹ as a stated condition. Fourth, the authors explicitly warn that even when the number of f-evaluations is reduced (e.g., when δ⁻¹ ≲ D), the total wall-clock runtime or T-count might not decrease because of the expensive jump operations and deeper circuits. Finally, they note that earlier PRN-based quantum Monte Carlo methods traded qubit savings for increased circuit depth, underscoring an ongoing depth-versus-qubit resource tension in their approach as well.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-009, C-012, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors state that future work will explore alternative ways to exploit the structural properties of pseudorandom sequences beyond the specific nested-QAE construction presented, with the goal of making quantum Monte Carlo algorithms more efficient.
    [codes: C-031]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution claimed is a QAE-based Monte Carlo method that explicitly speeds up a previously overlooked type of repeated computation in high-dimensional integrals: repeated, similar calculations over separated terms such as per-obligor loss contributions. By requiring a separable integrand and leveraging PRN-based indexing, they introduce a nested QAE that performs quantum-parallel evaluation over term indices and samples, theoretically reducing the number of calls to the expensive per-term circuit in regimes where the dimension D exceeds the inverse error tolerance. They further claim a concrete, finance-specific example—credit portfolio risk measurement using a PCG PRN generator—where this structural speedup translates into an estimated several-tens-of-percent reduction in total T-count.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is fully analytical: it reviews the standard QAE-based Monte Carlo framework using amplitude encoding, then extends an earlier PRN-based quantum Monte Carlo approach. The evaluation relies on asymptotic query counts and detailed T-count models for specific circuit components (PRN progression/jump, digital arithmetic, and inverse CDF implementations) to compare the previous and new methods. No empirical quantum hardware runs, noise models, or datasets are used; instead, a stylized credit portfolio with specified bit-width parameters serves as a theoretical testbed for the T-count comparison.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-018, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None.
    [codes: —]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as an evolutionary computing paradigm aimed at addressing complex, data- and computation-intensive problems in financial services, particularly in banking, insurance, high-frequency trading, and fraud/risk management. It formulates finance problems mainly as constrained and uncertain optimization, targeting three application groups: targeting and prediction (personalized services, fraud detection), trading optimization (portfolio rebalancing, derivatives valuation), and risk profiling (scenario simulations under regulatory pressure).
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-046, C-053, C-054, C-061, C-067, C-081]

It discusses quantum logic gates, entangling gates, and system-level characteristics such as coherence time, connectivity, gate fidelity, and logical (error-corrected) qubits as key elements in realizing useful financial applications, and it notes superconducting and trapped-ion/atom-based qubits as primary hardware approaches.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-065]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: As a conceptual review, the paper reports no experimental or quantitative quantum results; instead it presents speculative performance claims. It asserts that entanglement and superposition can yield much higher speed and lower energy use than classical computers, that several computational issues could be solved more efficiently with quantum algorithms, and that as few as ~50 high-quality qubits could run certain algorithms in minutes. In finance, the authors claim that quantum computing could enlarge solution spaces beyond supercomputers, nearly double "power" with each added qubit, improve pattern discovery for targeting and prediction, enhance portfolio diversification and rebalancing, streamline settlement, accelerate and improve risk simulations, and improve investment gains, reduce capital needs, create new investment opportunities, and strengthen fraud, risk, and compliance management.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-014, C-018, C-028, C-030, C-037, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-060, C-065, C-066, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-073, C-074, C-080, C-081]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast quantum and classical computing primarily at a conceptual level, arguing that classical machines encode information strictly in 0/1 bits, which restricts their ability and leads to intractability for certain combinatorial problems, whereas qubits can exist in multiple states simultaneously and be entangled. They claim quantum computers process data differently, excel at complex simulations and data analysis, and have solution spaces orders of magnitude larger than even supercomputers, while also emphasizing that everyday office applications may not see speedups. They further contend that some problems may never be solvable by traditional computers regardless of time, highlighting combinatorial growth of variables as a bottleneck that quantum approaches can mitigate by not testing all solutions sequentially.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges multiple limitations and caveats. On hardware, it notes that quantum computers are difficult and expensive to manufacture, require ultra-cold environments, and involve fragile quantum states where even minor disturbances cause decoherence and destroy computation; all operations must complete before decoherence, and gate errors accumulate quickly, so low gate fidelity and limited gate depth can render large qubit counts relatively useless. Architecturally, superconducting systems are constrained by physical adjacency of qubits, and identical qubits plus sufficient fidelity (roughly enabling n×n gates for n qubits) are needed for useful computation. Application-wise, the authors explicitly state that quantum computing will not speed up routine applications such as Word or Excel, that real-time behavioral analytics and accurate fraud detection are currently difficult with existing systems (e.g., high false positives, slow onboarding), and that Monte Carlo-based risk models are constrained by error scaling. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses consumer credit card default prediction, described as a critical capability for credit card issuers, focusing on industrial‑scale, high‑dimensional, temporally correlated datasets with severe class imbalance and a target of predicting default within the next 18 months. The authors frame the problem as a supervised binary classification task on an anonymized public competition dataset, evaluated mainly via a Composite Default Risk (CDR) metric that combines normalized Gini and default capture rate at 4%. They motivate exploring quantum–classical hybrids because such datasets challenge the scalability and performance of traditional classical algorithms.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses a hybrid quantum–classical approach based on quantum feature maps that encode classical data into an n‑qubit Hilbert space, followed by projective measurements to obtain projected quantum features (PQFs) which are then fed into classical models and ensembles. Specifically, the authors employ a Heisenberg feature map derived from the one‑dimensional Heisenberg model, adapt the circuits to IBM superconducting hardware via Qiskit’s level‑3 preset transpilation pass manager, and apply the TREX (Twirled Readout Error eXtinction) technique for readout‑error mitigation. The method is positioned within near‑term variational/hybrid quantum computing and is contrasted with direct quantum kernels by emphasizing that PQFs generate classical feature vectors with only linear quantum invocations, which may also help retain predictive power under hardware noise.
    [codes: C-003, C-006, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On balanced subsamples and simulator/hardware runs, quantum models achieved test performance close to but slightly below strong classical baselines, while projected‑feature ensembles combining classical and quantum predictions provided slight but consistent improvements over purely classical models. The main business‑relevant evaluation uses the CDR metric on an unbalanced 10,000‑sample subset, where the best simulator‑based ensemble improves over the classical baseline by Δ ≈ 0.0041 and the corresponding hardware‑based ensembles on ibm_marrakesh show smaller gains of Δ ≈ 0.0018 (logistic‑regression ensemble) and Δ ≈ 0.0009 (mean‑probability ensemble). The authors also report that, at the studied scale, quantum model accuracy remains high as the number of qubits/features increases in simulator studies, and that hardware quantum performance is close to classical (albeit marginally lower), suggesting that NISQ‑level noise did not completely obscure the informative signal.

The key comparative claim is that ensembles built from both classical and quantum prediction probabilities outperform the purely classical models by a small margin, leveraging the observed diversity between the two model families’ prediction‑score distributions and feature emphasis on top‑ranked customers. However, the authors caution that earlier classical benchmarks were obtained on a larger one‑month dataset than the restricted subsamples used for quantum experiments, so cross‑dataset comparisons require care.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly state that achieving a rigorously established quantum advantage over classical methods remains an unresolved and formidable goal, and that the practical utility of their proposed quantum–classical models relative to established classical methods on CPUs/GPUs/TPUs is still unresolved. They acknowledge that some classical benchmarks are based on the full one‑month dataset while the quantum and ensemble methods use restricted subsamples, so those comparisons should be interpreted with caution. In their conclusions they further emphasize that the ensemble performance gains are of the same order as the reported errors, implying that more experiments are required to confirm the robustness and statistical significance of the observed improvements.

They introduce several operational machinery analogized to quantum physics: a risk-squeezing operator that redistributes an effective vacuum noise between price and structural depth; a Temporal Contractivity Field as a warning signal; and a holographic bulk–boundary map where renormalization-scale flow captures risk evolution across horizons. Geometrically, the authors argue that as risk or leverage increases, proper time to exit positions dilates, the Lag Horizon diverges as a system approaches a “black-hole” state, and hyper-stable, low-volatility markets correspond to squeezed states where structural fragility is hidden and zero volatility implies near-certain crash via a WKB tunneling argument. Empirically and architecturally, they report that their FPGA-based Systolic Drift Monitor/MQE achieves deterministic end-to-end observation latency of about 1.4 μs, far below assumed drift timescales (>100 μs), enabling pre-symptomatic detection of hyper-stable crashes and heralded erasure in dual-rail qubits, and they present forensic BTC case studies showing large pre-crash bulk winding and symmetry breaking that precede boundary price failures by thousands of ticks.

=== PAPER 7f5135581c08 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles financial risk management by focusing on predicting "fallen angels", i.e., credit rating downgrades, on a highly imbalanced real-world dataset where only 9–12% of instances are downgrades and the goal is to increase precision for this minority class while maintaining recall above about 80%. The prediction task is cast as a supervised classification problem whose operating point is explicitly defined in terms of precision–recall trade-offs tailored to risk management needs.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a QBoost-style heterogeneous ensemble where binary weights select weak learners, and this combinatorial selection is reformulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem to be solved on a neutral-atom quantum processor. They exploit the analog implementation of an Ising Hamiltonian on neutral atoms to sample bitstrings, with Random Graph Sampling (RGS) that leverages random loading to explore many atomic configurations and uses a classical relabeling step to better match the QUBO structure, explicitly avoiding iterative closed-loop variational optimization that would be costly given the low repetition rate of the hardware. Tensor-network methods (TEBD on tensor networks with polynomial parameter count) are additionally used as a quantum-inspired numerical tool to validate and explore scaling of the proposed optimization strategy.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the credit downgrade prediction task, the classifier trained via the neutral-atom QPU reaches a precision of about 27.9% at roughly 83% recall, which the authors describe as competitive with the Random Forest benchmark, while using only 50 learners instead of 1200 and achieving total runtimes around 50 minutes. They show that RGS with relabeling converges to low-cost QUBO solutions with an empirically polynomial repetition scaling of approximately 0.2 × N^1.55, and that its performance becomes comparable to simulated annealing at larger problem sizes. A tensor-network–optimized boosting variant already matches or slightly surpasses the Random Forest benchmark in precision (around 29%), reinforcing the performance potential of their ensemble formulation.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QPU-based classifier is directly compared against a state-of-the-art Random Forest baseline with 1200 trees, which attains about 83% recall and 28% precision but requires more than three hours of classical training and hyperparameter optimization; the quantum-enhanced model achieves essentially the same precision–recall operating point with fewer learners, improved interpretability, and shorter total runtime. At the QUBO-optimization level, RGS with relabeling is benchmarked against classical simulated annealing and random sampling, showing better-than-random performance and approaching simulated annealing as problem size grows, while a tensor-network–optimized boosting model already attains benchmark-level or better precision using fewer learners than the Random Forest.
    [codes: C-003, C-009, C-010, C-013, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that variational or closed-loop quantum optimization methods would require O(1/ε²) measurement samples to estimate energies with precision ε, which is impractical on current neutral-atom hardware due to its low repetition rate on the order of 1–5 Hz. This hardware throughput constraint explicitly motivates their choice of a sampling-based RGS approach that avoids iterative quantum–classical feedback.
    [codes: C-020, C-021]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Using tensor-network simulations, the authors explore how performance could be improved in the near term and use these results to motivate future scaling of their approach.   DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors conduct a theory‑driven review of three quantum (or quantum‑inspired) approaches: (1) continuous‑variable quantum neural networks (CV‑QNNs) for anomaly/fraud detection in financial data, implemented as hybrid quantum‑classical models where classical layers control parameters and an encoding layer converts bits into qumode states with a specified layered gate sequence; (2) the lattice‑based CRYSTALS‑Kyber post‑quantum cryptographic scheme (CPAPKE/CCAKEM) for securing financial communications, with tunable parameter sets and retrofitting into TLS handshakes via replacement of Diffie–Hellman; and (3) quantum‑enhanced Monte Carlo for risk modeling using Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), where probabilities are encoded in qubit amplitudes and a generic QMC circuit structure is outlined and connected to IBM/Qiskit implementations.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles simulation-based optimization problems where the objective is expensive to evaluate and must be approximated via simulation, targeting objective functions expressed as expectation, variance, CDF, or (C)VaR of random variables and functions thereof. It frames these as optimization tasks over continuous or discrete decision variables, including illustrative cases such as a quadratic loss, the newsvendor inventory problem, and portfolio optimization with a VaR-based risk penalty.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-005, C-023, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum-enhanced simulation-based optimization (QSBO) approach that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) to accelerate evaluation of expectation-based objectives, encoding probability distributions into amplitudes and mapping function values via Taylor-based approximations and controlled rotations. They support both continuous decision variables treated as parameters in f(X, y) and discrete decision variables represented on qubits with a parameterized trial state and linear entangling ansatz, evaluated with continuous-estimate QAE variants that reduce width/depth compared to canonical QAE; specific financial mappings rely on comparators and value-register constructions for piecewise costs and VaR.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that QAE provides an estimation error scaling of O(M^-1) with circuit depth O(M), in contrast to classical Monte Carlo’s O(M^-1/2) error, leading to a quadratic speedup for objective evaluation in QSBO. In experiments, they show that canonical QAE induces a stepwise objective landscape, whereas a maximum-likelihood QAE variant yields continuous estimates that better mirror smooth objectives, and that in toy applications the method identifies the optimal or best portfolio or decision with high sampling probability—for example, stock level s = 2 in the newsvendor problem with probability close to one, and selecting only the first asset in the portfolio example with probability about 0.9.

This comparison is presented at the level of asymptotic error scaling and not as an empirical runtime benchmark.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core technical problem as applying sequences of affine transformations within quantum circuits, which is challenging because quantum operations must be unitary while affine maps are not, and because directly adding or subtracting bias terms from amplitudes breaks normalization (C-006, C-014, C-020). Within finance, this is instantiated as a portfolio-return / financial risk–assessment setting, where combinatorial amplitude patterns are used to compute portfolio returns via sums of amplitudes in a knapsack-like construction (C-003, C-004, C-020, C-033).
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-014, C-020, C-033]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The method is a gate-based routine that embeds each linear part A of an affine map into a unitary via block encoding while handling the translation term B through Hadamard-supported conditional initialization on ancilla branches (C-002, C-009, C-012, C-015, C-017, C-021, C-026). Hadamard-supported element-wise addition generates scaled sums and differences of amplitudes while preserving normalization, using measurement on an ancilla to select the desired branch, and realizing a sequential, recursively defined series of affine transformations with known global scaling (C-014, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-028). For the finance application, the authors iteratively grow the register and apply Hadamard-supported add/sub steps with asset blocks Bk to construct combinatorial signed sums of asset amplitudes, and for signal processing they apply QFT, a single affine transformation in the Fourier domain, then inverse QFT (C-018, C-021, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-034, C-040).
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-034, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their routine can encode both element-wise sums and differences of amplitude vectors, scaled to maintain normalization, and that after k affine steps the final state represents the desired sequential affine transformation up to a known factor 1/2^k that can be corrected classically (C-016, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-043, C-044). In a gate-count comparison on a small instance, they claim their approach uses a smaller block-encoded matrix (4N^2 vs 16N^2) and achieves about 32% fewer total gates than an augmented-matrix block-encoding baseline, although with more multi-qubit gates (C-011, C-030, C-031). For the finance use case, they derive a closed-form combinatorial expression for amplitudes over portfolio configurations and note that measurement frequencies estimate squared amplitude magnitudes, with a bias such that larger assets are more likely to appear; in the signal-processing example, they state that the affine-in-frequency workflow enables selective enhancement or suppression of signal components (C-003, C-004, C-016, C-023, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044).
    [codes: C-011, C-016, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-041, C-043, C-044, C-003, C-004]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The only explicit comparison is against another quantum block-encoding construction rather than a fully classical algorithm: the authors compare their block encoding of A with a block-encoded augmented-matrix approach that embeds an enlarged matrix Ã, reporting a reduction from 16N^2 to 4N^2 in matrix size and 32% fewer total gates on a toy instance (C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030). They acknowledge that this advantage in total gate count is tempered by a higher number of multi-qubit gates, which may change the effective hardware cost (C-031).
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly note that standard block-encoding procedures become increasingly computationally demanding as matrix size grows, motivating their alternative construction but also indicating scaling challenges (C-010). Their divide-and-conquer state-preparation scheme achieves exponential depth reduction at the expense of using O(N) ancilla qubits instead of O(log N), highlighting a substantial qubit-overhead trade-off (C-018, C-019). They also acknowledge that many of the generated quantum basis states store "useless" values that are never measured, implying wasted Hilbert space and potential inefficiency (C-025). In their gate-count comparison, they concede that the proposed method introduces more multi-qubit gates than the baseline, which may raise implementation cost on actual hardware (C-031).
    [codes: C-010, C-018, C-019, C-025, C-031]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that their affine-sequence framework could underlie further applications in quantum combinatorial optimization, signal processing, and quantum machine learning beyond the exemplars presented (C-013). They also propose extending the portfolio-return construction with techniques like amplitude amplification to increase the probability of sampling desirable configurations (C-038). In the signal-processing context, they envision stacking multiple affine layers in the frequency domain to implement different filters, and more generally, they point to extending their routine to multidimensional transformations (C-042, C-045). They further speculate that their gate-count advantages may grow with the number of qubits, hinting at better performance at larger scales (C-032).
    [codes: C-013, C-032, C-038, C-042, C-045]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce a novel technique and routine for applying sequences of affine transformations to the probability amplitudes of a quantum state, addressing the challenge of implementing non-unitary affine maps within unitary quantum circuits (C-001, C-006, C-043).   DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is primarily constructive and illustrative: the finance and signal-processing examples are toy constructions without real financial datasets, focusing instead on synthetic amplitude encodings and closed-form expressions for the resulting amplitudes (C-003, C-004, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-040). === PAPER 858a41cdb5b2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as designing quantum algorithms that can efficiently handle and manipulate arrays (including matrix-like data structures) by directly embedding their entries into quantum amplitudes, and providing an end-to-end pipeline from data loading through arithmetic manipulation to information extraction that can support such array-based tasks. The authors argue that direct amplitude embedding simplifies subsequent algebraic operations on the stored information compared with register-based encodings.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method is a direct amplitude-embedding framework where array entries f(i,j) are stored as amplitudes c_ij of a two-register 'quantum matrix' state, with indices i and j representing rows and columns respectively, and arithmetic is performed directly on these amplitudes without square-root encodings or register-based value representations. The pipeline is modularized into separate stages for data loading (including pointwise loading under an efficient-oracle assumption and specialized constant-array loading), an arithmetic toolkit on arrays (reversal, permutations, pairwise sums, reductions, scalar and array multiplication, scalar products), and information extraction via a Quantum Coin amplitude-estimation scheme enhanced by an iterative Grover-style zoom-in procedure and amplitude shifts over confidence intervals. Specific gate-level mechanisms include masking and controlled-X for row reversal, pivot-based recursive multi-controlled-X permutations and cyclic permutations with added controls, Hadamard-based pairwise addition and Walsh–Hadamard reductions, controlled rotations for multiplication by constants within [0,1], array multiplication with products encoded in specific ancilla branches, and composition of array products with reductions to obtain scalar products.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-013, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that state-of-the-art generic n‑qubit state preparation requires a number of CNOT gates scaling as 2^{n+1}, motivating their search for more efficient loading in structured cases such as constant arrays. For constant arrays, they state that their loading procedure uses, in the worst case, n_I X-gates, two Y-rotations, and a single multi-controlled NOT, and from this they infer that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed on a quantum computer to load a constant array than in the generic case. Within the arithmetic layer, they quantify that whole-matrix reversal can be more efficient than row- or column-only reversal, that reductions place row sums into the first column, and that array multiplication encodes the product of two arrays in the joint |0⟩ ancilla branch, which can then be combined with reductions to yield scalar products. For readout, they show that their Quantum Coin method with amplitude shift and iterative Grover amplification increases the measurement probability of the target basis state according to the standard amplification relation, effectively boosting the success probability within a specified confidence interval.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily contrasts quantum vs. quantum approaches to state preparation, noting that existing generic loading techniques require exponentially many CNOTs in the number of qubits, whereas their constant-array loading uses only a number of gates scaling with the number of row qubits and a single multi-controlled NOT. On this basis, they claim that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed to load constant arrays on a quantum computer, though the detailed comparison to classical loading costs is not elaborated beyond this asymptotic statement.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and conditional assumptions. They state that pointwise loading of generic arrays is 'generically not efficient', underscoring that their loading advantages are restricted to structured cases such as constant arrays and that the overall efficiency of their array multiplication procedure is tied to the efficiency of the underlying loading process. They explicitly assume the existence of a suitable efficient oracle for data loading, without which the end-to-end scheme would not be efficient. They also note that multiplication by a constant via controlled rotations is initially restricted to numbers between 0 and 1. At the operation level, they point out that swaps of two entries in an array are demanding operations, reflecting a cost overhead for fine-grained permutations. For their approximation of linear shifts via step functions, they caution that the method becomes inefficient if the required precision scales as 1/N in the number of discretisation points, indicating unfavorable scaling for high-accuracy piecewise approximations.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The provided codes do not report explicit statements about future research directions or proposed extensions beyond the presented framework and examples.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its novelty in offering a general-purpose framework for quantum algorithms that operate on arrays via direct embedding into amplitudes, thereby avoiding square roots and register encodings and, according to the authors, enabling simpler handling and combination of stored information. They highlight the modularization of the quantum algorithm pipeline into data loading, arithmetic manipulations, and read-out, and the construction of an efficient toolkit of quantum arithmetic operations on arrays, including explicit examples on manipulating generic oracles such as constant shifts and step-function approximations to linear shifts. They further claim that for constant arrays this framework can, in principle, achieve an exponential reduction in the number of operations required for loading compared with generic state-preparation methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-017, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors emphasize a modular pipeline that treats data loading, arithmetic operations, and read-out as separable components, allowing each to be analyzed in terms of gate counts and efficiency. For resource estimates, they adopt the customary use of CNOT counts as a primary complexity indicator for state preparation and articulate explicit gate-level procedures (e.g., masking with controlled-X for row reversal, recursive pivot-based permutations, Hadamard-based reductions, controlled rotations for scalar multiplication, and Quantum Coin Grover iterations for readout). However, the codes do not indicate the use of real financial datasets, benchmark instances, or reproducible code artefacts; rather, the work is presented at the level of abstract array manipulation and oracle examples, with performance characterized via analytical gate counts and scaling arguments.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Some codes provide additional detail on the behavior of specific example constructions: for example, the constant-shift oracle example stores the difference array f − s, and the step-function shift is described as the most rudimentary approximation to a linear function. These details contextualize how the general arithmetic framework can be instantiated on concrete oracle transformations but do not substantially alter the broader methodological or problem-framing dimensions.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames its objective as surveying supervised and unsupervised quantum machine learning techniques that have actually been executed on quantum hardware, with a specific emphasis on real‑world applications in high‑energy physics, finance, and healthcare rather than toy problems. It focuses on how data (classical vs quantum) are defined and encoded into quantum feature spaces, highlighting efficient data loading and representation as central challenges for making these applications practical.

It systematically reviews encoding strategies (basis, amplitude, angle, data re‑uploading, Hamiltonian encodings), circuit structures (feature map vs model circuit separation in VQCs, Swap‑test classifier), and optimization and gradient techniques (SPSA, quantum gradient methods, parameter‑shift, quantum natural gradient and QN‑SPSA, shot‑frugal optimizers, local cost functions) as the key levers for making these methods workable on near‑term devices.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across domains, the authors report that amplitude encoding can in principle offer exponential memory savings and that randomized measurement strategies can improve the scaling of quantum kernel estimation. They highlight observed robustness and faster convergence of certain optimizers (SPSA under noise and quantum natural gradient methods, including QN‑SPSA) and cite results such as exponential speedup claims for qPCA, high‑fidelity quantum GAN state replication, and tensor‑network approaches whose qubit requirements scale only logarithmically or are input‑size independent. Application‑wise, they note that high‑energy‑physics studies largely pursue gains in small‑data regimes, finance feature‑selection with QN‑SPSA converged on 20‑qubit hardware, quantum‑data‑driven models appear more promising than those on classical data, and some healthcare image‑classification experiments on real hardware achieve accuracies comparable to classical baselines, though vulnerabilities and hardware‑induced performance gaps are also observed.

In high‑energy physics and healthcare, the authors report comparable AUC‑ROC or accuracy to standard classical classifiers, with specific examples where more expressive encodings yield no improvement on real hardware relative to simpler encodings or classical baselines. They also emphasize that there may exist efficient classical algorithms that achieve performance comparable to quantum approaches, underscoring that convincing empirical evidence of a clear quantum advantage over classical learning remains limited so far.

They emphasize data‑related bottlenecks including the difficulty of efficiently encoding classical data (data‑loading problem), amplitude encoding’s potentially exponential gate cost, quadratic scaling and noise in quantum kernel estimation, and the lack of efficient, standardized data loaders or QRAM. On the algorithmic side, they highlight barren plateaus in variational training, the need for careful ansatz design, inefficiency of backpropagation for PQCs, and scaling issues for methods like qPCA on larger datasets. They also note that more complex encodings can amplify hardware noise without improving performance, that QGANs risk mode collapse, that quantum hardware’s noise and coherence constraints limit attainable circuit depth, and that full quantum error correction introduces overhead that can erode speedups. Further, they stress security and privacy gaps—including vulnerability of QML classifiers to adversarial examples, lack of built‑in privacy mechanisms, and insufficient exploration of differential privacy—as well as meta‑level limitations such as the lack of standardized benchmarks and quantum datasets, limited empirical evidence of quantum advantage, possible parity with unknown classical algorithms, and poor transparency around hyperparameter choices, all of which hinder interpretability, reproducibility, and progress.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the challenge of efficiently loading classical probability distributions into quantum states for financial applications, noting that exact state preparation scales as O(2^n) and undermines quantum advantage for large n (data-loading bottleneck) and that existing qGANs are unstable and not robust on NISQ devices (noise and expressivity limits) (C-001, C-008, C-010). It specifically frames qGANs as approximate probability loaders for tasks such as derivative pricing and risk assessment, where distributions like 2D Gaussians and log-normals need to be embedded into quantum states for downstream algorithms including Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) (C-009, C-020, C-026, C-027, C-060).
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-010, C-009, C-020, C-026, C-027, C-060]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a noise-resilient hybrid qGAN architecture that extends the Zoufal et al. framework by combining advanced loss functions (WGAN-GP and MMD) with expressive variational ansätze—EfficientSU2 and a 6-qubit QCNN—and explicit NISQ noise modeling via depolarizing channels on CX gates (C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-043). Training uses a differentiable PyTorch–Qiskit workflow with parameter-shift gradients, ADAM optimization, and a WGAN-GP objective plus gradient penalty to stabilize learning, while target distributions are discretized to 8×8 grids for loading (C-003, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-050, C-029). For the financial-pricing demonstration, this qGAN-based loader prepares log-normal distributions that feed into Quantum Amplitude Estimation on up to 10–20 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware (C-006, C-025, C-050, C-059, C-060, C-061).
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-033, C-034, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-043, C-003, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-036, C-041, C-050, C-006, C-025, C-059, C-060, C-061]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across 2D Gaussian and log-normal benchmarks, the EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP (R8) variant achieves sub-0.01 Wasserstein distances, with a reported mean WS ≈ 0.0027 ± 0.0004 and fidelity > 0.9, and is visually almost indistinguishable from the target PMFs, with t-SNE analysis suggesting that the generators learn the underlying distribution manifold rather than memorizing samples (C-014, C-030, C-052, C-054, C-055, C-064). Noise sweeps under depolarizing noise up to p = 0.02 show approximately linear degradation and then saturation, with the best model maintaining WS ≈ 0.0046 ± 0.0004 and high relative entropy, while hardware experiments on IBM’s 20‑qubit devices indicate that EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP achieves lower VaR estimation error than QCNN, evidencing relative robustness under realistic noise (C-056, C-057, C-058, C-059, C-065). In the financial application, QAE with qGAN-loaded log-normal distributions attains European call pricing errors below 1%, with hardware estimates around 5.47 ± 0.07 and claims of 100× reduction in required shots for a given precision in simulation (C-006, C-060, C-061, C-062).

  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The proposed hybrid qGAN variants are benchmarked against both a baseline RY–CZ qGAN and classical WGAN-GP and MMD-GAN models, with the EfficientSU2–WGAN-GP circuit reporting substantially lower Wasserstein distances and statistically significant improvements (Wilcoxon p < 0.01) over the RY–CZ baseline on the 2D Gaussian task (C-046, C-052, C-053). The authors also report that their architecture achieves lower VaR estimation error under noise on IBM hardware compared to QCNN-based quantum models, and they highlight a 25% hardware error reduction in QAE-based pricing relative to a baseline qGAN loader and 100× fewer shots than a classical Monte Carlo-based estimate at matched precision in simulation (C-058, C-059, C-061, C-062).

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The QADQN framework reportedly achieves superior risk-adjusted performance, with higher Sharpe ratios (0.82 and 0.77), elevated Sortino ratios above 1.1, and constrained maximum drawdown of 19.24% across overlapping and non-overlapping test periods (C-003, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027). It delivers cumulative returns of 78.91% and 71.26% in these respective periods, while exhibiting selective trading behavior that identifies favorable entry and exit points and avoids unnecessary trades, and training completes within about six GPU-hours (C-024, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-033).
    [codes: C-003, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Compared with classical baselines, the QADQN agent is reported to consistently outperform both a Buy & Hold strategy and a DDPG reinforcement learning agent in terms of cumulative returns and risk-adjusted metrics over both overlapping and non-overlapping evaluation periods (C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030). The authors interpret these results as indicating that QADQN can better identify profitable trading opportunities and generalize to both familiar and unseen market conditions than the classical benchmarks (C-023, C-025, C-030).
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that all quantum-inspired components are executed via classical simulation, explicitly stating that they do not claim any quantum speedup or hardware-level advantage and that the quantum formalisms (portfolio encoding, QUBO, Hamiltonians) are only motivational rather than actually solved quantum processes (C-015, C-016, C-017). They acknowledge that the experiments are limited to a single S&P 500 asset with overlapping train-test windows and omit real-world trading frictions in parts of the setup, which restricts generality (C-018, C-038). They further note that current NISQ hardware constraints such as decoherence, noise, and limited qubit connectivity are not modeled, so results likely overestimate what current devices could deliver, and that their 4‑qubit attention design may not scale well since larger qubit counts would require deeper, noisier, and more expensive circuits (C-036, C-037).
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors propose broader validation via multi-asset portfolios and cross-market indices such as NASDAQ, FTSE 100, and Nikkei 225 to strengthen evidence of generalizability (C-034, C-040). They also suggest stress-testing the approach under extreme market events like the COVID-19 crash, and ultimately deploying QADQN in simulated real-time trading platforms and controlled live environments (C-035, C-039).
    [codes: C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing the Quantum Attention Deep Q-Network (QADQN), a quantum-inspired reinforcement learning framework that integrates a multi-head quantum attention mechanism into deep Q-learning for financial trading and risk management, intended to reduce overhead and enhance interpretability relative to standard transformer attention (C-001, C-002, C-008). It also highlights the use of quantum-motivated portfolio encoding and QUBO/Hamiltonian formulations to inform feature mapping, and the combination of POMDP modeling, Dual Thrust–style replay buffer initialization, and imitation-based learning to improve trading policy learning (C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors position their work as addressing shortcomings of GARCH, GBM, and standard deep learning models, which they describe as insufficient for nonlinear dependencies, regime shifts, and fat-tail risks, and as computationally demanding and sensitive to data irregularities (C-005, C-006, C-007). The experimental setup is specified with training on S&P 500 data from 2016-01-15 to 2020-01-15 using a 24-day rolling window, with both overlapping and non-overlapping evaluation periods, and transaction costs of 0.2% per trade with no leverage (C-019, C-020, C-022). They document that each quantum attention module uses four qubits, analyze that training complexity remains polynomial with a manageable quadratic factor from quantum attention, and report that training on four years of data completes within six GPU-hours, suggesting practical feasibility under their simulator-based setup (C-021, C-032, C-033).
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes qualitatively that the learned QADQN policy behaves in a risk-sensitive manner, implementing timely exits and dynamic position adjustments during downturns, which the authors link to its ability to mitigate downside volatility while maximizing returns (C-026, C-031).
    [codes: C-026, C-031]
