=== PAPER a143717759af (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the challenge of assessing banking system stability in emerging and developing economies where reliable, comprehensive financial and market data are often missing or opaque, especially for unlisted banks. It formulates this as a need for a simple, transparent, country-level reverse stress-testing metric that can approximate system-wide resilience to credit shocks using accounting data and a focus on the weakest banks in the system.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-018]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Not addressed in this paper; no quantum computing methods, algorithms, or hardware are discussed.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Applying the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP) metric to about 1,500 banks in 59 EMDEs during COVID-19, the authors find a median country CDBP of 9.8 percentage points, with two countries having Banks at Risk that are already undercapitalized. Regional patterns show substantial dispersion, with Sub-Saharan Africa having the highest median CDBP but wide interquartile range, while South Asia exhibits the lowest median CDBP at 3.8 percentage points. Empirically, the CDBP is only weakly associated with EIU banking risk measures and with standard macro-financial and financial soundness indicators, suggesting that it encapsulates complementary information; robustness checks including profit buffers yield very similar assessments (correlation 0.953).
    [codes: C-004, C-016, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The CDBP is compared against traditional macro-financial and financial soundness indicators, as well as the EIU banking risk indicator, and the authors report that these associations are relatively weak and explain little of the variation in CDBP. They interpret this as evidence that the CDBP provides complementary information to standard country-level indicators, and suggest it could be used alongside them rather than as a replacement.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-043, C-046, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors emphasize that the CDBP is a very rough approximation of systemic banking resilience with several important limitations. Conceptually, it focuses only on credit risk, excluding other key risks such as currency and liquidity risk, contagion and second-round effects, contingent liabilities, bank resolution frameworks, and non-linear distress dependencies among banks. Methodologically, the minimum capital requirement is applied uniformly across banks without bank-specific buffers; the reverse stress test mechanically computes an NPL breakpoint without assigning a likelihood or time horizon; the provisioning rate for new NPLs is fixed and collateral is ignored; and the approach assumes additional provisioning is fully absorbed by capital and effectively excludes profit buffers in its baseline. Data-wise, NPL information is backward-looking, lagged, and may be underreported; the bank sample can be incomplete; COVID-19 policy support measures may have reduced balance-sheet transparency; and the authors stress that the metric should ideally be complemented by richer supervisory data and additional stress tests.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that the CDBP could be developed and used as a basic monitoring tool and as a useful input to form a preliminary view of a banking sector’s resilience, particularly in data-poor EMDEs. They argue it should complement, rather than replace, traditional country-level indicators and be used in conjunction with more detailed stress tests and richer supervisory information. They also propose that high or concerning CDBP signals could trigger more in-depth supervisory risk reviews and targeted analytical work.
    [codes: C-007, C-017, C-049, C-051, C-052]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution claimed is the development of a simple, transparent, reverse stress-testing based country-level indicator—the Consolidated Distance to Breakpoint (CDBP)—that uses bank-level accounting data to approximate system-wide resilience to credit shocks in EMDEs. The novelty lies in focusing on the tail of the most vulnerable banks that together hold at least 20% of system assets (Banks at Risk), consolidating their balance sheets to derive a systemic breakpoint measure, and demonstrating that this tail-risk-focused indicator provides complementary information to existing aggregate measures.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-006]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper defines a bank-level Break Point as the NPL ratio at which increased loan-loss provisioning depletes capital buffers above minimum requirements, and then computes a Distance from Break Point (DBP) as the difference between this threshold and the current NPL ratio. It aggregates by selecting the most vulnerable banks (lowest DBP) until they represent at least 20% of system assets, breaking ties by bank size, and consolidates their balance sheets to compute the CDBP. Key modeling assumptions include that incremental provisioning is fully absorbed by capital, a fixed 55% provisioning rate for new NPLs, uniform minimum capital requirements, and ignoring collateral and profits in the base case, with a profit-buffer robustness check. The empirical application uses Fitch balance-sheet data for around 1,500 commercial banks in 59 EMDEs as of Q3 2020, falling back to the latest data not older than 2019 when necessary, and the authors explicitly note potential issues with NPL data lags, underreporting, incomplete bank coverage, and COVID-19 support measures that may obscure true asset quality.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-048]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The application during the COVID-19 pandemic is framed within broader macro-fiscal and sovereign risk concerns: the authors note that large projected GDP contractions in some countries could impair bank resilience and that weak banks may contribute to a bank–sovereign doom loop by undermining sovereign debt sustainability.
    [codes: C-044, C-045]

=== PAPER a4cb146201fc (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper reframes economic decision-making by replacing utility with a propensity function that gives the probability of transacting, motivated by the perceived failure of neoclassical equilibrium models during the 2007/8 financial crisis and the inability of behavioural economics to capture non-classical cognitive phenomena. It positions this quantum-inspired propensity framework as a way to model decision uncertainty and anomalies such as preference reversals and the disjunction effect in economic and financial contexts.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-023, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Methodologically, the authors adopt quantum probability and qubit-based formalisms: they represent decision states as qubits and use the 2-norm to allow amplitudes with negative projections that yield superposition, interference, and entanglement. They construct quantum circuits where order effects are modeled via sequential projections, with specific gates used to simulate phenomena like the disjunction effect and preference reversal, and show how a general (classical) propensity function can be "quantized" by treating propensity curves as wave-function analogues and mapping their dynamics to a quantum harmonic oscillator model; an appendix proves the equivalence of a one-qubit and a two-qubit circuit used in the analysis.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-027, C-037]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that a simple quantum circuit can reproduce observed order-effect probability tables and flexibly simulate multiple cognitive phenomena, including the disjunction effect and preference reversal, with a specific threshold condition for switching from a more attractive to a less attractive option when the associated costs differ by a factor greater than three. In the economic propensity framework, they derive that a normal propensity distribution leads to a linear restoring entropic force, with the effective mass inversely related to the variance, and that buyer and seller propensities combine multiplicatively to give a joint (scaled normal) transaction propensity. Extending this, higher quantum harmonic oscillator states are argued to generate non-normal distributions akin to market behavior, and the authors link the work against the entropic force—and thus the energy or information required to change a decision, such as a preference reversal—to log ratios of propensities at different points and to a base quantum energy scale.
    [codes: C-003, C-012, C-014, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-038]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The approach is explicitly contrasted with classical probability and utility-based economics: classical probability, based on the 1‑norm and positive numbers, cannot naturally represent superposition, interference, and entanglement, whereas quantum probability with the 2‑norm can. Similarly, the paper critiques neoclassical models that assume rational utility maximizers driving markets to stable equilibrium, and argues that both standard and behavioral economics—rooted in classical logic—struggle to accommodate empirically observed decision anomalies that their quantum propensity framework can represent.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-016, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The main acknowledged limitation is conceptual and sociological: the authors note that many social scientists will regard it as inappropriate or contentious to quantify constructs like social power or mental energy, even though their framework does so by relating decision changes and propensities to energy-like quantities. They also imply that capturing the interplay of subjective and objective forces that constitute power requires a more fully developed framework, indicating that their current proposal is an initial step rather than a complete theory.
    [codes: C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors call for the development of a more suitable and comprehensive framework to describe the interplay between objective and subjective forces that constitute social and economic power, building on their quantum propensity and entropic-force concepts.
    [codes: C-036]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in proposing a quantum-inspired economics framework that replaces utility with a propensity function expressed in quantum-probabilistic terms and can be quantized to include interference and entanglement effects characteristic of human decision-making. It further claims that this framework allows unified modeling of diverse phenomena—from cognitive interference and decision anomalies (order effects, disjunction effect, preference reversal) to financial pricing (such as option prices)—thereby shifting the expression of value from classical utility to quantum propensity and entropic forces.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-008, C-020, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is conceptual and analytical rather than empirical: it constructs toy models (e.g., coin-based qubits, quantum circuits, quantum harmonic oscillators) and derives closed-form relationships such as entropic forces and mass–variance links, supported by an appendix that formally proves the equivalence between a one-qubit and a two-qubit circuit used to simulate order effects, while noting that intermediate probabilities differ despite matching final probabilities. There is no mention of implementation on actual quantum hardware, empirical datasets, or statistical validation against financial market data, suggesting the results are at the level of theoretical modeling and mathematical analogy.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper includes standard structural elements such as an explicit outline of the subsequent sections and an appendix detailing circuit equivalence; these do not materially affect the substantive quantum-economic claims but help organize and formalize the exposition.
    [codes: C-009, C-037]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper is relevant to risk_management because it offers a quantum-inspired way to model decision uncertainty, threshold effects, and non-normal behavior that can matter when assessing tail risk, stress responses, and risk-taking under changing information. Its strongest overlap is conceptual rather than empirical, but the propensity and entropic-force framework could be mapped to risk models that need to capture non-classical shifts in behavior.
    [silo_relevance_score: medium]
  KEY_POINT 1: Quantum propensity replaces utility with a transaction-probability view of decisions, which is directly relevant to modeling uncertain risk-taking behavior.
    [codes: C-002, C-023, C-033  dim_source: dimension_1]
  KEY_POINT 2: The paper’s qubit and circuit formalism is designed to represent order effects, interference, and sequential information updates.
    [codes: C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020  dim_source: dimension_2]

=== PAPER a75f8f16f267 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames financial forecasting and portfolio optimisation as increasingly intractable for traditional machine learning and classical computing due to the scale, uncertainty, and complex constraints in modern markets, highlighting specific bottlenecks in Monte Carlo simulations, regression, classical SVMs, and convex portfolio optimisation under real‑world constraints such as cardinality limits, transaction costs, and non‑linear risk factors. This motivates a "critical need for enhanced computational paradigms" and positions QML as a response to this complexity in finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-042]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: As a review, the paper surveys several QML approaches rather than implementing a single method: Quantum Support Vector Machines that use quantum feature mapping to embed data into high‑dimensional Hilbert spaces for faster inner‑product computation in classification tasks (e.g., bullish vs bearish markets, risk profiles); Variational Quantum Circuits as hybrid quantum‑classical models for regression/supervised learning, trained by classical optimisers and designed to be compatible with noisy NISQ devices, with claimed richer functional forms due to superposition and entanglement; Quantum Principal Component Analysis for dimensionality reduction to identify principal components exponentially faster in theory and to compress portfolio, macro, and trading data; and quantum annealing plus QAOA for portfolio optimisation, encoding constraints into QUBO form so that quantum tunnelling can better escape local minima and produce comparable or better optimisation outcomes more quickly. The paper also conceptually discusses embedding quantum solvers within traditional data pipelines and hybrid architectures that integrate quantum models with classical financial systems.
    [codes: C-003, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-043, C-054, C-056]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper, being conceptual, mainly reports claimed or cited results rather than new empirical metrics: it states that QML algorithms can offer significant improvements over classical methods in speed, accuracy, and scalability, including promises of exponential speedups and superior generalisation for big, complex financial data. Specific algorithmic claims include faster inner‑product computation in QSVMs and theoretically exponential speedups for QPCA. The authors report that quantum annealing can yield comparable or better portfolio optimisation outcomes in a fraction of the time versus classical solvers, and that quantum‑powered Monte Carlo is already being used by JPMorgan for asset price simulations with significantly reduced computational time for risk modelling. Hybrid quantum‑classical models are described as having demonstrated improved accuracy in predicting volatility indices and yield curves, and QML more broadly is said to have demonstrated improved efficiency in forecasting, optimisation, and trading. The paper also cites market and adoption metrics such as projected rapid growth in the QML and financial‑services quantum markets and high levels of institutional engagement.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-018, C-022, C-023, C-032, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-058]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper consistently contrasts quantum approaches with classical baselines, arguing that classical methods such as Monte Carlo simulations, linear regression, classical SVMs, and Markowitz‑style convex optimisation are increasingly insufficient for the scale, uncertainty, and real‑world constraints in modern finance. QML is claimed to offer significant improvements over these classical methods in speed, accuracy, and scalability, including exponential speedups and superior generalisation in complex big‑data environments. For specific techniques, QSVMs are said to compute inner products faster via quantum feature maps, QPCA is claimed to identify principal components exponentially faster in theory than classical PCA, and quantum annealing is presented as escaping local minima more effectively than simulated annealing while delivering comparable or better optimisation outcomes in a fraction of the time required by classical solvers.

On the algorithmic and methodological side, the paper notes a lack of standardised benchmarks and proven performance on real‑world financial datasets, the complexity of designing effective quantum circuits for high‑dimensional and noisy financial data, and that many quantum methods are still experimental and untested. Regulatory and governance limitations are also highlighted: because the technology is at an early stage, regulators find it difficult to craft specific rules beyond generic requirements for transparency and accountability. These limitations collectively reinforce that the current state of QML for finance is exploratory rather than production‑ready at scale.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets accurate estimation of catastrophe tail risk—specifically VaR and TVaR at extreme percentiles such as the 99.5th percentile—which it frames as a severe computational challenge due to exponential sample growth in classical Monte Carlo for low‑probability, high‑severity events. This tail‑risk estimation is then embedded in a reinsurance portfolio optimization problem via a Capital Efficiency objective for non‑proportional treaty design.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-009, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed hybrid architecture integrates physics‑based catastrophe calibration with two quantum components: QAE for sampling loss distributions and tail probabilities, and a VQE‑style parameterized ansatz for preparing tail‑focused loss states, both using non‑linear, tail‑weighted amplitude encoding on an 8‑qubit register. Error mitigation is handled primarily through zero‑noise extrapolation and symmetry‑based sample filtering, while a dynamic backend scheduler routes workloads across heterogeneous QPUs and simulators based on a normalized, weighted scoring function over precision, latency, and cost.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-012, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a synthetic Florida coastal hurricane portfolio, the hybrid system is reported (in noisy simulation) to match classical tail precision using 7.5×10^2 quantum shots versus approximately 2.0×10^4 classical Monte Carlo samples, corresponding to a 96.25% reduction in sample complexity and a 35% reduction in estimator variance at the 99.5th percentile. The authors report VaR and TVaR estimates with much tighter confidence intervals than the classical baseline and claim that the resulting optimization recommends a non‑proportional treaty (10M attachment, 50M limit, two 100%‑premium reinstatements) that improves Capital Efficiency from 0.35 to 0.42 and allows reinsurers to free up capital by narrowing confidence bands around tail metrics.
    [codes: C-007, C-033, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The hybrid quantum‑classical pipeline is benchmarked against a classical Monte Carlo baseline that requires about 2.0×10^4 samples to attain confidence at the 99.5th percentile, whereas the hybrid approach reportedly attains equivalent tail precision with 7.5×10^2 quantum shots, implying a 96.25% reduction in sample complexity and 35% lower estimator variance. The classical VaR estimate of $37.3M (±$4.1M) is contrasted with a hybrid VaR of $32.0M (±$0.8M), and the authors interpret the higher classical VaR as a variance‑induced upward bias that leads to over‑capitalization relative to the tighter hybrid estimates.
    [codes: C-002, C-033, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that fully quantum algorithms for high‑dimensional, highly correlated insurance portfolios are currently impractical on NISQ devices due to decoherence, limited connectivity, and regulatory auditability constraints, motivating their hybrid partitioning. They explicitly caution that their gains are reported in terms of sample complexity rather than wall‑clock runtime, emphasizing that theoretical quadratic speedup does not translate directly to real‑time acceleration. They further note that their implementation requires about 7.5×10^2 shots—around a 53× constant‑factor overhead relative to idealized QAE—because of noise and mitigation overheads, and thus their empirical results remain simulator‑based and subject to NISQ hardware realities.
    [codes: C-011, C-036, C-037]

=== PAPER b43110ee807d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the computation of market risk metrics—Value at Risk (VaR) and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR)—for portfolios of financial derivatives, formulated on a scenario-based distribution of portfolio values where the portfolio is priced under a finite set of market scenarios V = {V(s_i)} and VaR/CVaR are defined over the resulting loss distribution. The authors specifically target the efficient estimation of VaR as the probability mass below a threshold and CVaR as the expected loss beyond that threshold for derivative portfolios. They highlight that risk metrics may be more amenable to quantum advantage than raw derivative pricing, motivating algorithms that operate on the scenario-based risk-analysis level rather than only on single-price estimation.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-007]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper develops two quantum approaches for scenario-based VaR and CVaR: a QAE-based method and a Quantum Signal Processing (QSP)–based method. In the QAE-based derivative VaR algorithm, scenario information is encoded by preparing a superposition over scenarios such that an operator A_S encodes the portfolio value under all scenarios, followed by a binary comparison that flags whether each scenario’s value lies below a threshold μ and uses amplitude estimation to recover the probability P[V ≤ μ]. The QSP-based method instead block-encodes the relevant operator and uses QSP to apply polynomial transformations to its singular values so as to approximate a threshold function θ_μ(x); QAE is then used only as an outer readout to estimate the probability associated with the flagged subspace, and the VaR threshold μ_α is found via a bisection search over μ with adaptive allocation of QAE accuracy and confidence between iterations. For CVaR, the authors modify the function implemented by QSP by inverting the threshold below μ to avoid a discontinuity and enable more efficient estimation of the expected tail loss, noting that this CVaR routine structurally depends on first having computed the correct VaR threshold.
    [codes: C-002, C-006, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that, for a fixed target VaR/CVaR accuracy, the QSP-based approach requires significantly fewer quantum resources than the QAE-based approach in their simulations, despite both having similar asymptotic scaling. Quantitatively, they find numerically that using QSP in practice yields a more efficient algorithm and that, in a quantum-advantage benchmark based on derivative VaR, the logical clock-rate threshold required for advantage in derivative pricing tasks can be lowered by up to roughly 30× relative to previously published thresholds, contingent on assumptions about scenario preparation. They also specify the classical complexity baseline for scenario-based VaR via nested Monte Carlo as scaling like O(N/ε²_p), providing a point of comparison for their quantum resource analyses.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-008, C-021, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares its quantum VaR and CVaR algorithms to classical nested Monte Carlo, taking the classical complexity for general VaR estimation to scale as O(N/ε²_p) and positioning both quantum methods as offering the usual quadratic improvement from amplitude estimation under the same scenario-sampling assumptions. At the algorithmic level, the authors argue that although QAE- and QSP-based VaR methods have similar asymptotic scaling, QSP is more resource-efficient in practice, effectively reducing the quantum overhead relative to classical baselines. They further discuss how classical adaptive sampling combined with Multi-level Monte Carlo can reduce classical VaR/CVaR complexity to Õ(ε⁻²) for sufficiently smooth densities and note that analogous adaptive ideas could, in principle, be incorporated on the quantum side by adjusting the accuracy with which derivative prices are encoded.
    [codes: C-008, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations of their approaches. First, they note that a prior QAE-based VaR method that assumes direct access to a unitary for the loss random variable is not directly applicable to derivative VaR because scenario-based derivative pricing does not provide the required unitary, necessitating an extra QAE layer and more complex oracles. They further highlight that finite binary registers cannot represent all scenario values exactly, so approximate binary encoding introduces discretization error and causes probability leakage where each scenario may contribute weight to the wrong comparison flag, degrading classification around the VaR threshold. Additionally, because their approach requires coherent approximation of scenario values, high-performance iterative QAE variants cannot be used in the inner layer, restricting algorithmic choices. For the QSP-based CVaR routine, they explicitly state that CVaR estimation depends on first reliably computing VaR and identifying the correct threshold, adding an extra dependency and potential source of error. At the implementation level, the authors leave the design of efficient scenario-preparation procedures as an open question and stress that the performance and any quantum advantage of their algorithms rely critically on being able to prepare a superposition of scenarios efficiently; if scenario loading is expensive, the advantage could be significantly weakened or lost.
    [codes: C-010, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-024, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper points to several avenues for future work, most notably the need to design and analyze efficient scenario-preparation schemes capable of loading market scenario distributions into quantum superposition at acceptable cost, since their current treatment leaves this as an open problem. They also suggest that ideas from classical adaptive sampling and Multi-level Monte Carlo might be ported to the quantum setting by adaptively tuning the accuracy with which derivative prices are encoded as amplitudes, potentially extending or preserving quantum advantage even when classical methods improve. More broadly, the authors imply that refining polynomial approximations and threshold functions (e.g., for CVaR) could further improve resource efficiency in realistic risk-management settings.
    [codes: C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim as their main contribution the introduction of two quantum algorithms for computing VaR and CVaR of financial derivatives that operate on scenario-based portfolio values encoded in superposition, leveraging QAE and, more prominently, QSP to estimate risk metrics more efficiently. They argue that by focusing on risk metrics—rather than just derivative pricing—and by using a QSP-based polynomial thresholding construction that requires fewer quantum resources than a straightforward QAE-based extension of prior asset-risk methods, they can lower the logical clock-rate threshold required for quantum advantage in derivative-related tasks by up to about 30× under their benchmark assumptions. This positions the work as both a methodological extension of existing quantum risk analysis to derivative portfolios and a refinement of resource estimates for quantum advantage in financial risk management.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-009, C-021, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper builds on and extends a prior QAE-based VaR algorithm that assumes direct access to a unitary encoding the loss random variable, carefully explaining why this assumption fails for derivative portfolios and how they instead construct scenario-superposition operators and binary comparison oracles to recover VaR probabilities. The authors discuss error sources such as finite-precision binary encoding and misclassification near thresholds, and they formalize how these affect amplitude estimates, indicating an awareness of precision and discretization issues. On the QSP side, they follow a published minimax-Chebyshev approach to construct polynomial approximations to discontinuous threshold functions and then adapt these constructions (e.g., via an inverted linear threshold for CVaR) to improve numerical behavior, which suggests attention to numerical stability and approximation quality. While the supplied codes do not detail software environments or full reproducibility infrastructure, they do emphasize how accuracy and confidence parameters are allocated in the bisection and amplitude-estimation stages, indicating a systematic treatment of algorithmic error management rather than ad hoc parameter choices.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all provided codes map to the primary reporting dimensions.
    [codes: —]

    [silo_relevance_score: high]

=== PAPER b524b2fc9631 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the problem of estimating full loan-level loss/risk distributions, rather than just point estimates, to enable true account-level pricing and decisioning in retail lending. It frames this within a competing-risks cash-flow and survival modelling setup that incorporates multiple sources of uncertainty (including lifecycle and macro-environment effects) to obtain a probability distribution for individual-loan default and attrition outcomes.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-016, C-017, C-019]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors consider quantum Monte Carlo methods based on quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) to estimate loan-level tail risk more sample-efficiently than classical Monte Carlo, using amplitude encoding of probability density functions into qubit registers. They explain how distributions are encoded via binary representations in qubit superposition, rely on entanglement to reuse sampled values across calculations, and decompose the quantum algorithm into three components while referring to existing quantum Monte Carlo / QAE work for acceleration of risk-estimation tasks.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Classically, Monte Carlo simulations of loan-level loss distributions for example accounts fit very well to lognormal distributions; normal fits are rejected in favour of lognormal, and once this shape is assumed, only tens of simulations are needed to estimate tail risk instead of thousands. With 50 simulations, the classical method computes an account’s risk distribution in about 1.9 seconds, which the authors note is sufficient for real-time use, and they also report empirical patterns from the APC decomposition (e.g., default peaks around the 2001 and 2009 recessions, payoff dynamics). On the quantum side, they reiterate the theoretical QAE result that the accuracy achieved with M classical Monte Carlo samples can be achieved with O(M) operations yielding O(1/M) error scaling, giving a quadratic sample-complexity improvement over the classical O(1/√M) convergence, but do not report hardware experiments.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper develops a classical Monte Carlo method as the main practical solution for estimating loan-level loss distributions and explicitly contrasts its O(1/√M) convergence with the theoretically faster O(1/M) error scaling of QAE-based quantum Monte Carlo. However, because the simulated distributions are well-approximated by lognormal, the authors show that only tens of classical simulations are required to estimate mean, variance, and tail risk, leading to runtimes of about 1.9 seconds per account and arguing that this is already fast enough for real-time use, thereby undercutting the near-term practical need for quantum speedup despite the theoretical quadratic advantage.
    [codes: C-002, C-009, C-023, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations of their quantum approach and modelling assumptions. For quantum computing, they note that quantum registers cannot be copied, requiring entanglement workarounds, and that current hardware noise may render present-day results largely unreliable even as hardware improves. They emphasise that efficient loading of distributions into quantum registers is only possible when an efficient classical integration algorithm exists, and that the full competing-risks quantum formulation scales poorly in qubits (best-case 4Nm qubits and 4N registers), far exceeding likely commercial qubit counts in the next few years. They explicitly state that the full competing-risks approach will require additional quantum algorithm development to become feasible, and that including a full yield model and additional cash-flow components may break the lognormal or beta distribution fit, undermining both the classical and proposed quantum shortcuts that assume a simple closed-form distribution for the final loss distribution.
    [codes: C-005, C-012, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests that if quantum computing can make some of the estimation processes fast enough for real-time use, it may change lending practices, but this is framed as a longer-term possibility. As a nearer-term direction, the authors propose focusing on simplified, single-risk models with unconditional distributions as the likely initial application of quantum computing to account-level decisioning. They also suggest exploring quantum algorithms that exploit assumed closed-form distribution families (e.g., lognormal or generic beta) for the final loss distribution, which would allow QAE to estimate parameters rather than tail points directly, potentially reducing quantum resource requirements for more realistic competing-risks settings.
    [codes: C-010, C-032, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors present a combined classical–quantum analysis of loan-level risk-distribution estimation: they develop and empirically validate a classical Monte Carlo framework for competing-risks loan-level loss distributions, including demonstrating robust lognormal fits that dramatically reduce required simulations, and they map this problem to quantum Monte Carlo/QAE, outlining how distributions and survival components can be encoded in qubit registers and entangled for reuse. Their contribution is positioned as identifying where quantum amplitude estimation could in principle offer a quadratic sample-complexity advantage for loan-level tail-risk estimation, while also showing that, under current modelling assumptions and lognormal fit, classical Monte Carlo already delivers real-time performance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-009, C-014, C-016, C-018, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-039]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is grounded in a real-world public dataset from Freddie Mac, focusing on 30-year fixed-rate conforming mortgages with rich account-level variables, and it constructs a multihorizon competing-risks survival framework based on APC decomposition of lifecycle and environment components. The authors estimate separate PD and PA models via panel logistic regression at each horizon, propagate uncertainty by including 95% confidence intervals on coefficients and environment functions, and model environmental dynamics using a second-order mean-reverting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Classical Monte Carlo then samples conditional PD and PA from these distributions, tabulates lifetime default and payoff densities, and tests distributional assumptions by comparing lognormal and normal fits, including goodness-of-fit testing and discussion of simulation counts and runtimes; no actual quantum hardware or code implementation is reported, and the quantum analysis remains theoretical.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Not addressed in this paper

=== PAPER c0182e500e61 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses high-dimensional Monte Carlo integration for estimating expected values E[F] of functions F(X1,…,XD), with a particular focus on credit portfolio risk measurement (e.g., VaR under a Merton-style loss model) as an industrial finance use-case where many random numbers are required and thus many qubits would naively be needed.
    [codes: C-002, C-006, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors build on quantum Monte Carlo integration using quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), and propose a 'PRN-on-a-register' implementation where pseudo-random numbers are generated sequentially on a single quantum register via deterministic recursion and jump oracles. The integrand is evaluated sequentially using intermediate variables, with an initial superposition over sample indices, and the final amplitude encoding the sample average which is then estimated by QAE. For integrands with a specific separable structure, they introduce a nested QAE scheme using a term oracle to evaluate terms in quantum parallel and sum them via QAE, after reformulating inputs into common and individual stochastic variables.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper states that quantum Monte Carlo integration with QAE achieves a quadratic reduction in oracle calls, O(ε⁻¹) versus classical O(ε⁻²), and that the proposed PRN-on-a-register approach can 'tremendously' reduce the number of qubits by requiring only one register regardless of the number of random numbers. For separable integrands, combining nested QAE with PRNs can reduce the query complexity for estimating intermediate sums and F(j) to O(ε⁻¹) oracle calls, and potentially yields a query reduction factor of O(ε⁻¹/D) compared to a naive O(D) iterative computation when ε⁻¹ ≲ D.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-016, C-019, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors compare their quantum Monte Carlo integration approach to classical Monte Carlo by noting that classical methods require O(ε⁻²) oracle queries to achieve error ε, whereas QAE-based quantum methods use O(ε⁻¹) queries, constituting a quadratic speed-up. They also contrast their PRN-on-a-register implementation with a classical-style register-per-random-number design in quantum circuits, where the latter would scale qubit requirements proportionally with the number of random numbers in high-dimensional finance problems such as credit portfolio risk.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-012, C-013]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that while the nested QAE and PRN approach can reduce the number of oracle queries, this does not automatically translate into time complexity gains because PRN jump operations are typically more time-consuming than simple PRN updates; the effective time reduction factor depends on the relative runtimes T_jump and T_up and scales as O(T_jump·ε⁻¹ / (T_up·D)). The authors also point out that the query reduction advantage for the nested QAE method is conditional, applying only when the desired precision satisfies ε⁻¹ ≲ D, and they defer a more strict error estimation of the QAE-based method to follow-up work, implying that error analysis is not fully resolved in this paper.
    [codes: C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest exploring additional industrial and scientific use-cases of quantum Monte Carlo integration, especially in domains where speeding up high-dimensional Monte Carlo integration is a central challenge.
    [codes: C-033, C-034]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in proposing the 'PRN-on-a-register' quantum Monte Carlo integration scheme, where pseudo-random numbers are sequentially generated on a single register via recursion and jump formulas, leading to a substantial reduction in required qubits compared to register-per-RN implementations. It further claims that by leveraging separable integrand structures and nested QAE, the method can achieve additional time or query complexity reductions with respect to the number of dimensions.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The authors refer to companion works where they provide detailed circuit-level implementations of the PRN-on-a-register scheme, including concrete pseudo-random number generators, comparisons of error bounds, and more stringent error analysis for the QAE-based method, indicating that key implementation and analytical details are elaborated outside this conference paper.

=== PAPER c434305b37fb (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit risk analysis within a Gaussian Conditional-Independence (GCI) framework, focusing on loading standard Gaussian latent factors and mapping them to conditional default probabilities for a single asset. The authors concentrate on the uncertainty-model sub-circuit that is common to both VaR and CVaR estimation, encoding the conditional default probability as the chance of measuring |1⟩ on an asset qubit with rotation angles depending affinely on the latent factor. This is framed as constructing quantum circuits that can reproduce distributions relevant to credit risk models on current NISQ hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-009, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hardware-aware, variational, gate-based method that prepares discrete Gaussian distributions on small superconducting QPUs and plugs them into a GCI credit-risk sub-circuit. The Gaussian loading ansatz consists of single-qubit Ry rotations followed by entangling gates, whose parameters are variationally trained via parameter-shift gradients and Adam to match a target histogram, with analytic angle relations derived to enforce symmetric bell-shaped outputs. Implementation is tightly coupled to the Quantware Contralto-D sQPU: native CZ gates, specific qubit triplets, pulse-level schedules, and hardware-aware transpilation (including SABRE routing, subcircuit replacement, and pulse-level retuning) are used to minimize depth, respect connectivity, and tune rotation angles as device-specific hyperparameters.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-010, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-047]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their hardware-aware variational circuits can synthesize two- and three-qubit Gaussian-like distributions whose probability amplitudes follow periodic trends with respect to rotation angles, allowing identification of optimal angle settings for specific qubit pairs and triplets. They claim that the method and hardware scale well from two to three qubits, and that analytic angle relations provide practical guidance for shaping symmetric, bell-like histograms on today’s superconducting QPUs. For the integrated GCI credit-risk sub-circuit, they find experimentally that certain Ry angles control the relative heights of the Gaussian lobes, identify an angle combination that best matches simulated output, and observe that the 95% VaR conclusion at a given loss level is consistent across simulator, hardware-ready, and experimental outputs, supporting a proof-of-concept viability claim for quantum adaptation in this financial context.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-021, C-022, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-039, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily compares hardware runs against noiseless quantum simulations and classical GCI outputs rather than against full classical Monte Carlo baselines. For the GCI sub-circuit, they state that the best-tuned hardware-ready circuit yields output distributions and VaR estimates that align with those from the simulated transpiled circuit and a classical baseline, concluding that the simulator cannot directly reproduce experimental behavior without modeling hardware noise. They also emphasize that standard transpilation and noiseless simulation, while useful references, ignore device-specific noise, in contrast to their hardware-informed retuning.
    [codes: C-040, C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: current NISQ hardware has few addressable qubits, high gate errors, and decoherence, necessitating very small proof-of-concept circuits. They note that SPAM and other noise sources cause asymmetries in the experimentally prepared distributions even when the analytical target is symmetric, and that optimal rotation angles are highly dependent on the specific qubit pair or triplet, limiting parameter portability. They explicitly state that noiseless simulators and standard transpilation flows do not capture device noise or sensitivity to particular error sources, and that no readout error mitigation was applied in their experiments, which they present as a methodological caveat.
    [codes: C-006, C-031, C-032, C-038, C-043, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include integrating readout error mitigation and error-amplification techniques into their quantum algorithm implementation pipeline, and developing or using quantum compilers that more fully adapt circuit structures and parameterizations to specific QPUs, thereby incorporating noise-awareness beyond basic transpilation.
    [codes: C-046, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as the first experimental investigation and implementation of a key Gaussian-loading sub-circuit within a QAE-based credit risk analysis algorithm on a superconducting QPU, serving as a small-scale, finance-inspired proof-of-concept. They also claim that their study bridges a gap between quantum algorithm specialists and hardware engineers by combining financial modeling (GCI) with pulse-level, hardware-aware transpilation and parameter tuning tailored to a specific superconducting processor.
    [codes: C-005, C-008, C-011]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study is explicitly hardware-aware: circuits are compiled to minimize depth and connectivity violations, then further adapted at the pulse level on a specified Contralto-D sQPU with documented native gates and DRAG-based single-qubit pulses. The team performs benchmarking of coherence and fidelity parameters immediately before experiments, selects specific qubits and parking strategies, and uses a combination of Qiskit’s preset pass manager, SABRE routing, and manual subcircuit replacement based on hardware tests. The uncertainty model sub-circuit is chosen because it is common to both VaR and CVaR, and the work derives analytic angle conditions for symmetric distributions to guide shallow ansatz design. At the same time, reproducibility is somewhat constrained by device-specific tuning, the lack of readout mitigation, and the absence of real market datasets, as the experiments rely on synthetic Gaussians and a stylized GCI model.

=== PAPER c46b48afaa7c (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum computing for financial risk measurement, focusing on Monte Carlo–style estimation of Value-at-Risk (VaR) for market risk and Potential Future Exposure (PFE) for counterparty credit risk, both of which require simulating high‑dimensional risk‑factor evolutions and repricing to obtain P&L or exposure distributions. It frames these problems as expectation and quantile estimation tasks over future ‘states of the world’, with market risk quantified by VaR on P&L distributions and CCR modeled as exposure to replacement cost summarized via quantile-based exposure profiles over discretized time. The authors emphasize that suitable quantum targets are precisely such simulation/optimization problems that require many algorithmic repetitions over large scenario sets and risk factors.
    [codes: C-002, C-008, C-009, C-015, C-021, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is built around quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) and its use for expectation and quantile estimation, exploiting its quadratic convergence improvement over classical Monte Carlo and using interval or bisection search on thresholds to obtain VaR and PFE quantiles. Risk‑factor return distributions are encoded via amplitude encoding into qubit registers, using either direct state preparation or distribution loading based on piecewise polynomial fits for empirical marginals combined with a Gaussian copula to handle dependence, after which P&L or exposure is computed and a comparator circuit flags whether outcomes lie below or above quantile thresholds. The authors discuss hybrid CPU–QPU architectures where only time‑critical Monte Carlo components are offloaded to a QPU in a highly optimized format to leverage QAE speed‑up while keeping calibration and other tasks classical.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the positive side, the authors confirm in simulation that their quantum circuits can reproduce the intended risk‑factor and P&L distributions, validating the construction of the VaR circuit and the correctness of the distribution‑loading approach. However, quantitative accuracy remains modest at realistic qubit budgets: even with three qubits per risk factor the 99% VaR estimate deviates by around 14% from the reference value, and in the CCR case exposure quantiles show errors of roughly 5–10% even in the more refined discretization. Circuit complexity is also substantial: for market risk, circuit depths of 9,387 and 22,589 are reported for two and three qubits per risk factor, respectively, and for the CCR setup depths of 1,015 and 2,237 are required. Noise studies on the CCR circuit show that even a base bit‑flip noise level of 0.1% induces about 15% relative error in a 90% quantile, and typical noise levels can push relative errors beyond ±25%, significantly perturbing the CDF and making the resulting risk estimates practically unusable.
    [codes: C-010, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper motivates its use of QAE by the theoretical quadratic speed‑up it offers over classical Monte Carlo, improving convergence from the classical square‑root rate to linear scaling in the number of oracle calls for expectation estimation. At the same time, the authors stress that classical risk engines in large financial institutions already compute VaR and CCR measures within minutes or at most a few hours and are therefore operationally mature and efficient, resulting in a currently weak business case for replacing them with quantum solutions. In the market‑risk case, they also show that a simple parametric normal VaR underestimates tail risk relative to a model using empirically calibrated marginal distributions, highlighting that quantum implementations must at minimum match the modeling sophistication of incumbent classical approaches.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-013, C-016, C-034, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors are explicit that practical, real‑life deployment of their quantum risk‑measurement approach remains far away: current qubit counts severely limit the number of risk factors and time steps that can be modeled, making commercially relevant, realistic risk‑measurement use cases out of reach for the foreseeable future. They identify limited hardware capacity—measured in number of qubits—as a major bottleneck, noting that several orders of magnitude more qubits than the current ~10^2 would be required; even accurate representation of marginal distributions alone demands at least five qubits per risk factor dimension, and multi‑period CCR setups scale qubit use as 2^qN, quickly exhausting NISQ devices. Quantum noise is a second central obstacle: they report that typical noise levels significantly distort CDFs, with base‑case noise already causing about 15% quantile errors and higher noise easily exceeding ±25%, effectively rendering even otherwise promising circuits unusable. They also stress that using too few qubits per risk factor (e.g., two qubits in the CCR example) leads to large discretization errors, and even at three qubits per factor VaR and exposure estimates still deviate by around 5–14%, which is substantial in a risk‑management context. Overall, the paper concludes that given these qubit, depth, and noise constraints, coupled with already fast and mature classical systems, the business case for moving to quantum risk measurement is currently not very strong.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-017, C-018, C-040, C-042, C-044, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For this line of work to become practically relevant, the authors argue that substantial progress is needed in quantum hardware scale and quality as well as in noise control and error‑mitigation techniques, since current noise levels and qubit counts are inadequate for realistic risk‑measurement tasks. They also implicitly point toward further development of hybrid CPU–QPU schemes and better noise‑robust implementations of QAE‑based risk algorithms as part of the broader active quantum‑research agenda upon which any path to real‑world risk‑measurement applications will heavily depend.
    [codes: C-005, C-017, C-019, C-048, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main contribution is presented as moving beyond textbook‑style illustrations of quantum finance to more realistic risk‑management use cases by implementing QAE‑based circuits for empirically calibrated VaR and PFE calculations and analyzing their resource requirements and limitations. The authors also situate their work within a landscape where practical quantum applications in quantitative finance are still comparatively limited, highlighting their detailed treatment of market and counterparty credit risk with empirical marginals, copula‑based dependence, and explicit circuit‑size and noise‑sensitivity analyses as advancing the discussion of near‑term feasibility and hybrid strategies.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-019, C-023, C-031, C-041, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper bases its examples on empirically calibrated stock‑return data, using four years of historical prices to construct leptokurtic marginal distributions, modeled via low‑order piecewise polynomials, and a Gaussian copula to represent dependence in line with industry practice. The authors provide concrete circuit‑level details such as the gate counts for direct state preparation, circuit depths for both market‑risk and CCR cases, and the qubit scaling for multi‑period setups, and they validate their quantum circuits on a simulator by confirming that the loaded distributions match the classically constructed targets. Noise is incorporated via an explicit bit‑flip noise model applied to gates and measurements, and its impact is quantified through perturbations in CDFs and quantile errors. These choices yield reasonably transparent and reproducible toy‑scale benchmarks but also reflect simplifying assumptions (e.g., Gaussian copula, coarse discretization) that may limit direct transferability to production‑grade risk systems.
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper normalizes P&L by removing constants before applying quantum estimation, and it emphasizes that risk calculations typically require large‑scale scenario generation and repricing across many risk factors, reinforcing the suitability of Monte Carlo‑type problems for exploring quantum speed‑ups. It also notes that the use of empirically calibrated marginal distributions, rather than simple Gaussian marginals, can materially change VaR outcomes in their example, underscoring the importance of realistic distributional modeling in quantum risk algorithms.
    [codes: C-009, C-015, C-023, C-028, C-034]

=== PAPER c4e919f71785 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles transaction settlement in a central clearing house, where the objective is to settle as many (possibly weighted) delivery-versus-payment transactions or payments as possible within a batch, subject to legal, balance, credit, and collateral constraints that make the problem difficult but systemically important. It formulates this as a mixed binary optimization (MBO) problem combining binary settlement decisions with continuous variables (e.g., slack and credit-collateral facility variables), enabling inequality constraints to be represented via slack variables and penalties. The authors explicitly model party balances, credit constraints, and shared credit-collateral facilities, and then reformulate the resulting inequality constraints with nonnegative slack variables so they can be handled by their quantum optimization framework.
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors extend variational quantum optimization methods originally designed for QUBO/Ising problems to mixed binary optimization, allowing joint treatment of binary and continuous decision variables. They present two heuristics: one maps the MBO to a continuous optimization over quantum circuit parameters (and continuous variables), and another constructs a QAOA-style Hamiltonian H(y) parameterized by continuous variables, along with a slack-variable-based heuristic that iteratively optimizes, projects, and reoptimizes to help escape local minima. Equality constraints are enforced via quadratic penalty terms, and transaction-settlement-specific constraints are incorporated through this penalty and slack-variable framework before applying these variational quantum algorithms, which are tested both in classical simulation and on IBM quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-029, C-030, C-005]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On small transaction-settlement instances, the proposed heuristics find optimal or near-optimal settlement patterns, with classical simulations and IBM quantum hardware showing good agreement for the three-transaction test cases (with and without a credit-collateral facility), where the optimal bitstring that settles T2 and T3 (011) is sampled with the highest probability. In a seven-payment instance, a straightforward variational run with COBYLA fails to reach the global maximum objective value, saturating at a suboptimal level, whereas the explicit slack-variable heuristic enables the objective to reach the maximum value corresponding to four settled transactions, though only one among several globally optimal solutions is found. The authors also provide illustrative optimal solutions and note cases where a simple greedy algorithm settles fewer transactions than their optimization-based approach.
    [codes: C-005, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper positions its quantum methods as heuristics that can be warm-started from classical relaxations, and in at least one small test case, the authors report that a simple greedy classical algorithm may settle only a single transaction, whereas the formulated optimization yields a solution settling two transactions. They also emphasize that any potential quantum advantage is empirical and case-specific, as their algorithms cannot be analyzed via asymptotic complexity, and they thus stop short of claiming systematic performance superiority over classical methods.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-019, C-020, C-032]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress that their quantum optimization procedures are heuristics without rigorous complexity guarantees, so any advantage must be assessed empirically on a case-by-case basis rather than through big-O analysis. They note that current evidence suggests any quantum advantage, if it exists, is likely to appear only for problem sizes above roughly 100 variables, which is beyond their small test instances. They also highlight hardware-related constraints: solution quality improves with circuit depth, but near-term devices suffer from noise, and additional SWAP gates needed to map problems to native qubit connectivity further increase circuit depth and degrade performance. Methodologically, they acknowledge that their algorithms currently exploit very little of the specific structure of the underlying optimization problems. Finally, at the heuristic level, they show that their slack-variable approach may locate only one of multiple globally optimal solutions, limiting solution diversity.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-039, C-042]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that better quantum (and hybrid) algorithms could increase settlement efficiency by enabling more transactions to be settled per batch, thereby shortening the interval between trade and settlement. They propose designing algorithms that more deeply exploit problem structure—for example, focusing on problems with convexity in the continuous variables—to potentially outperform current methods, and recommend exploring problem-specific variational forms such as QAOA-style ansätze tailored to the transaction-settlement structure. They also note that adjusting transaction weights in the objective function could be used to steer the heuristic toward preferred optimal solutions, such as prioritizing higher-volume transactions.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims as its core contribution the extension of variational quantum optimization algorithms from quadratic unconstrained binary optimization to the broader class of mixed binary optimization problems, thereby enabling simultaneous treatment of discrete and continuous variables, including inequality constraints via slack variables. It introduces the transaction settlement problem as a novel and practically relevant financial application for demonstrating these methods and proposes two new heuristics for MBO, including a slack-variable-based scheme to help escape local optima in the variational landscape.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper formulates a clear MBO framework with explicit binary and continuous variables, uses standard quadratic-penalty methods for equality constraints and slack-variable reformulations for inequalities, and connects these formulations to its quantum heuristics in a structured way. It demonstrates the approach on several hand-crafted, small-size settlement instances, reporting the exact optimal solutions, multiplicity of optima, and the behavior of both direct variational optimization and the slack-variable heuristic. The evaluation includes both classical simulation and runs on IBM quantum devices, with reported agreement between the two for the smallest instances, but remains limited in scale and largely illustrative rather than statistically extensive.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-018, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Beyond the core methodological and empirical content, the authors emphasize that transaction settlement in clearing houses is a process of systemic importance due to the large volume and value of transactions, and that legal constraints combined with collateral and credit optionality contribute to the complexity of the optimization problem they study. They also remark that their proposed structure supports the integration of problem-specific variational forms like QAOA, reinforcing the flexibility of their framework.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-044]

Drawing on cited work and industry pilots rather than new experiments, the authors report that QAOA-based portfolio methods and hybrid models have been shown to outperform traditional solvers on small portfolios, reduce computational power requirements, and in some cases deliver more accurate customer clustering and risk estimation than classical models; they also assert that quantum Monte Carlo can significantly enhance the speed and accuracy of VaR calculations. === PAPER c7d33a63a50e (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses risk measurement in finance, extending quantum approaches beyond standard Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) to alternative tail risk measures: Expectile Value-at-Risk (EVaR) and Range Value-at-Risk (RVaR). EVaR is framed as a compromise between VaR and CVaR, while RVaR is presented as a qualitatively robust risk measure that encompasses both VaR and CVaR as special cases. The overall problem is situated in the emerging area of applying quantum computing to financial mathematics.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: All proposed algorithms are built around quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), leveraged for its quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods and its ability to estimate expectations via appropriate payoff mappings. For expectiles, the authors use an equivalent mathematical reformulation and a hybrid scheme where a quantum circuit evaluates an objective function inside a classical bisection root search, implemented via an operator that loads the loss distribution, applies a comparator and controlled rotations; for RVaR, they construct an operator combining two comparators and a controlled y-rotation and then reconstruct RVaR directly from the resulting interval probability. The implementation assumes a discretized support encoded in a qubit register, uses comparator-based operator A constructions, and includes practical QAE variants—Maximum Likelihood QAE and Iterative QAE—in addition to the canonical QAE.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-025]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On quantum simulators, the authors report that all four quantum algorithms for VaR, CVaR, EVaR and RVaR perform sufficiently well and that, in a credit-risk case study, the average estimate converges to the exact value as the number of ancilla qubits increases, with expectile and VaR showing similar accuracy and RVaR being less accurate. Across both the credit and insurance examples, accuracy improves when more ancilla or distribution-loading qubits are used, with the authors noting that good results are obtained once the number of qubits is sufficiently large. Under noise (including a real-device setting and noisy hardware emulation), they find that EVaR/expectiles and VaR estimates remain robust, while CVaR and especially RVaR are significantly degraded; hardware noise is observed to distort the loaded density function, yet expectile calculations with three distribution qubits are still described as sufficiently reliable. They also emphasize that EVaR and VaR are robust against noise on real hardware, in contrast to CVaR and RVaR.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their approach as leveraging quantum amplitude estimation to obtain a quadratic speedup relative to classical Monte Carlo-based methods for estimating risk-measure expectations. Conceptually, expectiles are described as providing a compromise between classical VaR and CVaR, and RVaR as a robust alternative that subsumes both as special cases, but the paper does not report explicit empirical runtime or accuracy head-to-head benchmarks against specific classical algorithms.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. First, the canonical QAE implementation relies on quantum Fourier transform and controlled Grover-type operations, which lead to deep circuits with many CNOT gates and thus pose challenges on current NISQ hardware. Second, the discretization of continuous distributions for state preparation introduces an approximation error that depends on the number of qubits used to load the distribution, constraining accuracy via the granularity of the domain discretization. Third, the RVaR algorithm explicitly requires prior knowledge or estimation of the tail interval probability p, adding a dependency that is not needed for all measures. Finally, the authors’ results show that RVaR is significantly affected by hardware noise and that state-preparation circuits suffer from noise-induced inaccuracies in the encoded density, indicating practical robustness limitations for some risk measures on present devices.
    [codes: C-014, C-016, C-030, C-031, C-035]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors explicitly state that additional risk measures beyond those treated in the manuscript are of interest for future research. In particular, they point out that expectiles are special cases of shortfall risk measures and suggest that shortfall- and utility-based risk measures could be promising extensions for quantum implementation and analysis.
    [codes: C-036, C-037]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The work claims novelty in being, to the authors’ knowledge, the first to construct and implement quantum algorithms for alternative risk measures EVaR and RVaR, going beyond the previously studied VaR and CVaR. They emphasize that these alternatives to VaR/CVaR had not been calculated on a quantum computer before and that their constructions show how existing complexity results for QAE-based VaR/CVaR can be transferred to expectiles and RVaR. Conceptually, they also stress the roles of expectiles as a compromise between VaR and CVaR and of RVaR as a robust measure encompassing those as special cases.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-028]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper uses two case studies: a synthetic two-asset credit-risk portfolio with explicitly specified parameters and a real-world insurance claim-size dataset calibrated from the Norwegian automobile data, lending some domain realism. The authors describe the state-preparation strategy for the loss distribution in the credit case, splitting loading into two circuit steps, and in the insurance case they discuss the discretization–approximation tradeoff as qubit count increases. They also incorporate worked analytical examples (e.g., the expectile function under a normal distribution) and explore multiple QAE variants (canonical, MLQAE, IQAE), including experiments on simulators and noisy/real hardware, which helps interrogate robustness. Accuracy and convergence behavior are primarily presented qualitatively (e.g., convergence as ancilla or distribution qubits increase), and the reported convergence of results as qubit resources grow supports the internal consistency of the approach.
    [codes: C-018, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-017]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper frames the application of quantum computing in financial mathematics as a relatively new and emerging area, and it restates in the conclusion that expectile calculations on current devices can be sufficiently reliable while RVaR remains significantly more sensitive to noise. These contextual and summarizing remarks do not introduce additional distinct methodological or problem-framing elements beyond those already captured in other dimensions.
    [codes: C-008, C-034, C-035]
